This study offers a preliminary error analysis for two-layer neural networks designed to compute eigenpairs of the Schr\"odinger operator, addressing the challenge of the curse of dimensionality in quantum mechanics. We demonstrate that the generalization error for neural approximations of eigenfunctions scales polynomially with respect to the number of parameters. These findings are derived from a prior analysis of the PDE's local structure, which establishes that the PDE can be reformulated as a system of integral equations. Leveraging this approach, we construct a neural network model to numerically resolve these integral equations. Our results indicate that the generalization error for the resulting neural approximations can be bounded by polynomial functions of the parameter counts for both the neural network and the integral equation system. This work extends the prior posterior error analysis of the authors, which was specifically dedicated to proving the efficiency of the neural network model in solving the Schr\"odinger operator. Furthermore, we present numerical experiments to validate our theoretical findings. These experiments illustrate that the neural approximations achieve high accuracy for eigenvalues and eigenfunctions across various dimensions, including up to 100 dimensions. Finally, we discuss the limitations of our approach and outline potential future research directions. The code used for the numerical experiments is accessible at https://github.com/ChenchenWang1997/Neural-Network-Eigenvalue-Solver. Keywords: High dimensional Schr\"odinger operator, eigenvalue problem, integral equation, deep neural network, approximation theory, error analysis. 2020 Mathematics Subject Classification: 65J20, 65N30, 65N99, 65Y20, 68T07, 81Q10.

We demonstrate that the local limit of the fixed point forest, a model from statistical mechanics, corresponds to a Galton-Watson tree with an infinite mean, where the degree distribution follows a power law of $-3$. The analysis of this tree's properties relies on a stochastic differential equation. This equation was previously derived in the context of the half-integral Bessel process and a random walk on $\mathbb{Z}^2$ featuring a repulsive origin. We establish that this Bessel process exhibits a repulsive origin and investigate its connection to the fixed point forest. Furthermore, we examine the specific case where the differential takes the form of a Bessel process, a scenario that arises in the study of the two-dimensional Ising model. A strong Gelfand pair (G,H) consists of a group G and a subgroup H where every irreducible character of H induces a multiplicity-free character on G. This paper classifies the strong Gelfand pairs for the special linear groups SL(2, p), where p denotes a prime number. Furthermore, we identify specific characters within these groups that do not arise from any strong Gelfand pair. Additionally, we determine which characters of SL(2, p) have Galois conjugates with inductive multiplicities exceeding 1. The characterization of those groups contributing to strong Gelfand pairs mirrors the pattern observed in symplectic groups. The relevant characters fall into three categories: unipotent, quasi-unipotent, and quasi-split. This classification aligns with the pattern seen in symplectic groups, with the exception of unipotent characters. The proof relies on the properties of induced characters and their restrictions. Unipotent characters are not part of any strong Gelfand pair, a fact that also applies to sp(4,q). The number of strong Gelfand pairs in SL(2,q)) exhibits a periodic pattern with a period of 4. This number is closely related to the count of irreducible characters of H, where (SL(2,q),H) forms a strong Gelfand pair. This study investigates the hidden-charm molecular pentaquark $P_{c}(4450)^+$ as a compact three-body bound state comprising $c\bar{c}n$ ($n=u,d$), utilizing the three-body EFT formalism grounded in $P_{c}(4450)^+$'s molecular nature. We calculate its electromagnetic characteristics, including the charge radius, magnetic dipole, and electric quadrupole moments. Our findings indicate that the charge radius is negative, suggesting an internal structure where the charm quark is not at the center. Additionally, the magnetic dipole moment is positive and significantly larger than that of the proton, while the electric quadrupole moment is negative, confirming the presence of deformation. These results offer valuable insights for future experimental measurements. Furthermore, we explore the implications of these predictions for the internal structure of $P_{c}(4450)^+$ and its potential decay mechanism. Finally, we extend our analysis to other molecular pentaquarks, $P_{c}(4380)^+$ and $P_{c}(4337)^+$, which are also hypothesized to be compact three-body bound states. Our predictions for their electromagnetic properties are consistent with existing experimental data. This work aims to provide a theoretical basis for future studies on the electromagnetic properties of molecular pentaquarks. Additionally, we examine the influence of cutoff dependence on these properties, revealing that the electromagnetic characteristics of $P_{c}(4450)^+$ are highly sensitive to the cutoff value. This sensitivity underscores the necessity for precise experimental measurements to further elucidate the internal structure of molecular pentaquarks. Finally, we explore the potential for distinguishing between the three-body effective field theory and the diquark-antitriquetark model through such measurements. Our findings suggest that electromagnetic observables could serve as a critical tool for differentiating between these two distinct structural models. The primary instrument for this proof is a novel identity of multilinear form applicable to all Zinbiel algebras, a tool of independent significance. Additionally, we examine the concept of Zinbielness relative to a specific multilinear form and characterize this property for algebras of codimension one. We also analyze Zinbiel algebras within the context of multilinear identities and identify the identities satisfied by all such algebras of codimension one. Finally, we classify all Zinbiel algebras of dimension two and three. These classifications confirm that every Zinbiel algebra is nilpotent and provide a counterexample to the conjecture asserting that all Zinbiel algebras satisfy a nontrivial multilinear identity. Furthermore, we present a counterexample to the conjecture that all Zinbiel algebras of dimension five or less are commutative. The paper concludes with an exploration of Zinbiel analogues to various classical algebraic structures. Specifically, we demonstrate that a Zinbiel algebra can be defined as a commutative semigroup satisfying a specific identity, and we characterize those possessing a two-sided unit and an inverse relative to the Zinbiel operation. We also examine Zinbiel analogues of Lie algebras, associative algebras, and Poisson algebras. Notably, we prove that any Zinbiel algebra over a commutative ring that constitutes a Lie algebra is nilpotent, and we provide a counterexample to the conjecture that all Zinbiel algebras over a commutative ring that are associative are commutative. This paper investigates the scattering theory for cubic inhomogeneous Schrödinger equations featuring an inverse square potential, defined as $iu_t+\Delta u-\frac{a}{|x|^2}u=\lambda |x|^{-b}|u|^2u$ in $\mathbb{R}^3$, where $0\leq b<2$ and $-\frac{3}{2}<a<\frac{1}{4}$. We demonstrate the global well-posedness and scattering of solutions within the critical mass space $H^1_{crit}(\mathbb{R}^3)$. The primary challenge stems from the nonlinearity's inability to satisfy Strichartz estimates. To address this, we employ a novel approach combining the Morrey-Cauchy estimate with the Strichartz estimate. Furthermore, we establish the sharp mass threshold for scattering by utilizing the virial identity and profile decomposition. These findings extend the results of Kenig-Vi\c{c}ente (2017) regarding cubic nonlinearities to a broader class of inhomogeneous nonlinearities. Additionally, we provide a comprehensive analysis of the ground state's mass and energy for this specific inhomogeneous problem. Finally, we examine the scenario where the nonlinearity is defocusing. In this case, we demonstrate that the Cauchy problem is globally well-posed in $H^1_{crit}(\mathbb{R}^3)$ and that solutions disperse over time. Notably, this result represents the first instance of scattering theory for defocusing inhomogeneous nonlinearities of the form $|x|^{-b} |u|^p u$ in $\mathbb{R}^3$ with $p\neq 2$. Our findings extend the work of Liang-Zhang (2019) on the defocusing cubic NLS to a wider range of inhomogeneous nonlinearities. To achieve this, we develop a new method for handling defocusing nonlinearities that avoids the need for local energy estimates. We introduce a migration-contagion (MC) process that integrates two distinct mechanisms: migration, where a node is infected if any of its neighbors carry the contagion, and forgetting, where a node spontaneously recovers from an infection. We establish a sufficient condition guaranteeing the existence of a non-trivial stationary state for this process on a connected graph, and we examine the specific instances of the MC process where only the initial configuration influences the system's evolution. Furthermore, we analyze the asymptotic behavior of the MC process on complete graphs, trees, and unweighted, symmetric random graphs. For complete graphs, we derive an exact formula for the expected time until all nodes become uninfected, and we demonstrate that the migration-contagion process on a tree is equivalent to a random walk of a chip on a tree, where each node holds a chip and the chip at a node splits into two, moving to a randomly selected neighbor. These findings are supported by numerical simulations. We confirm the existence of a 3:2 mean motion resonance (MMR) chain within the K2-138 planetary system. This conclusion is derived from a comprehensive analysis of the system's dynamical stability, which incorporates the most recent transit data from the Kepler mission. Our investigation identifies a single stable configuration in which all planets participate in 3:2 MMRs, a finding that aligns with the outcomes of N-body simulations. Our research indicates that the previously proposed 2:1 MMR chain is unstable and thus unlikely to represent the true architecture of the K2-138 system. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the 3:2 MMR chain in K2-138 is more probable than the 2:1 MMR chain in Kepler-11, which is also believed to host a 3:2 MMR chain. We further examine the formation mechanisms of this 3:2 MMR chain, suggesting that convergent migration and disk truncation are the most plausible processes. Finally, we explore the implications of our findings for the broader understanding of MMR chains in exoplanetary systems. Our study underscores the critical role of long-term transit observations in elucidating the dynamical architecture of these systems. Additionally, we emphasize the necessity of integrating transit data with N-body simulations to accurately determine the true architecture of exoplanetary systems. We anticipate that our findings will significantly advance our comprehension of the architecture of exoplanetary systems. Specifically, our results suggest that 3:2 MMR chains are more common than previously thought, and that the discovery of such chains in other systems will be facilitated by the extended transit observations provided by the Kepler mission. We also note that the 3:2 MMR chain in K2-138 is likely the result of convergent migration and disk truncation, and that the presence of such a chain in the system is consistent with the predictions of the core accretion model. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the Euler--Poincar\'e polynomial corresponds to the $q$-dimension of a specific indecomposable module within the category of modules admissible with respect to a genuine Whittaker datum. This result extends the quantum affine Schur--Weyl duality, originally established by the second author, to this general setting. Additionally, we investigate the properties of these genuine covers and their associated Whittaker modules. As an application, we derive the Euler--Poincar\'e polynomial for the $G_2$ case, which had previously been an open problem. Finally, we provide evidence supporting the conjecture that our findings offer a geometric formulation of the classical Schur--Weyl duality between the symmetric group and general linear groups. The SiD Detector is a proposed instrument for the future International Linear Collider, designed to achieve precise particle identification and high-resolution tracking within a robust magnetic field. This paper updates the concepts originally outlined in 2014, incorporating advancements from the SIDETC and SiDdet50 toolkits. These updates reflect new insights gained from the LHC and its detectors, as well as innovations proposed during the subsequent five years. The current design features a compact inner tracking system optimized for vertexing and low-momentum tracking, a vertex calorimeter for high-precision energy measurement, and a large detector section designed for particle identification. Additionally, the paper introduces a novel design for the outer tracking system. The configuration is optimized to deliver outstanding physics performance while maintaining a cost-effective budget. The development of the SiD Detector continues to be driven by the collaboration, with a strong desire to apply this design to an energy range of 350 to 400 GeV. Furthermore, the collaboration is actively exploring design options to extend the detector's operational reach to 500 GeV. This paper will outline the scientific rationale, technical feasibility, and cost estimates for SiD operation at both 350–400 GeV and 500 GeV. Ultimately, the SiD Detector aims to advance our understanding of the fundamental laws of nature. Its development is anticipated to be highly motivating for physicists and engineers, offering an opportunity to demonstrate the creativity and ingenuity of the SiD community. The collaboration welcomes new members to join in this endeavor. For additional details, please visit www.slac.stanford.edu/sid or contact sid@slac.stanford.edu. Amorphous ice exhibits local structural order comparable to that of ice Ih, yet it lacks long-range ordering. Determining whether this local order extends over larger distances is a critical inquiry. While some studies suggest the presence of larger ordered domains, others indicate that ice is completely structureless beyond the first coordination shell. This work employs large-scale molecular dynamics simulations to investigate long-range order in hypersonic amorphous ice. We developed a novel order parameter designed to detect long-range order within ice structures. Our findings reveal a significant reduction in long-range order as temperature rises, with the transition to a fully disordered state occurring at approximately 150 K. Furthermore, we identified a sharp peak in the temperature derivative of the order parameter at roughly 140 K, which we interpret as a first-order phase transition. This event marks the most extended range of order in hypersonic ice prior to the eventual transition into the liquid phase. We attribute this phenomenon to the annealing of larger ordered regions within the ice. These results offer a novel perspective on the long-range order in amorphous ice and suggest a potential method for inducing order in ice films, which could be valuable for technological applications. Additionally, our work introduces a new metric for detecting long-range order in ice, a tool applicable to various other systems. Finally, we demonstrate that this order parameter can distinguish between low and high density amorphous ice. These discoveries significantly enhance our understanding of ice's structural properties and its phase diagram. This report outlines my second-year project conducted at the Centre for Nanoscience and Nanotechnology, Indian Institute of Technology Roorkee, utilizing a variable temperature scanning tunneling microscope (STM). The primary objective was to employ STM to investigate the electronic structures of various materials, specifically graphite, gold, silicon, and boron-doped diamond. The project was divided into three components: (i) achieving atomic-resolution images of highly oriented pyrolytic graphite (HOPG) at room temperature and low temperatures, (ii) examining the influence of substrate temperature on the atomic-resolution imaging of gold deposited on HOPG, and (iii) studying the temperature-dependent tunneling current of silicon and boron-doped diamond at atomic resolution.

To achieve atomic-resolution imaging of HOPG at room temperature, a tungsten tip was utilized. The tip was prepared by cleaving a tungsten crystal to create a sharp apex, followed by a procedure known as "breaking in" to remove surface contaminants. The STM was then positioned over a graphite lattice, and the tip was brought close to the surface by applying a small bias voltage and a tunneling current of approximately 1 nA. By adjusting the tip-sample distance to maintain a constant current, an image of the graphite lattice was obtained. The tunneling current between the tip and the graphite surface was analyzed using Bardeen's theory, which describes tunneling as a quantum mechanical process where electrons traverse a potential barrier between two states.

The tunneling current between the tip and the graphite surface was found to be exponentially dependent on the tip-sample distance, a relationship derived from Bardeen's theory. This distance dependence was measured at room temperature and compared with low-temperature measurements taken at 4.2 K and 1.5 K. The data revealed that tunneling current is not only exponentially dependent on the tip-sample distance but also on the bias voltage and temperature.

Gold was deposited onto HOPG at room temperature using an evaporator, and the effect of substrate temperature on the STM imaging of gold was studied. Gold was deposited at room temperature, 300 K, 200 K, 150 K, and 120 K. The STM images indicated that gold forms clusters on the graphite surface, and the tunneling current showed a strong dependence on the substrate temperature.

This paper introduces a novel framework for capturing and exploiting mathematical structure within formalized proofs, utilizing the Isabelle AFP as a case study. We present a new data format that encodes both the content and dependencies of Isabelle theories, enabling the analysis of large-scale collections of formalized mathematics. Leveraging this format, we developed a suite of tools designed to facilitate the discovery and utilization of pre-existing formalized knowledge. Our findings reveal that, contrary to common assumptions, there is no substantial evidence of a "long tail" of rare structures within the AFP; instead, a vast array of useful formalized mathematical structures is already accessible. We demonstrate several examples of how these tools can enhance the accessibility of this pre-knowledge. Furthermore, we propose a new approach to managing dependencies among formalized theories, which significantly reduces redundancy and enhances the overall quality of the AFP. Finally, we outline several directions for future research regarding the application of these tools to other formalization efforts. Ultra-low-frequency (ULF) waves are a key component of the dynamic interaction between the solar wind and Earth's magnetosphere. Although these waves are frequently visualized through color plots, they can also be effectively represented as audio. This study introduces a method for converting ULF wave data into the audible spectrum and explores various parameters to optimize the fidelity of these audio files. The results are evaluated using both visual representations and human perception. This work is particularly relevant to ULF wave researchers, as it enables the creation of audio recordings that complement visualizations, thereby enhancing data interpretation. Furthermore, the paper includes a web-based ULF wave "sonification" tool that implements the discussed approach and allows users to adjust various sonification parameters. This free tool is accessible at http://www.astro.ucla.edu/~michael/ulf-sonification. The underlying Python code is available on GitHub at https://github.com/mjgk/ulf-sonification. The findings are also valuable to geophysicists and space weather researchers, as they demonstrate that human perception is a critical factor in analyzing ULF waves. Additionally, the study highlights that current visualization methods for ULF waves may not fully represent the data, suggesting that incorporating audio could improve the overall data analysis process. The paper concludes with a discussion of the pros and cons of ULF wave sonification. This research was conducted by undergraduate students at UCLA. Michael G. This study introduces a text data representation framework grounded in declarative memory-based structure (DMBS), which we contend is more intuitive and natural than prevalent alternatives like natural language processing (NLP) or statistical machine learning (SML) models. We contend that the DMBS model is essential for advancing both NLP and SML methodologies. The proposed framework encompasses four core components: (1) a text corpus model, (2) a text memory model, (3) a text attention model, and (4) a text retrieval model. We demonstrate that various NLP and SML techniques can be reformulated using these four primitives. Both algebras appear as subalgebras within the Cuntz-Toeplitz algebra $\mathcal{O}_{n^2}$. This result serves as a continuous analogue to an earlier discrete result established by the first author in [10]. Furthermore, this finding provides an affirmative response to a question posed in [11]. Finally, we examine the implications of this result for the classification of endomorphisms on the Cuntz algebra $\mathcal{O}_{N^2}$. Specifically, we establish that for any $N \geq 2$, the set of all endomorphisms on $\mathcal{O}_{N^2}$ that implement a gauge action on either the CCR or CAR algebra constitutes a Borel set. Additionally, we prove that for any $N \geq 2$, the collection of all irreducible endomorphisms on $\mathcal{O}_{N^2}$ implementing a gauge action on the CAR algebra is Borel. However, we also note that the set of all gauge actions on the CAR algebra is not Borel within the space of endomorphisms on $\mathcal{O}_{N^2}$. These findings are achieved through a novel approach that relies on a free product construction. Specifically, we show that $\mathcal{O}_{n^2}$ is isomorphic to the free product of $n$ copies of $\mathcal{O}_{n}$. The language GP 2, introduced by Boudol and the author in 1995, is a non-deterministic, non-interleaving process calculus that extends the $\pi$-calculus with choice operators and early name passing. Although its corresponding big-step semantics was published in 2000, a small-step semantics has been missing until now. This paper presents a small-step operational semantics for GP 2 and demonstrates its correspondence with the big-step semantics. Furthermore, it leverages the properties of the proposed small-step semantics to establish the non-interleaving behavior of GP 2. Specifically, it is shown that concurrent processes with distinct names cannot interact, and that the order in which internal actions are executed does not influence the resulting set of traces. These findings are achieved by integrating the concept of "barbs" with that of "weak transitions." The latter concept is introduced here for the first time and is subsequently utilized to prove the congruence of the weak transition relation. The paper also includes a detailed comparison between GP 2 and the $\pi$-calculus. Additionally, the work extends GP 2 with a guard operator, which functions similarly to the $\pi$-calculus's guard, and provides a corresponding small-step semantics for this extension. The primary distinction between the two semantics lies in how the guard operator is handled. Finally, the paper extends the $\pi$-calculus with this guard operator and establishes a correspondence between the $\pi$-calculus's small-step semantics and the added guard-based semantics. The distinction between these two correspondences is analyzed. The methodologies employed in this work are applicable to other calculi, such as the $\pi$-calculus with choice and the $\pi$-calculus with relabeling. The photoevaporation model, which attributes disk dispersal to the erosion of the outer layers by stellar radiation, has been the primary explanation for the young, low-mass TW Hydrae variable's persistent, large-scale disk structure. However, this model struggles to account for the star's observed radio emission. In contrast, magnetohydrodynamic (MHD) wind models, which generate radio-emitting jets driven by magnetic fields, offer a viable alternative. This study aims to test the MHD wind model against the photoevaporation scenario by analyzing the TW Hydrae disk's evolution and comparing it with observations of other protoplanetary disks. We developed a model of the disk's evolution using the photoevaporation framework, calibrated against existing millimeter-wavelength data, and simulated its radio emission. Our results indicate that the photoevaporation model fails to reproduce the current radio emission, suggesting that an MHD wind mechanism is likely responsible for the observed signal. Furthermore, we predict that the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array (ALMA) will detect approximately 10 mJy of radio emission from TW Hydrae within a 1 arcsecond beam, with a characteristic size of roughly 100 au. These predictions can be verified using future high-angular resolution radio observations. Additionally, we propose that the MHD wind model explains the evolution of protoplanetary disks, including the "dead zone" observed in the TW Hydrae disk. Finally, we discuss the implications of this research for the future study of protoplanetary disks. This work is based on the thesis by J. M. This study examines various factored forms of Chebyshev polynomials, utilizing the minimal fields of $\cos(\frac{2\pi}{d})$ as a foundational element. By employing the explicit formula for these factorizations, we analyze the degree and coefficient sizes of the resulting factors. Furthermore, we explore the connection between these factorizations and the cyclotomic polynomial $\Phi_d(x)$. We also investigate the irreducible factors within these factorizations and establish an upper bound for their coefficient sizes. Finally, we provide a lower bound for the coefficients of the factors of $T_n(x)$ in the case where $n=p_1p_2\cdots p_k$ and $p_i$ denotes the $i$-th prime number, for $1\leq i\leq k$. This result is derived from a general theorem concerning the coefficients of irreducible factors of $T_n(x)$, which also finds application in determining the coefficients of irreducible factors for other factored variants of Chebyshev polynomials. Our findings are supported by computational evidence. Additionally, we present a formula for the coefficients of the irreducible factors of $T_n(x)$ when $n$ is a prime number. These results have applications in cryptography, specifically regarding the security of the polynomial equation degree problem. We also address the factorization of Chebyshev polynomials using the explicit formula and provide a method for computing the coefficients of the factors. This approach enables the calculation of the coefficients of the cyclotomic polynomial $\Phi_d(x)$ for $d\leq 1000$ with a time complexity of $O(d^2)$. We conclude with several conjectures and propose them as avenues for future research. Finally, we outline several open problems. This study introduces a new transient classification method designed to identify and differentiate between internal faults, external faults, and various types of transients—such as switching transients, load loss of flux, load re-energization, and open conductor transients—occurring in two-core symmetric phase angle regulating transformers. The proposed approach relies on analyzing the envelope of the rectified and filtered phase angle error signal. By extracting specific features from this signal's envelope, the method achieves accurate classification. To validate the technique, a detailed model of a two-core symmetric transformer was developed and simulated using PSCAD/EMTDC. The results demonstrate that the proposed method outperforms existing techniques, which typically depend on voltage or current data, by offering superior accuracy and robustness. Furthermore, the method exhibits strong performance even when transient data is corrupted by noise. The paper also discusses the implementation of intelligent protection for these transformers, highlighting the advantages of the approach regarding accuracy, reliability, and cost-effectiveness. Finally, the method is successfully applied to detect and isolate faults, with the transformer remaining undamaged during the fault-clearing process. The paper concludes by addressing potential challenges and suggesting future research directions. Overall, this technique is well-suited for integration into modern intelligent protection systems for two-core symmetric transformers. Additionally, the approach is versatile and can be extended to other power system components, including single-core transformers and transmission lines. The source code is available for replication. This study investigates hybrid precoding techniques for downlink multi-group multicasting in millimeter-wave (mmWave) systems. We introduce a greedy selection method that identifies the optimal full-digital precoder by evaluating the performance of every possible digital precoder. Subsequently, we develop an analog precoder with a reduced number of RF chains using selection criteria based on mmWave channel characteristics. Finally, we propose a hybrid precoding strategy that derives the precoders from the optimal full-digital configuration. Numerical results demonstrate that this hybrid approach achieves a performance near that of the optimal full-digital scheme while utilizing fewer RF chains. Furthermore, the proposed algorithm exhibits rapid convergence, requiring only a few iterations to reach the optimal solution. A group exhibits near exponential residual finiteness growth if the size of its smallest normal subgroup with a finite quotient increases just below exponential rates as one considers smaller subgroups. We demonstrate that the direct product of a finite simple group and a locally finite group is near exponential in this sense precisely when the finite simple component is not of prime order. Furthermore, we establish that every locally finite group possesses a subgroup that grows near exponentially, and we identify a broad class of finitely generated infinite locally finite groups that achieve near exponential residual finiteness growth. Additionally, we present examples of infinite residually finite groups where normal subgroups with finite quotients display near exponential, exponential, and subexponential varying degrees of finiteness. Finally, we offer specific examples of infinite groups with finite quotients whose normal subgroups have indices growing near exponentially, even within the realm of finitely presented groups. This study examines the stretched Euler-Bernoulli beam on a star-shaped graph, where the rotational inertia of the beam is modeled by negative constants. We establish the well-posedness of the system and demonstrate its exponential stability when the rotational inertia parameters are sufficiently close to zero. Furthermore, we provide a counterexample illustrating that prior counterexamples do not apply to the stretched beam scenario. Finally, we outline several directions for future research. This work extends the findings of [10], which addressed beams on simply connected graphs. Additionally, this research builds upon the stabilization of stretched beams found in [1], which utilized transverse forces. The current paper focuses exclusively on rotational inertia and excludes the effects of axial forces and rotational viscoelasticity. We derive new counterexamples that extend those in [1]. The $r$-process, a nucleosynthetic phenomenon occurring in extreme astrophysical environments, is responsible for creating heavy elements in the periodic table. Its primary function is to synthesize these elements by capturing neutrons onto seed nuclei. Consequently, a robust understanding of nuclear masses is essential for accurately modeling this process. This study employs machine learning techniques to predict nuclear masses, achieving an accuracy that meets the requirements for $r$-process simulations. We utilized a graph neural network to forecast masses for all isotopes, training the model on a comprehensive dataset of 3,000 nuclei derived from various experimental and theoretical sources. Our findings indicate that the predicted masses align with experimental data to within 100 keV. Furthermore, we compared these predictions against other mass models and applied them to simulate $r$-process events, successfully reproducing observed abundance patterns. This research represents the first instance of a machine learning model predicting nuclear masses with sufficient precision for $r$-process studies. Additionally, we have made our code and the associated training dataset publicly available. This work paves the way for future investigations into novel machine learning methods for nuclear physics. The code can be accessed at https://github.com/abhishekkumar123456789/nuclear-masses. The training dataset is available at https://github.com/abhishekkumar123456789/nuclear-masses/tree/master/data. The supplementary material is located at https://doi.org/10.1093/mnras/stad1002. The dissipation rate, defined as the inverse of dielectric loss tangent, serves as a critical metric for characterizing microwave dielectric materials. This rate governs the relaxation times of dielectric-based superconducting qubits and phase qubits, making its precise measurement essential for developing high-performance quantum components. We present a high-precision method for measuring the microwave dielectric loss of sapphire, a vital substrate for superconducting qubits, achieving a sensitivity of 1 part per billion (ppb). This approach surpasses the current sensitivity limit of 10 parts per million (ppm) by four orders of magnitude. Our findings indicate that the dissipation rate of high-quality sapphire varies with temperature and exhibits a minimum value near 10 ppb at 4.2 K. These results provide a quantitative basis for optimizing sapphire substrates in the temperature range relevant to superconducting qubits. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the dielectric loss of sapphire is independent of the microwave field amplitude up to 100 ppm, a level significantly exceeding the electric field strengths encountered in superconducting qubits. These insights facilitate the development of high-performance dielectric materials for next-generation superconducting qubits. Additionally, our results suggest that the dielectric loss in sapphire originates from a two-level system (TLS) reservoir, with a TLS lifetime of approximately 10 microseconds. This finding offers a quantitative explanation for the observed saturation of microwave dielectric loss in sapphire. Finally, we discuss the potential for enhancing the dissipation rate of sapphire through the application of an external magnetic field. These outcomes are expected to advance the design of high-performance dielectric materials for future superconducting qubits. Our methodology is broadly applicable to the precise measurement of microwave dielectric loss in other materials. We present a novel method for transporting and manipulating particles using a continuous-wave optical dipole force. This technique relies on a linear relationship between force and velocity, known as optical drag, which becomes apparent in the moving frame of the beam. This phenomenon is termed "anomalous" because it opposes the direction of light propagation in the lab frame, a stark contrast to the "normal" optical momentum transfer (radiation pressure) that drives standard optical tweezers. We demonstrate that this anomalous optical drag can be engineered in three-dimensional standing-wave traps, offering a new capability for particle manipulation. Furthermore, we show that this drag effect is intrinsically linked to the quantum interference between opposing momentum states of the light, a relationship that clarifies the underlying physics and establishes a fundamental link between radiation pressure and optical interference. These insights are expected to have broad applications across diverse fields, including quantum optics, quantum electrodynamics, and quantum information science. Finally, we explore potential extensions of this mechanism to other platforms, such as metamaterials and quantum electrodynamics circuits.

This paper addresses two-stage robust optimization problems where first-stage decisions remain fixed during the calculation of second-stage costs. We introduce a method to derive a lower bound for the original problem by transforming it into a more tractable form. This approach is applicable to a broad range of scenarios, including cases with numerous binary uncertain parameters. We demonstrate that the resulting lower bound is tight and prove the finite convergence of our proposed algorithm. Furthermore, we illustrate the method's effectiveness through various numerical examples. The code is accessible at: https://github.com/ahmadreza1390/Lagrange-Dual-2-Stage-RO. Our numerical results indicate that the lower bound is tight in most cases, and the method is computationally efficient. Additionally, the method is flexible and can be easily adapted to other problems. We conclude that this approach serves as a valuable tool for obtaining a lower bound in two-stage robust optimization. Finally, we note that extending this method to multi-stage problems is an interesting avenue for future research. We believe this work will inspire further research in this area. This paper introduces H4M, a heterogeneous, multi-source, multi-modal, multi-view, multi-distributional dataset designed for urban analytics. The dataset comprises four distinct data types: (1) transportation data, including taxi GPS trajectories and public transportation records; (2) social media posts from Weibo and Twitter regarding Beijing; (3) government data, specifically official Beijing Weibo posts and news articles; and (4) traffic data, such as camera observations and probe vehicle records. This collection offers a comprehensive, multi-dimensional, and multi-modal view of Beijing's transportation infrastructure and public sentiment. The data spans from January 1, 2016, to December 31, 2017, with a daily granularity of one hour. Furthermore, the study addresses the challenges of data heterogeneity, incompleteness, and imbalance, proposing a unified data fusion framework to derive a single, fused traffic state for each time slot. The resulting dataset and framework are made available to the research community to facilitate future research in urban analytics. The dataset can be accessed at https://github.com/zhongyuan1990/H4M. The findings were published in IEEE BigData 2019. Additional details regarding the dataset are available at https://data.over-blog-kiwi.com/2020/02/23/94/91/20200223102453700/file_222570c0.html. Pattern extraction serves as a critical step in analyzing and interpreting vast datasets, yet current methods often yield results that are difficult to comprehend and lack actionable insights. This paper introduces a new framework that integrates visual patterns with visual overviews to facilitate both human-in-the-loop exploration and automated data analysis. Ultimately, this framework is anticipated to enhance visual analytics applications by empowering analysts to investigate and interpret complex datasets. Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have become a cornerstone of machine learning, excelling in graph-based tasks like link prediction and node classification. However, their performance is often hindered by the scarcity of labeled data and the high costs associated with annotation. Transfer learning offers a potential solution to these challenges by applying knowledge gained from one task to another. This study investigates the efficacy of transfer learning within GNNs, specifically focusing on pretraining node classification models and reusing edge features. We evaluate this approach across various graph datasets and GNN architectures, comparing them against standard training methods. Our findings indicate that transfer learning yields significant performance gains, particularly in scenarios with limited labeled data. Furthermore, we analyze the underlying reasons for these improvements, offering insights into best practices for implementing transfer learning with GNNs. A collaborative filtering recommender system leverages the similarity between users and items to generate suggestions. This paper introduces a novel double feature allocation model (dfam) designed to simultaneously infer latent features for both users and items. We demonstrate that the expected value of the distinct user and item latent features learned by dfam vary based on their respective allocations to a discrete mixture component, a property that enables the system to calculate user and item similarity. Utilizing a real-world dataset, we conducted experiments comparing dfam against two baseline methods, as well as analyzing the model's learned parameters. The results indicate that dfam outperforms the baselines in recommendation accuracy and that the analysis aligns with our theoretical expectations. Furthermore, dfam exhibits superior scalability, allowing it to handle large datasets efficiently. The implementation is accessible at https://github.com/taiki-1234/dfam. We present a streamlined proof of a set disjointness protocol introduced by Baran, Braverman, and Linial (2009), utilizing a recent finding by Barak, Braverman, and Yehudayoff (2009). This approach is straightforward, relies exclusively on elementary probability, and yields a more robust lower bound. Furthermore, we extend this result to dynamic set disjointness, a scenario where parties can dynamically add or remove elements from their sets. Our findings indicate that, even under the randomized comparison model, identifying a pair of sets that are not disjoint necessitates $\Omega(n)$ comparisons, where $n$ represents the maximum set size. Additionally, we demonstrate that a single element can be inserted into a set with high probability using $O(1)$ comparisons, provided the sets remain balanced. Finally, we examine the communication complexity of set disjointness in data streams, a problem previously explored by several researchers. We establish that the randomized comparison model can resolve set disjointness with $O(1)$ comparisons and $O(1)$ communication per element, provided the number of elements is polynomial in $n$. This model also supports the efficient maintenance of a data structure capable of identifying a non-disjoint pair with a single query. Furthermore, we show that the randomized comparison model is at least as powerful as the standard communication model for set disjointness, thereby implying that any lower bound established for the comparison model applies to the communication model. Consequently, we conclude that the comparison model requires $\Omega(n)$ comparisons to identify a non-disjoint pair, whereas the communication model necessitates $\Omega(n)$ communication per element to achieve the same objective. Our primary contribution is a novel data structure for the comparison model that enables the identification of a non-disjoint pair with a single query using $O(1)$ comparisons per element, thereby establishing a lower bound of $\Omega(n)$ for the comparison model. This structure also facilitates the identification of a non-disjoint pair with $O(1)$ communication per element in the communication model, leading to an $\Omega(n)$ lower bound for that model as well. We anticipate that this comparison model will be valuable for addressing a variety of other problems. Notably, we demonstrate that the comparison model can solve the distinct element problem with $O(1)$ comparisons per element, a result that is impossible in the communication model. This finding suggests that the comparison model may offer a more efficient solution to the distinct element problem than previously established communication lower bounds. We investigate the momentum dependence of magnetic susceptibility in Heisenberg magnets by applying the high-temperature expansion method to the partition function. Our analysis of the magnetic susceptibility $\chi$ within the paramagnetic phase reveals a non-analytic momentum dependence, expressed as $\chi \sim k^{d-2} f(\beta k^{2})$, where $k$ represents the wave vector of the external field, $d$ is the dimensionality of the spin space, and $f$ is a function of $\beta k^{2}$. In the long-wavelength limit, this expression simplifies to $\chi \sim k^{d-2}$. This finding indicates that the critical exponent $\gamma_k$ governing the momentum dependence of $\chi$ is non-universal and relies on the dimensionality of the paramagnetic phase, which is determined by the spin space dimension $d$ and the spatial dimensionality $s$ of the system. Specifically, $\gamma_k = d + s - 2$ in this regime. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the critical exponent $\gamma$ associated with the temperature dependence of $\chi$ is not independent of $\gamma_k$; rather, $\gamma$ can be derived from $\gamma_k$ and the critical exponent $\delta$ via the relation $\gamma = (1 - s)\delta \gamma_k$. Consequently, the conventional scaling relation $\gamma = (1-s)\delta$ holds only in the long-wavelength limit of the magnetic field. Finally, we discuss the implications of these results for the critical behavior of the Ising model. In conclusion, the non-analytic momentum dependence of magnetic susceptibility in Heisenberg magnets represents a novel phenomenon that significantly influences the critical properties of these systems. This study also introduces a new perspective on the universality of the critical exponent $\gamma$. Our results suggest that the universality of $\gamma$ is contingent upon the long-wavelength limit, a hypothesis that warrants further investigation. We introduce a compact optical assembly utilizing multiple grating patterns to manage trapped single atoms within an integrated circuit. This system employs four distinct grating designs to execute the full experimental sequence, encompassing atom trapping, manipulation, and readout. We demonstrate the successful capture of a $^{87}$Rb atom at the center of an optical tweezer and illustrate the complete procedure for trapping and imaging $^{87}$Rb atoms within a $100\,\mu\text{m} \times 100\,\mu\text{m}$ area. This compact configuration is anticipated to be valuable for applications such as large-scale single-atom arrays, quantum information processing, and quantum simulation. Additionally, the design principles presented here may inform the development of other photonic devices and optical systems. This study investigates the nonlinear Hall effect in two-dimensional (2D) interacting systems characterized by quadratic dispersion, focusing on the influence of interactions and disorder. Employing the kinetic equation framework, we derive a closed-form analytical expression for the nonlinear Hall conductivity. Our findings indicate that while the nonlinear Hall effect vanishes in clean systems due to the cancellation of linear and quadratic velocity components, interactions induce a finite effect by shifting the Fermi surface and modifying the velocity composition. Furthermore, we demonstrate that this phenomenon persists in disordered systems through the interplay of interactions and disorder. Finally, we validate our analytical results using numerical methods based on the dynamical mean-field theory. These insights offer valuable guidance for achieving nonlinear Hall effects in interacting 2D materials. Additionally, our methodology is applicable to analyzing nonlinear Hall effects in other 2D interacting systems with higher-order dispersion relations. Finally, we outline potential experimental platforms for observing this effect. Optimal control theory has long been a cornerstone in the development of control systems, yet its application to decision-making has historically been hindered by the complexity of solving high-dimensional problems. Recent advancements in direct transcription methods have now made the use of optimal control for decision-making viable. This tutorial begins by outlining these mathematical foundations, followed by an explanation of how to formulate and solve optimal control problems using direct transcription. To demonstrate the method's utility, we apply it to a case study addressing dual-patient ventilation for COVID-19 patients, thereby highlighting its effectiveness in real-world decision-making scenarios. The accompanying Python code is provided in the supplementary materials. We aim for this guide to serve as a valuable resource for researchers interested in employing optimal control within various practical applications. A rational map $f:\widehat{\mathbb{C}}\to\widehat{\mathbb{C}}$ defined on the Riemann sphere is termed {\em bicritical} if it possesses precisely two critical points. This note provides a comprehensive classification of the groups (up to isomorphism) that function as deck transformation groups for iterates of such maps. Consequently, we establish necessary and sufficient conditions for this finiteness in terms of the monodromy and the orbifold invariants associated with the map. Furthermore, for every admissible orbifold $(\widehat{\mathbb{C}},\{p_1,\ldots,p_n\};b_1,\ldots,b_n)$, we demonstrate the existence of a corresponding bicritical rational map $f$ such that the orbifold data of the iterates $(f^m)_{m\geq 1}$ are given by the sequence $((\widehat{\mathbb{C}},\{f^m(p_1),\ldots,f^m(p_n)\};b_1^m,\ldots,b_n^m))_{m\geq 1}$. The analysis of the orbifold data for these specific bicritical maps is detailed in a separate publication. Additionally, we offer a characterization of the fundamental groups of the complements of the branch loci for maps with two or three critical points, which extends a result by J. Kollár. This paper establishes a uniform stationary phase estimate for a class of functions $f(x,\xi)$ that are piecewise $C^{\infty}$ in $x$ and $C^{\infty}$ across the entire space. The estimate demonstrates that the phase derivative $\xi \cdot \frac{\partial f}{\partial x}(\xi)$ vanishes only at isolated points, which are separated by a minimum distance. This result is applied to the study of wavefront sets for hyperbolic differential operators with piecewise smooth coefficients. Specifically, the paper proves that the wavefront set of a solution $u(x,t)$ to such an operator, given initial data with a known wavefront set, can be estimated based on the initial wavefront set and the wavefront set of the operator itself. Furthermore, the study examines the case where the coefficients are real analytic, showing that the initial wavefront set remains invariant under the operator. Finally, an appendix provides a proof of the uniform stationary phase estimate, which is derived from the implicit function theorem. This approach contrasts with the proof presented in [1], which relies on a more complex argument involving a priori estimates. Additionally, the appendix includes a remark on the applicability of this proof to other coefficient types, such as Lipschitz functions. The study begins by defining the ZNN model and outlining its design principles. Furthermore, the authors propose a unified framework for solving matrix problems using ZNNs, integrating the solutions for the aforementioned matrix operations into this structured approach. Additionally, the paper explores the application of ZNNs in other matrix-related contexts, such as time-varying low-rank matrix completion and image denoising. Finally, simulation results are provided to validate the efficacy of ZNNs in solving matrix problems and completing low-rank matrices. The proposed framework offers a systematic and unified methodology for addressing matrix computation problems through ZNNs. The findings indicate that ZNNs are highly effective for matrix computations, offering rapid convergence and the ability to handle time-varying matrix problems. The proposed framework serves as a valuable resource for researchers working on matrix computation problems using ZNNs. Ultimately, this work aims to facilitate further research and innovation in the field of ZNNs and matrix computations. Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) have become the standard for image classification, yet their receptive fields remain poorly understood. This study investigates the filters of a CNN trained for classification to determine if an optimal filter type exists. We demonstrate that an optimal filter can indeed be constructed using on-off center-surround receptive fields, which are simple yet effective for achieving accurate and robust image classification. Furthermore, these on-off center-surround receptive fields are straightforward to implement in neuromorphic hardware, offering a pathway to low-power, high-speed processing. The findings are validated through experiments on the MNIST and CIFAR-10 datasets. The resulting code is publicly accessible at https://github.com/DeepLearning4Brain/OnOffCNN. The dataset utilized in this work can be downloaded from https://drive.google.com/drive/folders/12422222222222222222222222222222. Finally, we conclude that on-off center-surround receptive fields represent a viable candidate for creating next-generation CNNs. These networks are expected to be more interpretable, robust, and energy-efficient than current architectures. Additionally, they hold significant potential for deployment in neuromorphic hardware, thereby advancing the field of brain-inspired computing. X-ray optics are currently being investigated for both fundamental research and potential future missions, such as the proposed Advanced Compton X-ray Spectrometer (ACXS). This study examines several methods to optimize ray-tracing performance, specifically targeting the ACXS Compton x-ray optical prescription. The objective is to determine the optimal arrangement of nested, axially symmetric, axially periodic, and axially symmetric periodic mirror shells that will reflect Compton electrons and positrons generated within the interaction volume onto a single focal point. We evaluate various optimization techniques, including the Nelder-Mead method, the Nelder-Mead method enhanced with a Levenberg-Marquardt algorithm, and a novel approach termed the "simulated optimization" method. This new technique employs a simulated annealing strategy to identify a superior mirror prescription. Our results indicate that the simulated optimization method surpasses both the standard Nelder-Mead approach and the Nelder-Mead method with Levenberg-Marquardt initialization when applied to this specific prescription. Furthermore, this method demonstrates robustness in locating a global optimum even when starting from a wide range of initial configurations. The techniques described here are applicable to any axially symmetric interaction volume and can be adapted for other Compton x-ray sources. Additionally, they hold promise for optimizing other x-ray optical systems, such as those intended for future missions. The source code is publicly accessible at https://github.com/abhishekbhagat/ComptonSourceOptimization. This work introduces a general framework for describing magnetic Bloch states in systems with lattice symmetry subjected to a magnetic field that breaks translational invariance but preserves lattice-site inversion symmetry. Within this framework, we investigate twisted bilayer graphene under a $2\pi$ flux per unit cell. The resulting magnetic Bloch bands exhibit reentrant flat bands at zero momentum, which can be viewed as distorted moiré flat bands. Furthermore, the phase of the magnetic Bloch states enables the construction of a non-Abelian gauge field, thereby extending the magnetic Bloch theorem to include spin-orbit coupling. Applying this extension to the twisted bilayer graphene model, we demonstrate that the reentrant flat bands transform into perfectly flat bands in the presence of spin-orbit coupling. These findings offer a pathway to experimentally detect the $2\pi$ flux phase using magneto-optical spectroscopy. Additionally, the developed framework holds broad applicability to other materials and magnetic fields that do not rely on large magnetic unit cells. Finally, these results suggest that the $2\pi$ flux state in twisted bilayer graphene may represent a new type of quantum spin liquid. This study was conducted using the open-source code MEGABAND. The accompanying paper, which details the theoretical analysis, is available at https://arxiv.org/abs/2201.07001. The code can be accessed at https://github.com/MEGABAND/MEGABAND. Driven by privacy concerns, we introduce a stegosystem that employs a Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) neural network to generate covert text within an innocuous cover. Our findings demonstrate that the network successfully hides messages with high capacity and undetectability. Furthermore, we show that the network's weights can be extracted from a single cover text, enabling the decoder to operate without prior knowledge of the network's architecture or parameters. Additionally, we prove that the network is robust against various attacks, including those designed to disrupt training or target the network directly. To facilitate future research, we have made the complete system, including the source code, available online. We hope this work inspires further advancements in the field of information hiding. Unit commitment (UC) is a critical challenge in power system operations, requiring the determination of optimal generation schedules for power plants over extended periods. While mixed-integer linear programming (MILP) is the standard approach for solving UC, its computational demands often result in excessively long solution times. To address this, the research community has increasingly focused on developing hybrid methods that combine learning techniques with traditional optimization to enhance computational efficiency. This study introduces a novel hybrid framework designed to significantly accelerate the solution of large-scale UC problems. The proposed method utilizes a deep neural network to forecast the costs of individual UC constraints, thereby identifying and filtering out non-binding constraints. By reducing the total number of constraints, the optimization problem becomes simpler to solve. Numerical experiments demonstrate that this approach accelerates the solution process by an order of magnitude compared to conventional methods. Furthermore, the method proves robust across various UC formulations and parameter settings. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/ChenYi2000/NNUC. We report high-pressure magnetization and $\mu$SR measurements on the Kitaev material $\alpha$-Li$_2$IrO$_3$, which contains both Kitaev and Heisenberg exchange interactions. At ambient pressure, the compound exhibits antiferromagnetic order below $T_\mathrm{N}=24$ K. Increasing pressure suppresses this transition, eliminating antiferromagnetism entirely at $p=1.5$ GPa. Spectroscopic data confirm that the collapse of magnetic order coincides with a pressure-induced dimerization of the Li$_2$IrO$_3$ lattice. This study demonstrates that the Heisenberg exchange interaction in $\alpha$-Li$_2$IrO$_3$ is mechanically fragile, a finding that offers crucial insights into the stability of Kitaev physics under external pressure. Furthermore, we discuss the potential for tuning Kitaev physics in this material through strain engineering. These findings are particularly significant for the search for Kitaev quantum spin liquid states, as they highlight the necessity of strain engineering to achieve the low-temperature Kitaev regime. Finally, we address the implications of these results for the realization of Kitaev physics in other related materials. Our work underscores the critical role of strain engineering in advancing Kitaev research. This conclusion is supported by the fact that Kitaev physics in $\alpha$-RuCl$_3$ was discovered via strain engineering, and that the elusive Kitaev regime in $\alpha$-Li$_2$IrO$_3$ remains inaccessible without applying pressure. Additionally, our findings suggest that strain engineering is essential for investigating Kitaev physics in other materials, such as Na$_2$IrO$_3$, which displays distinct pressure-induced structural and magnetic transitions compared to $\alpha$-Li$_2$IrO$_3$. These results are expected to guide future efforts in the search for Kitaev quantum spin liquid states. Synthetic control methods have gained significant traction for causal inference, yet they rely on two critical assumptions: the balance of covariates and the absence of interference. However, these assumptions are frequently violated in practical applications. This study introduces a proximal causal inference framework that derives identification conditions for the average treatment effect on the treated (CITIT) while simultaneously estimating the effect. The proposed model utilizes a machine learning approach to estimate the CITIT identification function, which is subsequently integrated into a proximal causal inference procedure to yield an estimator for the CITIT-weighted average treatment effect. Furthermore, the paper develops a semiparametric model to facilitate inference, enabling the construction of a point estimator for the synthetic control treatment effect alongside a corresponding variance estimator. Simulation results demonstrate that the proposed estimator achieves superior performance compared to existing synthetic control methods. Finally, the study applies this framework to evaluate the impact of the Affordable Care Act on Medicaid expansion. The analysis reveals that the proximal causal inference estimator offers a substantial performance advantage over traditional synthetic control estimators, particularly when covariate balance is compromised. Additionally, the proximal treatment effect estimate exhibits a notably larger magnitude than that of the synthetic control treatment effect. These findings underscore the potential of proximal causal inference methods to enhance the accuracy and reliability of synthetic control analysis. The code used to replicate the results is available at: https://github.com/ChenYi1997/SyntheticControl. Keywords: Proximal Causal Inference; Synthetic Control; No Interference; Covariate Balance. This paper introduces a privacy-preserving algorithm based on Gromov-Hausdorff distance to analyze and compare two unlabelled, undirected graphs from different sources without revealing sensitive structural information. We propose a method that applies the Gromov-Wasserstein (GW) discrepancy between node feature distributions to measure the distance between two unlabelled graphs. To ensure privacy, we integrate local differential privacy (LDP) into the GW discrepancy calculation, thereby protecting the distribution of node features. Our approach demonstrates that the resulting privacy-aware GW discrepancy maintains robustness and effectiveness in measuring graph distance while satisfying LDP guarantees. Experimental results indicate that this method outperforms existing state-of-the-art techniques in both accuracy and efficiency. Furthermore, our method proves highly effective for downstream tasks, such as graph classification and clustering, when used to learn a distance metric for graph representations. We introduce a new laser-plasma interaction mechanism driven by self-steepening, which enables polarization control of electron injection and acceleration during the collision of two plasma bubbles. This process occurs when two counterpropagating, polarization-mismatched pulses collide within a plasma. The resulting electron acceleration is facilitated by a polarization vortex generated through the interaction between the pulses' self-steepening effect and group velocity mismatch caused by group velocity dispersion. This polarization vortex creates a transverse electric field component that directs electron acceleration perpendicular to the laser propagation direction. We demonstrate that this polarization control remains effective even when the group velocity mismatch is negligible, relying instead on the self-steepening-induced intensity mismatch. Furthermore, we show that the self-steepening effect can be substituted by the Kerr effect, a phenomenon known as Kerr lensing mode locking in ultrafast lasers. Our findings suggest that this novel interaction mechanism can be readily applied to various laser-pulse-plasma systems, potentially offering new pathways for laser-pl interaction. Additionally, we explore the potential for generating and manipulating electron beams with transverse polarization. These results may have significant implications for applications in laser-based particle acceleration and electron tomography.

The renormalization of the flavor-singlet axial-vector current and its associated renormalization constant within dimensional regularization are examined. It is demonstrated that the renormalization constant connecting the bare field to the renormalized field exhibits a non-trivial dependence on the dimension-regularization parameter $1/\epsilon$, a phenomenon attributed to the renormalization of the $\gamma_5$ matrix. This dependence arises from loop diagrams involving the QCD vacuum insertion of the renormalized $\gamma_5$ matrix, a quantity that is non-zero in the four-dimensional limit of $\epsilon \to 0$ and therefore renormalizable. The resulting renormalized QCD vacuum insertion of the $\gamma_5$ matrix is directly linked to the renormalization of the axial anomaly, which is also renormalized due to the renormalization of the topological charge density. Furthermore, the renormalized topological charge density is shown to be independent of the renormalization scale $\mu_R$ and the renormalization scheme, adhering to the renormalization group equation. This finding is consistent with the fact that the renormalized axial anomaly remains independent of both $\mu_R$ and the subtraction scheme, as the renormalization of the $\gamma_5$ matrix is independent of the renormalization scale and scheme. Consequently, the renormalization of the axial anomaly is independent of both the renormalization scale and scheme. Additionally, the renormalization of the renormalized quark-gluon mixing coefficient $d_{tg}$ is derived, which is essential for renormalizing the renormalized quark-gluon mixing operator. The renormalization constant for this operator is determined by the renormalization of the topological charge density and the renormalized quark-gluon mixing coefficient. The derived renormalization constant for the mixing operator is independent of the renormalization scale and scheme, a result that aligns with the independence of the mixing matrix element of the operator, which is a physical quantity. Finally, the renormalization of the renormalized gluon field strength tensor is derived, a process that also requires the renormalization of the $\gamma_5$ matrix. The resulting renormalization constant for the gluon field strength tensor is independent of the renormalization scale and scheme, a conclusion consistent with the fact that the gluon field strength tensor is a renormalization scheme-independent quantity. Our approach leverages a convolutional neural network (CNN) to extract features from grayscale images taken by the uncaptured camera and combines them with existing color-image features to produce the final colorized result. This paper investigates the generalized Euler-Poisson-Darboux equation defined on the $l$-sphere. By applying separation of variables in Cartesian coordinates to an isopotential surface of this equation, we derive the generalized $n$-dimensional Euler equation, which represents a specific instance of the $n$-dimensional Ermakov system. Utilizing the Cartan-Karlhede algorithm, we determine all Lie point symmetries and conservation laws associated with this equation. Furthermore, we establish a link between the Lie point symmetries of the generalized $n$-dimensional Euler equation and its separability within Cartesian coordinates. Finally, we examine the link between the Cartan-Karlhede algorithm and the separation of variables, demonstrating that the latter can be derived from the former. As an application, we analyze the $3$-dimensional Euler equation, which corresponds to a special case of the $3$-dimensional Ermakov system. This system features a time-dependent potential with two centers, where the conserved quantities are identified as generalizations of the Laplace-Runge-Lenz vector and Runge vector. Additionally, we note that this system is integrable and possesses maximal symmetry. We also explore the connection between the Cartan-Karlhede method and the integrability of the Ermakov system. Finally, we extend our discussion to the $2$-dimensional Euler equation, which is linked to a special case of the $2$-dimensional Ermakov system involving a time-dependent potential with four centers. We show that this system is also integrable and exhibits maximal symmetry. These findings provide a novel approach to the integrability problem for the two-center potential. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the $2$-sphere is not separable in Cartesian coordinates using the Cartan-Karlhede algorithm. This work contributes to the broader field of mathematical physics by offering a new method for investigating the integrability of the Schrödinger equation. Specifically, it enables the derivation of the Schrödinger equation's conservation laws and the identification of its Lie point symmetries. We also address the associated eigenvalue problem. Our methodology is applicable to the $n$-dimensional Schrödinger equation with a time-dependent potential possessing a high degree of symmetry. As an illustrative example, we consider the $3$-dimensional Schrödinger equation with a time-dependent potential featuring two centers, which is known to be integrable and to have maximal symmetry. Public transportation systems are increasingly recognized as vital for societal mobility and environmental sustainability. However, their operation and management are complex, demanding substantial financial investment and extensive human resources. A primary challenge lies in planning and operating services efficiently, which necessitates a robust demand forecast. While public transit agencies possess rich data sources such as ticketing records and GPS tracking, they often lack the technical expertise to process this information effectively. Consequently, there is a growing need for data-driven methods that require minimal domain knowledge. This study introduces a recurrent neural network approach to enhance public transportation operations by utilizing only ticketing data to predict passenger demand. The findings demonstrate that this method yields superior results compared to ARIMA and XGBoost techniques when applied to time series data from multiple agencies. Furthermore, the research confirms that the proposed model can generate accurate demand forecasts even when critical operational data, like vehicle locations, is unavailable. Few-shot learning addresses a critical challenge in deep learning by enabling models to generalize from minimal examples. This study introduces a straightforward yet effective prototype-based method that learns class-level prototypes directly from support sets. Unlike conventional approaches that compute prototypes as feature mean or median values, our technique utilizes a neural network to derive prototypes through end-to-end training. We validate this method across three standard benchmarks: miniImageNet, miniCOIN, and miniSUN. Experimental results demonstrate that our approach surpasses state-of-the-art methods, achieving an accuracy of 69.4% in miniImageNet and 70.1% in miniSUN under the 5-way 5-shot setting. Furthermore, ablation studies reveal that our model can effectively reuse pre-trained weights across different datasets. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/ChenYi-1998/PP-LFS. Given its simplicity and robust performance, we believe this method holds significant potential for further research and application. Keywords: Few-shot learning, Prototype-based method.

We investigate systems featuring non-invertible global symmetries within four-dimensional quantum field theories. We demonstrate that if a continuous non-invertible symmetry is spontaneously broken, a massless Nambu-Goldstone boson inevitably emerges. This result is established by analyzing the behavior of correlation functions and employing a method to construct the would-be Nambu-Goldstone boson within an enlarged operator basis. Furthermore, we derive constraints on these massless modes, including the quantization of their couplings to higher-form currents and the constraint $2k \geq \Delta$ for its scalar interactions, where $k$ represents the spin and $\Delta$ the scaling dimension. Additionally, we show that conservation laws associated with invertible symmetries impose further constraints on continuous symmetries, allowing us to derive the central charge of the low-energy conformal field theory in terms of the ultraviolet central charges and the contributions from any spontaneously broken invertible symmetries. We also examine continuous symmetries in theories with chiral fermions, proving that if all fermion masses are non-zero, the continuous non-invertible symmetry must be unbroken. Finally, we explore the implications of these findings for dualities and for constructing quantum field theories that possess only non-invertible global symmetries. A directed graph is semi-transitive if and only if it is acyclic and satisfies the condition that for any directed path $u_1 \rightarrow u_2 \rightarrow \cdots \rightarrow u_k$, the edges $(u_1,u_2), (u_2,u_3), \ldots, (u_{k-1},u_k)$ all exist if and only if the edge $(u_1, u_k)$ exists. Graphs possessing this property are referred to as semi-transitive graphs. Bang-Jensen and Huang established in 1993 that every split graph is semi-transitive orientable, meaning it admits a semi-transitive orientation. This paper investigates the minimum out-degree of semi-transitive orientations for split graphs, demonstrating that this minimum out-degree is bounded by $n/2 + 1$, where $n$ represents the graph's order. Furthermore, we characterize the specific subclass of split graphs that achieve this bound. Additionally, we provide a complete characterization of $P_4$-free semi-transitive graphs, thereby confirming a conjecture by Chudnovsky et al. from 2009. Finally, we present a polynomial-time algorithm for determining the minimum out-degree of a semi-transitive orientation of a given split graph. As a consequence, we derive a polynomial-time algorithm for identifying $P_4$-free semi-transitive graphs. This approach contrasts with the current best-known polynomial-time algorithm for chordal $P_4$-free semi-transitive graphs, which was developed by Bui-Xuan et al. in 2019. Our findings also offer a novel, independent proof of the theorem by Chudnovsky et al. regarding $P_4$-free semi-transitive graphs, which was previously proven in 2009 to be solvable in quadratic time. We also address an open question posed by Bui-Xuan et al. in 2019 concerning the existence of a polynomial-time algorithm for recognizing $P_5$-free semi-transitive graphs. We demonstrate that such an algorithm exists specifically for $P_{5,5}$-free split graphs. However, we further show that no polynomial-time algorithm can recognize $P_5$-free semi-transitive split graphs unless $P = NP$. This study details the selection of hadronic tau decays via a deep neural network (DNN) within the CMS experiment. The DNN was trained to differentiate hadronic tau decays from QCD jets and fakes originating from light hadrons or electrons. The data used for training and validation comprised simulated particle-level events. A validation dataset at the reconstructed level, consisting of real CMS events, was employed to assess the DNN's performance. The results indicate that the DNN's efficiency and background rejection capabilities in identifying hadronic tau decays align well with predictions derived from Monte Carlo simulations. This DNN-based identification method is utilized in various physics analyses at CMS. The paper provides a description of the algorithm, its performance, and the agreement between the actual data and the Monte Carlo predictions. Additionally, it outlines the necessary steps for applying the method to new hadronic tau decay identification analyses. The source code is publicly accessible at https://github.com/cms-dp/dtau.
