The upcoming Rubin observatory is expected to generate vast datasets, including billions of light curves from the time-domain and hundreds of millions of images from its yearly surveys. This scale necessitates a shift from traditional methods toward scalable machine learning techniques, such as neural networks, to address challenges like object classification and property estimation. However, this transition introduces new issues, particularly the risk of neural networks overfitting on large data and the difficulty of quantifying prediction uncertainties. This work demonstrates that Bayesian Neural Networks (BNNs) offer a solution by learning uncertainty alongside data patterns. We validate this approach through simulations involving light curve fitting and classification, as well as galaxy morphology classification. Our findings indicate that BNNs can accurately estimate uncertainties for individual predictions and effectively identify overfitting during training. Furthermore, we show that transfer learning enables the training of Bayesian models on simulated data for application to real-world observations. These results confirm that Bayesian neural networks are a promising tool for addressing critical tasks in the Rubin era. The code for all analyses is publicly accessible at https://github.com/mauricio-fernandez-brito/bayesian-ml-rubin. The simulations are also available at https://github.com/mauricio-fernandez-brito/rubin-sims. Additional details regarding the analysis can be found in our supplementary material. Finally, we provide a tutorial on performing light curve fitting and classification using Bayesian neural networks at https://mauriciofb.github.io/bnn-rubin. This resource includes a step-by-step guide for fitting light curves, classifying objects, and assessing overfitting. The tutorial also covers transfer learning for Rubin data, with examples for both real and simulated observations. The user-friendly interface allows users to adjust hyperparameters, such as the number of network layers, and explore the impact of varying training set sizes. The interface also supports the selection of different datasets, including simulated or real observations, and enables the fitting of light curves for specific objects. The tutorial is available in both English and Spanish. We hope this resource will assist the community in applying BNNs to Rubin data. This study presents an experimental investigation of intermodal forward Brillouin scattering within a solid-core photonic crystal fiber, demonstrating the simultaneous excitation and detection of all three modes supported by the waveguide. The intermodal Brillouin bandwidth was measured at 100 Hz, with a mode coupling coefficient determined to be 0.0015 rad/W. These findings indicate that photonic crystal fibers can serve as a foundation for investigating multimode intermodal Brillouin scattering. Furthermore, the research suggests that the photonic bandgap structure inherent to such fibers could be leveraged to achieve high-temperature Brillouin spectroscopy. Additionally, the results highlight the potential of this fiber type for enhancing the sensitivity of distributed acoustic sensing systems. The Set-Union Knapsack Problem (SUKP) and the Budgeted Maximum Coverage Problem (BMCP) are two interrelated combinatorial optimization challenges. Both involve selecting a set of elements within a specific budget to maximize the union of their associated subsets. Suk et al. (2019) demonstrated that both problems are NP-hard and introduced a greedy algorithm achieving a $1/2$-approximation for SUKP, alongside a polynomial-time approximation scheme for BMCP when the budget equals the total number of elements. This paper introduces a local search algorithm for both problems that begins with the greedy solution and iteratively replaces the current best solution with a non-dominated one found through search. The algorithm's runtime is bounded by $O(m^2n^2)$, where $m$ represents the number of elements and $n$ the budget. Experimental results indicate that this local search approach significantly outperforms the greedy algorithm in terms of solution quality. Furthermore, applying the algorithm to the polynomial-time solvable BMCP with a budget of $m$ elements yields an optimal solution. The method also surpasses the state-of-the-art local search by Chen et al. (2019) regarding the number of non-dominated solutions discovered. Finally, the proposed algorithms were utilized to rank the top 100 news sources for 100 topics, with the resulting rankings validated by domain experts. The code is publicly accessible at https://github.com/ChenYi1996/LocalSearch. SUKP.

This paper introduces a new, straightforward machine learning approach for predicting churn in online gambling. Given the industry's high costs associated with acquiring new customers and the significant revenue loss from them, identifying at-risk individuals is crucial. The authors argue that the primary objective should be early warning detection to facilitate timely retention efforts. Their proposed method relies on a simple linear model that utilizes only a few features, specifically those that have changed recently. The study details the data collection process, feature selection criteria, and experimental results, concluding that the approach is both effective and efficient. The 2D Ising field theory, representing the continuum limit of the Ising model, is examined within a dual-magnetic field. In this framework, the Yang-Lee singularity manifests as a specific field configuration where the sigma field acquires a magnetic field but remains devoid of an Ising field. We demonstrate that the form factor expansion for the scalar particle field fails to converge in this regime. This outcome is consistent with the absence of analyticity in the form factors of scalar particles regarding their virtuality, a property previously established through finite lattice calculations. Consequently, the failure of the form factor expansion underscores the significant complexity introduced by the magnetic field in the two-dimensional Ising field theory. Furthermore, we explore the implications of these findings for the mass gap and the spectrum of the theory. Finally, we outline potential future research directions concerning this topic. Notably, the methodologies developed here are anticipated to be applicable to other two-dimensional field theories featuring a mass gap and a spectrum composed of stable, elastic particles. Such applications could yield novel insights into the structure of form factor expansions and the completeness of their series. The research was conducted using the FORM computer algebra system. Additionally, the appendix provides a detailed derivation of the one-loop correction to the sigma field propagator in the presence of a magnetic field, a result that may prove valuable for future investigations. We demonstrate that gluon transverse-momentum-dependent parton distribution functions (TMDs) can be expressed as correlations of large-momentum effective theory (TMT) gluon fields. This approach offers a straightforward method for determining the scale dependence of gluon TMDs and clarifies the physical significance of the Mellin moments of these functions. Furthermore, we establish a direct link between the gluon TMDs of one hadron and the gluon Sivers functions of a different hadron. These findings are derived using gauge-invariant field-strength operators. Additionally, we calculate the renormalization-scale dependence of the gluon TMDs, revealing that the gluon helicity distribution $g_1^{g[N]}(x)$ is scale-independent at leading twist. The findings regarding the scale dependence of gluon TMDs are validated by existing literature. Finally, we provide a gauge-invariant definition for the gluon TMDs, extending the framework previously established for quark TMDs. This enables a direct comparison of gluon TMDs extracted from various hadron-dispersion sum rules. Furthermore, our results facilitate the extraction of gluon TMDs from processes involving nucleon targets with large light-cone momenta. The paper concludes with a discussion of these implications. Ultra-relativistic heavy-ion collisions serve as an effective tool for investigating photon-photon interactions. Theoretical predictions for the cross sections of these processes are essential for comparing against experimental data. This study examines the interaction between an electron or positron and a heavy nucleus within an electron or positron-Ur or Pb system during ultra-peripheral ultra-relativistic heavy-ion collisions. We demonstrate that the electromagnetic interaction between the lepton and the nucleus can be modeled as the exchange of two photons. This approach is valid when the lepton's transverse momentum is significantly smaller than the nuclear charge. Furthermore, we have computed the corresponding cross sections. Our findings indicate that the cross section for electron-electron scattering is approximately two orders of magnitude greater than that for positron-positron scattering. Additionally, the cross section for electron-electron scattering involving a Ur nucleus is roughly two orders of magnitude lower than that for the same process with a Pb nucleus. These results suggest that photon-photon interactions involving electrons and positrons in electron-Ur or electron-Pb ultra-peripheral collisions could be observable in the near future. Additionally, we have established that the ratio of the cross sections for electron-electron and positron-positron scattering is independent of the target nucleus. This ratio is approximately 2.0 for a Ur nucleus and 2.1 for a Pb nucleus. We anticipate that our findings will be valuable for future experimental investigations. Our predictions regarding the cross sections for electron-electron and positron-positron scattering in ultra-peripheral electron-nucleus collisions are as follows: 1.1 mb for electron-electron scattering with a Ur nucleus, 2.2 mb for the same with a Pb nucleus, 0.005 mb for positron-positron scattering with a Ur nucleus, and 0.01 mb for positron-positron scattering with a Pb nucleus. These values are provided for an equivalent photon energy of 100 MeV. Additionally, the ratio of electromagnetic interactions between electrons and positrons with a Pb nucleus is approximately 2.1, whereas with a Ur nucleus, this ratio is approximately 2.0. These ratios are independent of the photon energy. The electromagnetic interaction between electrons and a Pb nucleus is roughly 200 times greater than that between positrons and a Pb nucleus. Similarly, the electromagnetic interaction between electrons and a Ur nucleus is about 200 times greater than that between positrons and a Ur nucleus. Cycling is a popular mode of transportation, yet it exposes riders to significant injury and fatality risks. To better understand and mitigate these dangers, it is essential to identify the factors contributing to cyclist accidents. This study introduces a risk descriptor for cyclists that integrates context-aware data, including vehicle type, cycling mode, and road surface conditions. By utilizing computer vision, the proposed descriptor analyzes video footage to extract context-specific risk indicators. These descriptors are computed across various cycling scenarios and compared against accident scenarios to identify statistically significant differences, thereby revealing context-dependent risk factors. The results indicate that the risk descriptor varies based on context, with notable differences observed in both cycling and vehicle modes. Furthermore, the study successfully identifies the presence of bicycles in video streams, demonstrating the descriptor's potential for real-world video analysis. This approach offers a promising method for analyzing context-aware risk factors and can be extended to other road users, such as pedestrians. Control Barrier Functions (CBF) are extensively utilized to ensure safety in high-dimensional robotic systems, yet their efficacy depends on the precise integration of dynamics models, making them vulnerable to model uncertainties. This paper introduces a motion planning framework that employs CBFs to generate safe trajectories for dynamically-constrained robots, accounting for model uncertainties. The proposed CBFs are defined as infinite-horizon cost functions, where the minimum value of this function represents a safe trajectory. We demonstrate that the CBFs satisfy a C1-continuity property, which facilitates the application of established optimization techniques. Furthermore, we prove that incorporating CBFs into the cost function enables the derivation of safe trajectories through standard optimization. To compute these CBF-based trajectories, we propose a novel optimization method that utilizes CBFs to guide a model-based planner. Experimental results on a 7-DoF robot arm validate the approach's ability to produce safe trajectories even when dynamics models are imperfect. The proposed method is general and can be integrated with various existing motion planning techniques. Additionally, we demonstrate that it enhances the safety of existing methods, such as Model Predictive Control (MPC), which often lack strict safety guarantees due to model inaccuracies. The numerical examples are implemented using the Robotics Toolbox for MATLAB. The Robotics Toolbox is an open-source library for robotics research and education, available at http://robotics.tamu.edu. For a ring $R$ and a positive integer $n$, the covering number $\operatorname{cov}(R^n)$ denotes the smallest possible size of a subset $S \subseteq R^n$ such that every element in $R^n$ can be expressed as a sum of two elements from $S$. This paper investigates the covering numbers for rings of integers, integers modulo $n$, and the rings of algebraic integers within number fields. Specifically, we establish that $\operatorname{cov}(\mathbb{Z}_p^k) = p^k - p^{\lfloor k/2 \rfloor} + 1$ for any prime $p$ and positive integer $k$, and that $\operatorname{cov}(\mathcal{O}_K^2) = 5$ when $\mathcal{O}_K$ is the ring of algebraic integers in a quadratic number field with class number 1. Additionally, we derive a lower bound for $\operatorname{cov}(R^2)$ when $R$ is a finite commutative ring with identity, and provide a lower bound for $\operatorname{cov}(\mathbb{Z}_n^k)$ when $n$ is a positive integer and $k$ is an even positive integer. These findings yield new results for the specific cases where $R = \mathbb{Z}_p$ or $\mathbb{Z}_{p^k}$, and where $K$ is a quadratic number field with class number 1. Furthermore, we demonstrate that $\operatorname{cov}(\mathbb{Z}_{p^k}^2) = p^k - p^{\lfloor (k-1)/2 \rfloor}$ for any positive integers $k$ and $p$. The proofs utilize a graph-theoretic approach, which we also apply to determine the covering numbers of matrix rings over a finite field. Finally, we present several open questions and conjectures regarding covering numbers in rings and modules. This work serves as a natural extension of the study conducted by P. Erdős, I. Z. Ruzsa, and E. Szemerédi in 1986. Our findings also partially address an inquiry posed by J. H. Smith in 2001. The techniques developed here may offer a foundation for future research into the covering numbers of more general rings and modules. Keywords: covering number, finite commutative ring with identity, finite ring, finite algebra

Deep neural networks (DNNs) are highly susceptible to adversarial examples, which are subtly altered inputs that cause incorrect predictions despite being imperceptible to humans. This vulnerability stems from the fact that models often rely on easily manipulable features that are not semantically aligned with the data. To address this, we introduce a robust training framework that enhances resilience by incorporating adversarial training alongside a novel robustness regularization technique. This regularization minimizes the impact of high-order derivatives within the input space, thereby reducing the model's dependence on features that are easy to exploit. Our approach is straightforward to implement and yields significant improvements, as evidenced by superior accuracy and AUC scores across multiple benchmark datasets. Furthermore, the method demonstrates strong generalization, with consistent performance gains observed on unseen datasets. Finally, we show that this framework effectively mitigates the overconfidence of DNNs, a key factor contributing to their adversarial weaknesses. The code for our framework is available at https://github.com/DeepRobustness/R-R.

We examine a conservation law incorporating nonlocal interactions, where the kernel is defined as the convolution of a non-negative, integrable, and bounded function with a non-negative Dirac delta function centered at $\theta \ge 0$. We demonstrate that when $\theta = 0$, the model simplifies to a local conservation law, which serves as the singular limit of the nonlocal formulation. We establish that solutions to the nonlocal problem converge to the unique entropy solution of the corresponding local problem, with a quantified convergence rate dependent on $\theta$. Furthermore, we prove that every entropy solution to the local problem satisfies the nonlocal problem in the sense of admissibility. Finally, we analyze the dependence of the convergence rate on $\theta$ and investigate the behavior of these rates as $\theta$ approaches zero. These findings are supported by various numerical examples. The study begins by presenting the nonlocal model and its associated entropy formulation, followed by a review of existing results for specific kernels. We then derive the singular limit for general kernels, utilizing a relative entropy argument to bound the nonlocal entropy solution by the local one. This enables us to prove the convergence of nonlocal entropy solutions to the unique entropy solution of the local problem, while providing an explicit estimate for the convergence rate. We subsequently examine the local limit for several kernels, including those used in prior studies. Additionally, we explore the behavior of the derived rates as $\theta$ tends to zero. The paper concludes with numerical experiments that validate our theoretical findings and offer further insights into the model's behavior. These experiments employ two distinct numerical schemes: a finite volume method for the local problem and a finite difference method for the nonlocal problem. We also present a numerical approach to verify the admissibility of entropy solutions. Finally, we discuss the observed behavior of the nonlocal solutions as $\theta$ approaches zero. The results indicate that the finite difference scheme converges to the local solution, but the finite volume scheme does not, despite both schemes being consistent with their respective problems. This discrepancy is attributed to the finite volume scheme's upwind nature, which introduces a bias in the nonlocal context. We also provide numerical evidence supporting the derived convergence rates. These findings suggest that while the finite difference scheme is more accurate, the finite volume scheme remains a viable option for practical applications. The paper concludes with a discussion of potential future research directions. The results are supported by various numerical examples. Dilation surfaces extend the concept of translation surfaces by allowing atlases with local charts to map into the plane under complex conjugation. These surfaces arise as small perturbations of translation surfaces and can be realized as quotients of dilation invariant sectors under actions of dilation groups acting on the upper half-plane. This paper investigates the dynamics of arbitrary dilation invariant open sets under group actions, demonstrating that minimal sets are either horizons or contain a non-wandering point. We establish that for horizon saddles—saddles where the stable and unstable horizons are straight lines—there exists a corresponding invariant line. Furthermore, we prove that a dilation surface is Morse-Smale if and only if it lacks non-wandering horizon saddles. This result parallels the characterization of Morse-Smale translation surfaces, which are defined as those without periodic directions. The study of horizon saddles parallels research on translation surfaces regarding closed geodesics, specifically the work of Masur and Smillie on interval exchange transformations. Additionally, we demonstrate that the set of dilation surfaces containing a non-wandering horizon saddle is dense. These findings underscore the significant distinction between dilation surfaces and translation surfaces, highlighting the necessity for new techniques and invariants to address fundamental questions in this domain. Notably, the existence of a closed geodesic does not guarantee that every dilation surface exhibits a horizon saddle. Consequently, we introduce a novel invariant, the dilation zeta function, which serves as a tool for analyzing the dynamics of dilation surfaces. This function is defined for any dilation surface and a dilation invariant open set and encodes information regarding the dynamics on that open set. We provide a formula for the dilation zeta function of dilation surfaces possessing a horizon saddle and derive a formula for the number of fixed points of horizon saddles based on this invariant. This approach offers a new perspective on the dynamics of dilation surfaces, as the fixed point count of a horizon saddle is determined by the surface's invariant. We also examine the relationship between horizon saddles and minimal sets, proving that a horizon saddle is either minimal or possesses a non-wandering point. Finally, we present a translation surface with a periodic direction that is not a horizon saddle, thereby illustrating the distinction between these two concepts. The paper concludes with an outline of future research directions. This work was conducted during the first author's visit to the University of Leeds, supported by the Leeds International Fellowship. This study introduces a novel framework for characterizing functional connectivity within the human brain using total correlation, thereby expanding the traditional concept of functional connectome. Defined as a probability distribution over functional connectome realizations, this new construct offers a more nuanced and comprehensive description of brain connectivity. The paper demonstrates that total correlation effectively captures complex, multifaceted dependencies among brain regions, distinguishing it from mutual information, which primarily identifies pairwise relationships. Furthermore, the authors propose a new method for estimating total correlation from time series data and apply this technique to resting-state fMRI recordings from the Human Connectome Project. The results reveal that brain regions exhibiting high total correlation with the region of interest display synchronized activity patterns. Additionally, the study finds that the total correlation of resting-state fMRI time series from distinct brain regions is significantly lower than that of synthetic data, such as white noise or first-order autoregressive processes. These findings indicate that the proposed framework successfully discriminates between brain regions that are functionally connected to the region of interest and those that are not. The research concludes by outlining potential future applications of this framework. The code required to replicate the results is accessible at https://github.com/DeepakSahoo1996/TotalCorrelation. This paper investigates the fixed Clifford algebra $Cl_{0,n}(\mathbb R)$-valued Segal-Bargmann transform, denoted $S_{MB}$, and its relationship with the Taylor isomorphism $T_{cl}$, which maps a $k$-th order continuous function $f: \mathbb R^k \to Cl_{0,n}(\mathbb R)$ onto the space of Taylor series $\mathbb C_n^{k[[z]]}$. We demonstrate that the composite map $T_{cl}^{-1}S_{MB}$ is an injective operator that links the weighted $L^2$-space $\mathcal H^2_{\lambda_{k,n}}(Cl_{0,n}(\mathbb R))$ with the Fock space $\mathcal F^2_{\lambda_{k,n}}(Cl_{0,n}(\mathbb R))$. Furthermore, we establish that the reproducing kernel for the latter space is the exponential function $\exp_{Cl_{0,n}}(\lambda_{k,n} z \bar z)$, and we derive several properties of this kernel. Finally, we outline several applications of these findings.

Keywords: Clifford algebra, Segal-Bargmann transform, Taylor isomorphism, Fock space, exponential function.

This paper introduces a pathwise conditioning framework for Gaussian processes. Unlike the conventional joint density conditioning approach, our method relies on reproducing kernel Hilbert space theory. We derive a closed-form expression for the conditional mean and demonstrate that the conditional covariance retains a diagonal kernel form, provided the original joint distribution does. The proposed framework is validated through simulations and case studies. Furthermore, we apply this method to create Gaussian process classifiers that integrate auxiliary data alongside the standard joint density conditioning technique. Simulation results indicate that the proposed classifier surpasses standard methods in both accuracy and computational efficiency. Finally, we demonstrate the application of this framework on two real-world datasets: the MNIST and CIFAR-10 image collections. In both scenarios, our classifiers achieve higher accuracy than state-of-the-art Gaussian process classifiers. This study examines a ground-based sensor network augmented by sensor balloons. We assess the network's connectivity using the Wiener index, a metric that correlates with both the diameter and average shortest path lengths. Our primary objective is to determine the optimal vertical spacing between the ground and the balloons. We demonstrate that minimizing the Wiener index leads to an optimal solution when the vertical distance is set to 1.5 times the distance that yields optimal coverage for a purely balloon-based network. Furthermore, we establish that as the number of balloon sensors grows, the optimal distance converges to 1.6 times the optimally spaced distance for the balloon-only scenario. Finally, we provide a complete characterization of the Wiener index for a specific class of graphs, which includes the relevant topologies, and derive a closed-form expression for the minimum Wiener index within this class. These findings are supported by numerical simulations. Additionally, we extend our analysis to evaluate the impact of balloon mobility on network connectivity. We find that balloon movement significantly enhances connectivity, with the Wiener index improving by a factor of 2.5. This improvement is achieved by allowing balloons to periodically shift to bridge gaps between ground sensors, thereby creating more regular graph structures. We also analyze the convergence of the Wiener index for these dynamic graphs and provide a characterization of the convergence rate. Finally, we generalize these results to broader graph classes and offer insights applicable to other graph metrics. This research is grounded in a real-world application involving a network of ground sensors monitoring a desert region, augmented by solar-powered sensor balloons. The ground sensors are deployed at a fixed distance, resulting in a network with a high diameter, which this work aims to address. The balloons are designed to maintain a fixed altitude, making the balloon-ground distance a critical parameter. We demonstrate that optimizing this distance substantially improves network connectivity. The proposed solutions are straightforward to implement and require no modifications to the existing sensor hardware. The past few decades have seen remarkable advancements in our understanding of the subatomic world, driven largely by particle physics. Among these achievements, neutrino research stands out, having revealed that neutrinos possess mass and offering the potential to solve fundamental questions regarding electroweak symmetry breaking, matter-antimatter asymmetry, and the nature of dark matter. This overview examines the current state of knowledge and the future prospects of neutrino physics, with a specific focus on the upcoming Deep Underground Neutrino Experiment (DUNE). DUNE represents a new frontier in accelerator-based neutrino research, aiming to achieve unprecedented precision in measuring neutrino properties and uncovering new phenomena. By utilizing a megaton-scale liquid argon time projection chamber, DUNE will investigate fundamental neutrino characteristics—including mixing angles, mass hierarchy, and CP violation—through high-statistics measurements of neutrino oscillation. Furthermore, the experiment will study supernova neutrinos and search for sterile neutrinos, while also leveraging its broad energy spectrum to explore electroweak physics, quantum chromodynamics, and hadronization. Additionally, DUNE is poised to make significant contributions to proton decay searches, dark matter investigations, and measurements of the cosmic matter-antimatter asymmetry. This paper details the scientific motivations behind DUNE, outlines its design and capabilities, and presents results from ongoing prototype experiments that validate its performance. Ultimately, DUNE is designed to advance our understanding of the fundamental constituents of the universe for the coming decades. The full text is available at http://arxiv.org/abs/1801.05775. Top tagging has become a critical area of research for the LHC, driven by the potential of extra-dimensional models to generate significant amounts of events featuring jets of highly boosted, decaying particles. This study enhances top-tagging discrimination by utilizing the boost distribution of the substructure within the tag. We demonstrate that this approach offers a substantial improvement over standard top-tagging techniques. Furthermore, we provide an interpretation of boosted-disk discriminants through Shapley values, demonstrating that these methods are interpretable. This capability is essential for assessing the robustness of the tag against background fluctuations and for guiding future developments in taggers. The analysis employs the same dataset used in the top discriminant training, ensuring that the proposed methods can be directly applied to existing taggers without requiring additional data. The code is publicly accessible at https://github.com/abernstein12/boosted-top-tagging. The findings presented here will serve as a foundation for our future research into the top tag. Deep Reinforcement Learning (RL) has demonstrated remarkable success in addressing complex decision-making challenges. However, the data efficiency of current methods often necessitates the exploration of vast state-action spaces, requiring agents to interact with environments for extended periods. This paper introduces a novel algorithm, Variance Reduction based Policy Optimization with Experience Replay (VRPO-ER), designed to enhance data efficiency. VRPO-ER integrates two established techniques: experience replay and variance reduction. Experience replay functions by storing past experiences in a buffer and sampling them for training, thereby mitigating the bias introduced by non-stationary targets. Concurrently, variance reduction accelerates the convergence of stochastic gradient descent by minimizing the variance of parameter updates. The synergy between these approaches is synergistic; variance reduction minimizes parameter update variance, which in turn reduces bias in the estimated targets used for parameter updates, while experience replay stabilizes the target estimates themselves. We evaluate VRPO-ER across various continuous control tasks and a benchmark discrete action problem. The results demonstrate that VRPO-ER achieves superior data efficiency compared to both the variance reduction-only and experience replay-only baselines. Furthermore, we provide theoretical insights into VRPO-ER, analyzing its convergence properties and the impact of a specific variance reduction method on parameter estimation. These theoretical findings offer valuable guidance for practical applications. The code is accessible at https://github.com/ChenYi2000/VRPO-ER.

The superbosonization technique extends the conventional Hubbard-Stratonovich transformation by employing Grassian supermatrices. This approach has proven highly effective in recent studies of the random matrix ensemble featuring the second type of analyticity. In this study, we compare two methods for calculating the average resolvent of the chiral Gaussian unitary ensemble (chGUE): the generalized Hubbard-Stratonovich transformation and the superbosonization formula. The superbosonization method yields a more compact expression, whereas the superbosonization formula is more intuitive. Both approaches yield identical results, confirming the validity of the superbosonization formula. Additionally, we demonstrate that the average resolvent can be derived from the average characteristic polynomial of chGUE. Finally, we discuss the potential of the superbosonization method for future research. This document serves as a tutorial on superbosonization. Spatiotemporal predictive learning is a critical research area with extensive applications in computer vision and computer graphics. However, current methods often overlook the fine-grained spatiotemporal details of motion, which are essential for generating high-quality predictions. To address this, we introduce a motion detail-aware learning framework called MoDeRNN. This approach employs a multi-level detail decomposition strategy to represent motion details at both coarse and fine granularities. Furthermore, we propose a multi-level detail reconstruction module that utilizes a coarse-to-fine strategy to recover these details from latent features, ensuring the motion details are preserved and aligned within the generated output. Additionally, the framework incorporates a detail consistency loss to enhance the quality of the predicted motion. Extensive experiments on two prominent public datasets demonstrate that MoDeRNN significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods in both qualitative and quantitative assessments. This paper introduces Josephine, a new memory management system designed to bridge the capabilities of garbage collection and ownership. Garbage collection ensures safe memory access by tracking the lifetimes of high-level language values, while recent Rust editions achieve similar safety through compile-time analysis of expression types. Although garbage collection traditionally incurs runtime overhead, garbage-free systems like Josephine retain this benefit by executing the tracking at runtime within garbage collectors. Josephine is implemented in C and C++, though the approach is language-agnostic. We demonstrate Josephine's feasibility through a detailed design, a formal model, and an implementation. Our model proves that Josephine can safely eliminate garbage collection overhead, and our implementation validates the feasibility of this optimization. Furthermore, we show that Josephine can dynamically select between garbage collection and optimization based on runtime conditions. This flexibility enables Josephine to outperform standard garbage collectors in both throughput and latency. To our knowledge, this is the first time such performance gains have been achieved. Our implementation comprises 1,500 lines of code, and we have integrated it into V8, the core of the Chrome browser, where it successfully optimizes memory usage for various JavaScript programs. This is the first time a JavaScript engine has demonstrated the ability to reduce memory consumption by 10% to 40% without any performance penalty. Additionally, Josephine can be toggled on or off by Chrome developers to enable or disable garbage collection as needed. We believe Josephine offers a novel method for garbage collectors to adapt to runtime conditions, thereby enhancing their efficiency. This work was conducted in collaboration with Chrome. We demonstrate that neutrinoless double-beta decay occurring within a collider presents an extended framework for investigating this phenomenon. In this regime, the process involves the production of heavy sterile neutrinos, which subsequently trigger the neutrinoless decay. We establish a comprehensive framework to analyze this mechanism and show that the resulting rate is governed by the interference between the Standard Model amplitudes of e+e- and W boson pair production and the contributions from heavy sterile neutrinos. This study underscores the significance of collider-based searches for neutrinoless double-beta decay and emphasizes the necessity of combining these experimental approaches with both accelerator and beta-decay studies of light sterile neutrinos. Furthermore, we outline the experimental requirements needed to explore this intriguing and potentially groundbreaking channel at the High-Luminosity LHC. Finally, we examine the potential of future high-energy colliders to investigate this phenomenon through the production of heavy sterile neutrinos. Our findings indicate that an HL-LHC with an integrated luminosity of 30 ab-1 could probe effective Majorana masses up to 100 eV, surpassing the sensitivity of next-generation beta-decay experiments. Additionally, we note that a future 100 TeV collider could probe effective masses reaching approximately 1 TeV. These results provide crucial guidance for upcoming experimental endeavors. In conclusion, we stress that neutrinoless double-beta decay in a collider offers a unique and complementary avenue for investigating neutrino nature, particularly in the context of sterile neutrinos. This approach is expected to play a pivotal role in the ongoing quest to determine whether neutrinos are Dirac or Majorana fermions. Our findings advocate for the inclusion of neutrinoless double-beta decay in the physics program of future colliders. We anticipate that the discovery of this phenomenon at a collider will open a new era in the investigation of neutrino properties. Such findings will necessitate a thorough re-evaluation of the theoretical framework and a complete re-examination of the entire body of experimental data. This will ultimately lead to a comprehensive understanding of the true nature of neutrinos. Such discoveries will undoubtedly have far-reaching implications for our comprehension of the universe. In the meantime, we hope that the proposed study of neutrinoless double-beta decay at colliders will be seriously considered and implemented. This work introduces a method for list decoding the polar codes of any length $N=2^u$ under a binary erasure channel (BEC) with erasure probability $\epsilon$, by integrating belief propagation (BP) list decoding with polar subcodes. The proposed algorithm begins by decomposing the polar code into polar subcodes of varying lengths. It then applies a recently developed BP list decoder specifically designed for polar codes of lengths $N=2^w$ where $w \leq u-1$. By integrating these subcode decoders and supplementing them with a tailored procedure for polar subcodes of lengths $N=2^w$ where $w \geq u-1$ (which utilizes standard polar subcode decoding), the algorithm generates a list of decoded messages. The size of this list is bounded by $2^{u(1-\epsilon^2)}$, which closely aligns with the polar coding bound of $2^{N(1-\epsilon^2)}$. Furthermore, the average decoding delay exhibits a sublinear relationship with the code length $N$. Numerical simulations conducted on the symmetric channels of the binary, ternary, and quaternary erasure channels demonstrate that the average decoding delay scales sublinearly with the code length across all three scenarios. Additionally, the results indicate that the sublinear complexity of the polar subcode decoders diminishes as the channel erasure probability decreases. Finally, the paper offers a comprehensive analysis of the algorithm's computational complexity and average decoding delay. The proposed approach is implemented in MATLAB, and a user-friendly interface is available at the following link: https://github.com/abdoalsharji/PolarSubcodeDecoder. This tool supports list decoding polar codes of any length under a BEC. The source code is open-source, allowing users to select any desired code length for decoding. The tool supports polar codes of lengths $N=2,4,8,16,32,64,128,256,512,1024,2048,4096,8192,16384,32768,65536,131072,262144,524288,1048576$. This study examines the point spread function (PSF) in coadded images generated by the Legacy Survey of Space and Time (LSST) and the Euclid satellite. We establish a straightforward and dependable approach for modeling the PSF of image stacks by analyzing the individual PSFs of the constituent images. Our findings indicate that the PSF of a stack is well-described by a Gaussian kernel, whose size is derived from the Gaussian components of the PSF models for each individual science camera. This model proves highly accurate for LSST stack simulations and remains applicable to Euclid, despite the satellite's non-Gaussian PSF characteristics. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the precision of PSF modeling for stacked images is superior to that of single exposures. These results are particularly significant for LSST, as they show that PSF modeling accuracy in final coadded images is independent of the number of exposures included in the stack. Consequently, this enables the use of a single PSF model for all coadded images, thereby streamlining the photometric pipeline. Additionally, we observe that PSF modeling accuracy improves as the stack size grows, a trend that is more pronounced in Euclid stacks compared to LSST stacks. This enhanced accuracy is crucial for Euclid, where high precision is essential for the photometric analysis of weak gravitational lensing. The methods presented here are implemented in the `psfutil` Python package, which is available on GitHub. The package includes a suite of functions for modeling PSFs in LSST stack images and is designed to be easily adaptable for Euclid. The `psfutil` package can be installed via pip. We encourage the Euclid photometric pipeline to adopt the methods described in this paper. This study theoretically examines the fracture toughness of crystalline solids, focusing on the influence of dislocation nucleation and propagation. We demonstrate that the theoretical fracture toughness is governed by the energy required to create new surfaces, the energy needed to nucleate a dislocation, and the energy associated with the dislocation's Burgers vector. Our findings indicate that the transition between dislocation-controlled and toughness-controlled regimes is influenced by the sample size and the specific geometry of the crack tip. Additionally, we observe that the theoretical threshold stress for brittle-ductile transition can be lowered by incorporating crystallographic anisotropy and non-hydrostatic stresses. Finally, we illustrate how these theoretical predictions can be applied to analyze the fracture toughness of various crystalline materials. These results offer a more precise framework for understanding the ductile-to-brittle transition in crystalline solids and can guide the design of materials with enhanced toughness. Furthermore, the proposed theoretical model is versatile and can be readily extended to investigate other fracture-related phenomena in crystalline materials, such as the ductile-to-brittle transition in nanoparticles and the effects of temperature and strain rate. This work investigates the probabilistic framework of a gas consisting of $N+2$ Schottky boundary conformal field theory (CFT) particles and $N$ Gaudin Schottky boundary conformal particles within the strip domain $\mathbb{H} = \mathbb{R} \times (0,1)$. The $N+2$ Schottky particles are fixed at positions $-1$ and $1$, along with $z_1, \ldots, z_N \in (0,1)$, while the $N$ movable Gaudin particles occupy locations $w_1, \ldots, w_N \in (0,1)$. The associated partition function is defined as $Z_{\mathfrak{g}}(z_1, \ldots, z_N; w_1, \ldots, w_N) = \langle e^{\xi(w_1) + \cdots + \xi(w_N)} \rangle_{\mathfrak{g}}$, where $\xi$ denotes a Gaussian free field (GFF) coupled with the conformal field $\phi$ and the logarithmic interaction fields $\psi_{\pm}$. This field configuration generates a stochastic process known as a stochastic log-gas, which yields $N$ multiple Schramm-Loewner evolutions (SLEs), denoted $\eta_1, \ldots, \eta_N$, originating from $w_1, \ldots, w_N$ and terminating at the imaginary axis. The primary objective of this paper is to demonstrate that the distribution of these multiple SLEs is independent of the specific values of $z_1, \ldots, z_N$. Consequently, the resulting collection of random curves constitutes a multiple SLE driven by a stochastic log-gas, a concept we term a "stochastic Schottky log-gas." This construction extends the concept of multiple radial SLEs driven by a log-gas, previously introduced by C. Hong and X. Sun in \cite{HS20}, to the half-plane setting. Furthermore, the multiple SLE generated by the stochastic log-gas exhibits invariance under the action of the real orthogonal group $O(2)$, a symmetry that is notably absent in the case of multiple radial SLEs. We establish that the distribution of the multiple SLEs is invariant under $O(2)$ transformations and derive the corresponding SLE differential equation.

This paper establishes a priori estimates for the Navier-Stokes equations with periodic initial data, expressing solution norms in the maximum norm using initial data norms. The proof relies on the Gronwall inequality and an $L^p$-estimate derived from the solution's integral representation. These findings are applicable to both the Cauchy problem and the scenario with periodic initial data. Furthermore, the study demonstrates that certain solutions remain bounded for all time and decays to zero as $|t|$ approaches infinity. This research represents a significant advancement in the theory of the Navier-Stokes equations, addressing a longstanding open question. Additionally, the methodology employed can be utilized to derive analogous results for other systems of partial differential equations. We introduce a quantum algorithm that enables a classical verifier to delegate the execution of a $T$-step quantum computation on $n$ qubits, where $T = \Omega(n)$, by performing only $O(T)$ classical interactions. This approach relies on a novel $n$-qubit code with distance $d = \Omega(\log n)$, which is amenable to $O(1)$-qubit syndrome measurements and supports the preparation of the code space with high probability. We demonstrate that the failure probability of this code space preparation can be mitigated to a constant using standard techniques. Furthermore, we establish that the code can correct any single error, including erasures, and that the constant failure rate can be further lowered to $1/T$ through repeated attempts. By integrating these error correction capabilities with interactive proof techniques, we achieve a classical verification process limited to $O(T)$ interactions and a constant failure probability. This result surpasses the $O(T \log T)$ interactions required by the approach of Fitzsimons, Fang, and Liu [arXiv:2009.00010]. Additionally, we extend our method to handle erasures, showing that the verifier interacts with the quantum prover at most $O(T)$ times with a constant failure probability. Our findings are applicable to various scenarios, including the delegation of quantum algorithms with $T = \Omega(n)$, the classical verification of quantum circuits of size $T$, and the classical verification of quantum states. In these contexts, the quantum prover executes $T$ operations on $n$ qubits using $O(T)$ classical queries to the prover's internal state. Our work also yields a new, efficient classical interactive proof system for $n$-qubit quantum states with distance $d = \Omega(\log n)$. This system utilizes $O(1)$-qubit syndromes and achieves $n$-qubit state preparation with a failure probability of $2^{-\Omega(\log n)}$. Finally, we demonstrate that our code can be implemented using $n$-qubit stabilizer states with distance $d = \Omega(\log n)$ and linear entanglement depth, a feature that may prove valuable for future research. Blockchain technology is increasingly recognized as a promising solution for enhancing transparency and traceability within the food supply chain. This paper introduces a novel blockchain architecture designed to manage the growing number of IoT devices involved in such systems. The proposed architecture employs smart contracts to automate the registration of new IoT devices and restrict their interactions to the blockchain environment. Furthermore, oracles are utilized to facilitate communication between the IoT layer and the blockchain layer. The architecture's efficacy is demonstrated through a practical application: managing a food supply chain. Additionally, the study evaluates the architecture's performance regarding throughput, transaction delay, and energy consumption. The results indicate that the proposed architecture outperforms both basic and advanced solutions in these areas. Finally, the paper outlines potential future research directions. Specifically, it suggests that future work could explore alternative solutions to oracles, such as utilizing IoT devices with sufficient computational power to validate and verify data, thereby reducing the reliance on cloud-based oracles. Additionally, the impact of the blockchain's consensus mechanism on the architecture's performance should be investigated. For instance, the proof-of-work mechanism, while effective for security, is not well-suited for resource-constrained IoT devices. Consequently, investigating alternative mechanisms like proof-of-stake is recommended. Furthermore, the potential of integrating machine learning with blockchain to improve security and efficiency is an area worthy of future research. We present early James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) observations of a sample containing 11 infrared-luminous, optically faint galaxies at redshifts $z\sim 1-3$, selected from the Hubble Space Telescope's CANDELS survey. These galaxies exhibit near-infrared luminosity functions that are approximately 1.5 dex fainter than those of Luminous Galaxies (LGs) at the same redshift. Our analysis reveals that the majority of these objects are strongly star-forming systems, with star formation rates (SFR) ranging from 10 to 100 $M_{\odot}$ yr$^{-1}$, and are predominantly classified as starbursts. Their stellar masses fall between $10^{9}$ and $10^{10}$ $M_{\odot}$, indicating that these LGs represent a population of low-mass, starbursting galaxies that are significantly more common than previously recognized. The observed star formation rates align with the star-forming main sequence (SFMS) at their respective redshifts, and their star formation rates relative to stellar mass (SFR/M*) are roughly 1.5 dex higher than LGs at the same redshift. Furthermore, the specific star formation rates (SSFR) of these LGs are comparable to those of LGs at the same redshift, suggesting that these galaxies are not in a transitional phase of evolution. The rest-frame optical colors of these objects are redder than LGs at identical redshifts, implying that LGs may be more evolved than previously thought. Finally, JWST imaging indicates that these galaxies are likely undergoing major mergers, a conclusion supported by their high gas fractions and low dust attenuation. These findings suggest that LGs are a distinct population of low-mass, starbursting galaxies that are more prevalent than earlier studies indicated. Additionally, we propose that the CANDELS field may be missing a population of infrared-bright, optically-faint galaxies due to the limited depth of its near-infrared imaging. This study underscores the necessity of JWST's superior sensitivity to uncover the true nature of these previously elusive galaxies. This study examines the jammed configurations of two types of disks with differing sizes and masses arranged in alternating sequences within a channel. We analyze the jammed density across various ratios of disk size and aspect ratio, comparing results for channels constrained by periodic boundary conditions versus those subject to repulsive walls. Our findings indicate that channel length significantly influences jammed density in the small disk regime under periodic boundary conditions. Furthermore, we observe that channel length effects are more pronounced when disks are nearly square, particularly for the periodic boundary condition case. Finally, we identify a distinct transition in jammed density as a function of disk size and aspect ratio, which is more evident in jammed sequences than in random mixtures. These results are supported by simulations and visualizations of representative jammed states. Additionally, we present a theoretical framework to explain the observed phenomena. This work extends our earlier research on randomly mixed disks of varying sizes and shapes, offering deeper insights into the physics governing jammed systems with polydisperse disk populations. Ultimately, our findings provide a foundation for future investigations into jammed systems involving polydisperse particles of diverse shapes. This study examines how distinct flavors of the El Niño-Southern Oscillation (ENSO) affect seasonal precipitation extremes across the Americas, Africa, and Australia. By analyzing observational data, we identify specific regions where very low or high seasonal precipitation occurs more or less frequently during El Niño years compared to neutral conditions. These areas are defined by a precipitation anomaly threshold of 20% and a statistical significance of p < 0.05. We observe that the regions most affected by the Southern Hemisphere's warm phase of ENSO (Niño34) differ from those influenced by the Northern Hemisphere's warm phase (Niño3). Furthermore, the regions responding to El Niño events show distinct patterns. The spatial distribution of these regions influenced by the three primary ENSO flavors shows limited overlap, indicating that the regions most susceptible to the warm phase of Niño3 or Niño3.4 are largely independent of the El Niño event. Additionally, the regions experiencing very low seasonal precipitation are not identical to those facing very high seasonal precipitation. These findings suggest that the mechanisms driving the impacts of El Niño on precipitation extremes are complex and likely vary across different regions. These results are derived from a new global dataset of seasonal precipitation extremes, which is available for research purposes. The concept of non-affine displacement, which quantifies the deviation of local particle motion from a uniform strain field, has been widely employed to investigate the dynamics of supercooled liquids and glasses. This study demonstrates that optical scattering experiments can directly measure the spatial correlation of the root mean square of the non-affine displacement, denoted as $\overline{u_N^2}(r)$, within a glass former near its glass transition. Specifically, we show that the radial dependence of $\overline{u_N^2}(r)$ observed in the scattered light intensity offers direct insight into the microscopic origin of the anomalous rheological behavior characteristic of these materials. Our findings indicate that the peak in $\overline{u_N^2}(r)$, which marks the length scale of non-affine expansion, shifts toward larger radii as the system approaches the glass transition. This trend aligns with the growth of the dynamic correlation length, thereby supporting the hypothesis that the non-affine expansion originates from regions of locally enhanced mobility. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the position of this peak in $\overline{u_N^2}(r)$ exhibits a linear relationship with the inverse of the scattered light intensity, a result that corroborates the dynamic heterogeneity hypothesis. These results are validated through both computer simulations and experimental data. Our findings underscore the potential of light scattering as a direct method for probing non-affine expansion in glass formers. Additionally, the radial profile of $\overline{u_N^2}(r)$ displays qualitative differences between fragile and strong glass formers, a distinction that mirrors the variations seen in the angular dependence of scattered light intensity. These observations reinforce the hypothesis that the non-local nature of non-affine expansion is more pronounced in fragile glass formers. Finally, we discuss the implications of these findings for the understanding of the glass transition. The manuscript includes supplementary material. We employ the S66 benchmark dataset, which includes 11 molecular dimers, to investigate how these interactions evolve under field exposure. Our analysis utilizes the CCSD(T)/aug-cc-pVQZ method for high-level energy calculations and the CCSD(T)/aug-cc-pVTZ/MP2/cc-pVTZ method for the corresponding density functional theory (DFT) approach. The DFT methods employed are B3LYP, M06-2X, and $\omega$B97X-D. Results indicate that the B3LYP method yields the most accurate outcomes when assessing the effects of external electric fields on dimers. Furthermore, we observe that the electric field influences both the equilibrium geometry and the interaction energy of the dimers. Finally, we demonstrate that the magnitude of this effect varies depending on the specific dimer involved. These findings are significant for understanding how external electric fields alter the behavior of molecular dimers. Additionally, this research holds relevance for applications involving molecular assembly and the design of molecular switches. The accompanying paper provides a Python script to calculate the energy changes of the S66 dimers under external electric fields. This script is written in Python and utilizes the PySCF package for quantum chemistry calculations. The script can be easily modified to accommodate different molecular systems and basis sets. We anticipate that this resource will be valuable to researchers studying the effects of external electric fields on molecular systems. The PySCF package is a powerful and versatile tool for quantum chemistry calculations, offering a wide range of methods and basis sets. Its user-friendly interface and extensive documentation make it an ideal choice for both novice and experienced users. We hope that this resource will assist researchers in their quantum chemistry calculations. Overall, this research contributes to our understanding of how external electric fields affect molecular dimers and provides valuable resources for future studies in this area. The Python script can be easily adapted for use with other molecular systems, and the PySCF package offers a wide range of methods and basis sets for quantum chemistry calculations. We believe that this resource will be highly beneficial to researchers in the field. The external electric fields studied in this work are relevant to various applications, including the design of molecular machines and the study of charge transfer processes. The findings of this study can contribute to our understanding of how external electric fields affect molecular dimers and can be used to predict the behavior of these systems under different conditions. The Fourth Industrial Revolution is characterized by the convergence of physical and digital technologies, fostering a highly interconnected industrial ecosystem. This integration facilitates the seamless exchange of data across all industrial stages, enabling real-time data-driven decision-making. However, inherent data incompleteness and the dynamic nature of industrial environments introduce uncertainties that are difficult to quantify precisely. Consequently, non-deterministic approaches are essential for modeling these uncertainties. This study examines the applicability of probabilistic, fuzzy, and non-deterministic robust models in industrial contexts, utilizing a stochastic capacitated project scheduling problem as a case study. The analysis compares these methods to evaluate their strengths and limitations. The findings indicate that non-deterministic approaches offer greater generality and flexibility, making them particularly well-suited for industrial applications. Furthermore, the study underscores the critical role of uncertainty modeling in Industry 4.0 and proposes that future research should focus on developing hybrid approaches that leverage the advantages of probabilistic, fuzzy, and non-deterministic frameworks. To support this direction, the paper also outlines potential strategies for integrating these diverse methods. Ultimately, this work aims to stimulate further investigation into hybrid modeling techniques. The associated Python code is accessible at: https://github.com/ahmedhassan1990/Non-deterministic-uncertainty-modelling. Supplementary materials can be found at: https://doi.org/10.6084/m9.figshare.14800008. Keywords: Industry 4.0; uncertainty; stochastic; fuzzy; non-deterministic; data-driven decision making.

This paper introduces a resilience formulation for cyber-physical systems (CPS) utilizing Signal Temporal Logic (STL). We propose a resilient robustness metric that evaluates how well a system's trajectory adheres to a specification under the influence of disturbances. Furthermore, we translate this metric into a Mixed-Integer Linear Program (MILP) to optimize resilient trajectories for a given dynamical system under disturbance effects. The approach is validated through a numerical case study. The accompanying code is accessible at https://github.com/ashishkumar1234/CPS-Resilience.

Keywords: Cyber-Physical Systems, Resilience, Signal Temporal Logic, Robustness, Disturbances.

Dark matter remains one of physics' most significant unresolved mysteries. While the leading candidate is the cold, weakly interacting massive particle (WIMP), numerous alternative hypotheses have been suggested, including ultralight scalar fields that interact with standard matter via scalar forces. These forces can generate minute, transient shifts in local gravity, potentially causing measurable accelerations in nearby free-falling objects. A proposed experimental strategy involves deploying a global network of accelerometers to detect these events. This study outlines the theoretical framework for such searches, deriving the signature of scalar field interactions and examining the feasibility of observing it. We demonstrate that a global network comprising roughly 100 accelerometers could achieve sensitivity to established theories within a few years. Furthermore, we identify specific targets for future experiments, such as the proposed Superconducting Gravity Gradiometer Network (SGGNet) in South Korea and the Space-Based Atomic Interferometer Constellation (SBAC) in Low Earth Orbit. We also address key technical challenges, particularly the need for high-precision accelerometers and the development of robust data analysis techniques. Although this approach demands substantial resources, it offers a promising avenue for advancing the search for dark matter. Ultimately, we argue that a global accelerometer network should be considered as a complementary method to direct WIMP detection experiments. This initiative would not only drive technological innovation but also make a substantial contribution to unraveling the nature of dark matter. We have made the source code for our analysis tools publicly available to facilitate this endeavor. Our findings are detailed in the paper "Scalar field dark matter searches using a global network of accelerometers," which can be accessed at https://arxiv.org/abs/2201.06001. The corresponding source code is available at https://github.com/sggnet/scalar-dm-search. Additional details regarding the analysis code can be found in our forthcoming publication, "Analysis of scalar field dark matter signatures using SGGNet," available at https://arxiv.org/abs/2201.06002. The SGGNet project is accessible at https://sggnet.org. Furthermore, we have established a dedicated GitHub repository dedicated to dark matter searches using free-falling objects, which can be found at https://github.com/sggnet/darkmatter. This repository includes a Python package named `scalar_dm_search`, available at https://github.com/sggnet/scalar_dm_search. The package features a module called `transient_gravity`, which contains the functions utilized in our analysis

The origin of compact, faint radio sources remains uncertain, with various theories suggesting they could be young or low-luminosity active galactic nuclei (AGN), star-forming galaxies, or radio galaxies viewed face-on. This study investigates the characteristics of these sources by stacking images of individual sources within radio galaxies. We analyzed a sample of 100 radio galaxies with redshifts $z<0.05$ and a median redshift of 0.02, selected from the 1.4 GHz VLA FIRST survey. Our results indicate that the mean stacked images of the most compact sources (smaller than 0.1 arcsec) are generally featureless and resemble thermal emission, with a mean brightness temperature of $T_{\rm mean} = 1.1 \pm 0.1$ K and a spectral index of $\alpha = -0.1 \pm 0.1$. In contrast, the mean images of more extended sources (larger than 0.1 arcsec) display a double-lobed morphology typical of AGN, characterized by a steeper spectral index of $\alpha = -0.6 \pm 0.1$. Furthermore, the spectral index of the most compact sources varies with redshift, suggesting that these sources are not a single population. We propose that the most compact sources represent a distinct population of young, low-luminosity AGN, while the more extended sources align with the morphology and spectral properties of standard radio galaxies. This finding supports the hypothesis that young, low-luminosity AGN are generally compact and faint. Additionally, we demonstrate that the spectral index of the most compact sources is consistent with the mean spectral index of radio galaxies, implying that the majority of radio galaxies may harbor a central, compact, low-luminosity AGN. Finally, we show that the mean image of the most compact sources is statistically indistinguishable from a Gaussian distribution, indicating that the sample is homogeneous. These results suggest that the most compact sources are either a single population or a mixture of populations with similar mean properties. We conclude that the mean image of the most compact sources is likely representative of the average young, low-luminosity AGN. The paper is available at https://arxiv.org/abs/2101.00010. Hidden Markov Models (HMMs) are extensively utilized to model information flow within stochastic systems. This paper introduces a non-standard extension of HMMs that allows for the quantitative analysis of information flow in both stochastic and deterministic systems. We demonstrate that the conditional distortion measure, which captures an observer's information gain regarding a hidden state based on system outputs, can be derived from a specific combinatorial operation on probability distributions. This operation is recognized in categorical probability theory as the "conditional expectation monad." Furthermore, we establish that the measures generated by our extended HMM framework align with those produced by an alternative method for quantitative information flow, which utilizes conditional distortion distributions. This method is notable for being the sole existing approach that supports a compositional analysis of information flow. Our findings suggest that the "conditional expectation monad" offers a promising pathway for future research into compositional information flow. Additionally, we provide a non-trivial example of a stochastic system to illustrate the method. This example involves a system that, with a probability of 0.5, leaks a single bit of information about its internal state through its outputs. We show that this system can be analyzed to prove that the information it leaks is independent of the observer's prior knowledge. Finally, we discuss the challenges and future directions for applying our framework to more complex systems. Specifically, we highlight that the current method relies on an exact, albeit computationally intensive, calculation of the conditional distortion distribution. We argue that future research should focus on developing approximate methods to make the approach more practical. This could involve either approximating the conditional distortion distribution directly or approximating the conditional expectation monad, which is known to yield accurate results in various contexts. We believe that such approximations would enable the application of our framework to a broader range of real-world systems. Ultimately, we hope that this paper will inspire further research into the application of the conditional expectation monad to information flow analysis. By doing so, we aim to advance the field towards a more compositional and modular understanding of how information is generated, transformed, and consumed. We believe that this more abstract and modular perspective will be essential for achieving a deeper understanding of information flow in complex systems. In summary, this paper presents a novel framework for analyzing information flow in stochastic systems, with the potential to significantly impact future research in the field. By providing a more abstract and modular perspective, we hope to inspire new avenues of inquiry and contribute to a more comprehensive understanding of how information flows in complex systems. This study presents an analysis of the statistical characteristics of the two-dimensional Burgers equation, which incorporates a stochastic nonlinear term. The methodology relies on the concept of statistical nonlocality, a framework for analyzing the impact of nonlinear dynamics on the probability density function (PDF) of a system's state. We demonstrate that the equations governing the evolution of the PDF for the Burgers equation can be derived exactly and solved analytically. Furthermore, we provide a precise characterization of the equation's solutions, revealing the emergence of self-similar solutions and front-like structures. The paper concludes with a discussion of the Burgers equation's dynamics and its potential applications. These applications include the development of a novel approach to the statistical theory of turbulence, as well as the design of new neural network architectures for solving partial differential equations. The latter is specifically highlighted as a promising tool for addressing inverse problems in fluid dynamics. Additionally, the statistical analysis of the Burgers equation serves as a foundational step toward developing a statistical theory for the Navier-Stokes equations. The work also examines the statistical properties of a generalized Burgers equation, which models the dynamics of a statistically nonlocal system. This generalization is defined by the presence of a nonlinear term that depends on the system's state through a nonlinear integral operator. We show that the statistical evolution equation for such systems can be derived exactly and solved analytically, yielding self-similar solutions. Finally, the paper discusses the application of this methodology to the generalized Burgers equation, which models the behavior of a statistically nonlocal fluid. This model is shown to describe the interaction between two fluids with distinct densities and viscosities. The resulting statistical theory of the two-fluid system is demonstrated to be equivalent to the classical model of two-dimensional hydrodynamics. The paper concludes with a discussion of the statistical properties of the two-fluid system and its applications in the statistical theory of two-dimensional hydrodynamics. This review examines recent experimental and theoretical advancements in the phenomenology of elastic scattering. It focuses on the analysis of the hadrodynamic regime, characterized by high multiplicities and transverse momenta, as well as the low particle yield regime, which is influenced by the properties of the produced source. The text also explores the application of the Glauber model, the Glauber-Gribov framework, and the Eikonal model. Furthermore, it addresses the description of the Coulomb-Nuclear Interference (CNI) region and the phenomena of shadowing and diffraction dissociation. The discussion is grounded in data from major experiments, including those at the LHC, RHIC, and various fixed-target facilities. Additionally, it explores the potential of utilizing elastic scattering as a tool for investigating the spatial distribution of participants and spectators. Finally, the review addresses the relationship between the elastic scattering amplitude and the proton radius. This material is intended for physicists specializing in nuclear and hadronic physics. This paper investigates how electromagnetic radiation emitted by a blackbody is modified by the Casimir effect. We demonstrate that applying the first law of thermodynamics to this system yields an equation of state that differs from the standard Stefan-Boltzmann law. Specifically, we examine the scenario where two perfectly reflecting parallel plates enclose the blackbody cavity, and we explore the thermodynamic properties of the resulting radiated field. Our findings indicate that the field's temperature is no longer uniform throughout the cavity. Furthermore, we observe that the temperature gradient becomes infinite at a specific distance between the plates, marking the point where the system reaches its maximum efficiency. Finally, we discuss the implications of these results for the blackhole-cavity analogy. This study is the first in a series; subsequent papers will explore the influence of the electron's magnetic moment and analyze the thermodynamics of the resulting radiation field. Additionally, future work will examine how the radiation field is altered by the geometry of the blackbody cavity. In this context, we will analyze the radiation emitted by a blackbody situated within a spherical cavity. We anticipate that the radiation field in this configuration will exhibit both radial and angular temperature gradients. This research is conducted under the framework of the Casimir effect, which is widely regarded as the most precise experimental verification of quantum field theory. Consequently, this field has attracted significant interest from both experimentalists and theorists. Our work aims to contribute to this area of research. We believe that investigating the thermodynamics of electromagnetic fields within a blackbody cavity influenced by the Casimir effect holds both theoretical and practical value. From a theoretical perspective, this approach offers a novel method for studying blackbody thermodynamics. From a practical standpoint, the findings may have applications in the design of devices intended to manipulate electromagnetic fields. We conclude by noting that the Casimir effect is a well-documented phenomenon, and our findings regarding the thermodynamics of electromagnetic fields in a blackbody cavity under this effect are consistent with established literature. Recent advancements in anonymization have enabled the release of location data to support research and public health initiatives. However, these data releases carry inherent privacy risks, as adversaries may exploit external information to re-identify individuals. This study investigates privacy under the assumption that attackers hold prior beliefs regarding user movement patterns, modeled as a Markov chain with a potentially unknown transition matrix. We demonstrate that privacy is compromised when the transition matrix is estimated using an improper uniform prior. Conversely, we prove that a proper conditional prior—derived from the Markov transition model—guarantees privacy by ensuring data leakage remains bounded. Furthermore, we introduce a novel anonymization technique that minimizes the loss of data utility while maintaining this safety assurance. Our experimental results indicate that the proposed method achieves superior performance compared to existing approaches. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/abhishekkumar123/CTP. Additionally, the experimental dataset can be downloaded from https://github.com/abhishekkumar123/CTP/tree/master/data. The paper is available at https://arxiv.org/abs/2101.01001. This paper introduces NDT-Transformer, a new network designed for localizing 3D point clouds. It utilizes the Normal Distribution Transform (NDT) to convert raw 3D point clouds into a grid-based NDT representation, which is then fed into a Transformer encoder-decoder architecture. Transformer networks have recently demonstrated superior performance in various 3D deep learning applications, including point cloud segmentation and object detection. By leveraging the NDT representation, NDT-Transformer achieves state-of-the-art results on two prominent 3D localization benchmarks: KITTI and OpenScene. Furthermore, ablation studies reveal that NDT-Transformer outperforms other 3D localization methods when trained on limited data. Resting-state functional MRI (rs-fMRI) connectivity analysis is a widely used method for investigating brain function. Although it has successfully identified key neural mechanisms in conditions like schizophrenia and depression, it has also yielded inconsistent results. This discrepancy may stem from the inherent noise in the data, which can be mitigated by aggregating data across multiple scanning sites. However, the optimal number of sites to combine remains unclear. This study addresses this uncertainty by evaluating the gain in statistical power, prediction accuracy, and reproducibility achieved by pooling rs-fMRI data from up to 100 sites. We applied a connectivity-based predictive modeling framework to a large, open-access rs-fMRI dataset to examine classification performance and prediction accuracy. Our results indicate that combining data from 20 to 30 sites yields substantial improvements in statistical power and prediction accuracy. Furthermore, we observed a significant increase in reproducibility when pooling data from sites with similar scanner models. These findings suggest that, whenever feasible, it is advisable to combine data from at least 20 sites to maximize statistical power and prediction accuracy. Additionally, we provide a practical tool to assist researchers in selecting the appropriate number of sites to pool for their specific research goals. The code used in this study is available at https://github.com/NeurodataLab/rsfMRI_power.
