This study examines a non-local grazing model for dry-land vegetation, where predator mortality relies on a weighted average of plant biomass across the entire domain. Our primary objective is to demonstrate that, under specific conditions, this grazing strategy stabilizes an otherwise unstable homogeneous state. We show that for a broad spectrum of predator mortality rates, a Turing-type instability emerges in the spatially extended system, causing vegetation self-organization into either spotted or striped patterns. Furthermore, we find that this instability is more readily triggered in the non-local model compared to the local reaction-diffusion system, provided the local grazing intensity is low. These findings suggest that implementing non-local grazing in semi-arid ecosystems could be a viable method for promoting the spontaneous formation of diverse vegetation patterns. Finally, we validate these results by analyzing satellite imagery from a real-world dry-land ecosystem, revealing that certain observed patterns align well with the model's predictions. Additionally, we identify specific parameter regimes where the model successfully predicts patterns detected in the field. These outcomes underscore the potential of mathematical modeling to enhance our understanding of natural ecosystems and support the design of effective management strategies. Our results also highlight the existence of a wide range of grazing regimes capable of inducing pattern formation, thereby offering new insights into the mechanisms driving the emergence of these structures. Finally, we discuss the broader implications of these findings for future research and potential applications. CountSketch is a widely used dimensionality reduction technique designed to estimate the tails of the empirical distribution for heavy-tailed streams. This method projects high-dimensional vectors into a lower dimension, allowing for the computation of approximate quantiles. However, the theoretical analysis of CountSketch typically relies on the assumption that input vectors are chosen independently of the projection. In this work, we investigate the algorithm's behavior when input vectors are adapted based on previous outputs. We demonstrate that the algorithm fails in such scenarios by constructing a specific instance where the empirical $\alpha$-tail deviates significantly from the true distribution. Furthermore, we provide a more general counterexample applicable to any linear dimensionality reduction method that uses random Gaussian vectors for projection. Finally, we propose a straightforward modification to CountSketch that ensures consistent estimation even with adaptive inputs. We also present a general framework for analyzing linear aggregation algorithms on heavy-tailed data and establish a lower bound on the sample complexity for any algorithm attempting to estimate quantiles under adaptive conditions. Our modified CountSketch achieves an optimal sample complexity of $O(n^{(\alpha-1)/\alpha})$ for estimating the $p$-quantile, where $n$ represents the number of samples and $1 < \alpha \leq 2$ denotes the tail index of the underlying distribution. Additionally, we extend this result to the case of multiple estimators. Our proposed algorithm surpasses the lower bound established for general linear aggregation methods and outperforms prior approaches designed for adaptive inputs. Experimental results indicate that our method also maintains strong performance when inputs are independent. The code is publicly accessible at https://github.com/ashwinb/robust-countsketch. This paper examines a seller utilizing an intermediary to market a single unit of a good to a potential buyer. The intermediary, who possesses private information about the buyer's valuation, can either truthfully disclose this information or fabricate a false one. The seller is uncertain whether the intermediary will choose to lie. We analyze the seller's optimal revenue-maximizing strategy, which involves selecting a price for the intermediary to set and a price to set directly in the event of a reported lie. Our findings indicate that a seller can secure a positive revenue even when the intermediary is a guaranteed liar, provided the seller sets an appropriately high price. Furthermore, we establish that a seller can always achieve a revenue of at least $1/4$ by setting the intermediary's price at $1$ and establishing a threshold; if a lie occurs, the seller will set a price of $2$ whenever the threshold is exceeded. We also present a family of instances demonstrating that the seller's optimal revenue can approach $1/2$. Finally, we extend our model to scenarios where the seller must sell multiple units. Our results suggest that the seller can secure a constant fraction of the optimal revenue by setting a sufficiently high price, even when the intermediary consistently lies. Additionally, we present a family of instances where the buyer's valuation follows a uniform distribution, proving that the seller's optimal revenue can be arbitrarily close to $0$. Finally, we propose a mechanism that the seller can implement to ensure a constant fraction of the optimal revenue. This paper establishes several sufficient conditions for the differentiability of an $n$-variable real-valued function, relying on the differentiability of an $(n-1)$-variable real-valued function, which are less restrictive than traditional requirements. These results are demonstrated by proving the sufficient conditions for continuous differentiability of the respective functions. To support the proofs, we utilize a lemma concerning the differentiability of real-valued functions of vector variables, an outcome that stands independently. Finally, we apply these theorems to the joint differentiability of vector functions, deriving a sufficient condition that relies on the sufficient condition for scalar functions; this new finding supersedes a previously established sufficient condition for joint continuous differentiability based on continuous differentiability of the components. Additionally, we present examples illustrating that the sufficient conditions for continuous differentiability for $n$-variable functions are not necessarily satisfied when $n$ exceeds 2. The examples further show that the sufficient conditions for the continuous differentiability of vector functions are not necessarily met when the dimension is 2, even though the continuous differentiability of the vector functions is assured. Finally, examples are provided where the sufficient conditions for scalar functions are met, yet those for vector functions are not necessarily satisfied. These findings offer a novel approach to addressing the classical problem of sufficient conditions for differentiability. The discussion concludes with suggestions for future research directions. This study introduces a computational framework designed to measure vocal entrainment within conversational pairs. By employing hidden Markov models to characterize speech rhythm, the approach extracts computational features from raw audio to capture temporal dynamics in dyadic interactions. We evaluated this method's reliability and validity through both laboratory-controlled experiments and analyses of real-world conversations. Results indicate that the metric reliably detects entrainment in synthetic scenarios and accurately distinguishes between natural entrained speech and non-entrained baselines. Furthermore, the metric demonstrates sensitivity to entrainment strength, allowing it to differentiate between conversations with varying degrees of entrainment. Finally, the approach successfully identifies shifts in entrainment that correspond to changes in interpersonal rapport. Overall, the findings suggest that this metric offers a robust tool for quantifying entrainment in dyadic conversations, with potential applications for analyzing conversational dynamics in social robotics and clinical settings. The code is publicly accessible at https://github.com/ashwinb/entrainment.

We demonstrate that the triangulated categorical control category $\lambda S_1$, constructed from the sphere $S^1$ via the lambda-construction, satisfies two key properties: first, its freely generated triangulated subcategory within $\mathrm{CPTN}$ contains all unitary matrices as a full subcategory; second, $\lambda S_1$ serves as a compact-closed monoidal category. These findings imply that any quantum control scheme achievable using only paths on $S^1$ can be simulated within this restricted resource framework. Furthermore, we outline a potential extension of $\lambda S_1$ that incorporates magnetic flux as an additional resource. This proposed construction may facilitate the simulation of control schemes that lie beyond the capabilities of $\lambda S_1$ alone. Finally, we present a categorical model for this extended construction and discuss its relation to the recently proposed path-categorical $\mathrm{Loop}_1$. Collectively, these results establish that $\lambda S_1$ represents a significant step toward a categorical framework for quantum control theory grounded in homotopy theory. Such a framework would enable the analysis of controllability and the derivation of control schemes through categorical methods. Specifically, $\lambda S_1$ functions as a quantum control category where the available resources are limited to the fundamental group $\pi_1(X) \simeq \mathbb{Z}$. This work thus provides a foundational step toward a path-categorical model for quantum control theory based on the first homotopy group. The paper is structured into three main parts: the first presents our main results, the second details the construction of $\lambda S_1$ and its properties, and the third explores the path-categorical model for quantum control theory. Additionally, an appendix addresses the relationship between $\lambda S_1$ and $\mathrm{Loop}_1$. We introduce novel exact analytical findings regarding two quasiparticle excitations within fractional quantum Hall effect wavefunctions, specifically targeting the Laughlin states for filling factors $m=3,4,5,6$ and the Moore-Romney states for $m=2,3,4$. These findings include the derivation of new exact analytical expressions for the two-quasiparticle correlation functions, alongside the calculation of previously unresolved exact values for the total energy and angular momentum. Furthermore, we resolve an ambiguity noted in the literature concerning the angular momentum of two quasiparticle excitations in Laughlin states with $m>2$. We also provide exact numerical data for the $m=2$ case, which was previously unavailable. Additionally, we compute exact values for the total energy and angular momentum of two quasihole excitations in the Moore-Romney state with $m=5$. Finally, we present numerical results for various configurations involving multiple quasiparticles. These findings are anticipated to be valuable for future investigations into quasiparticle interactions and quasiparticle-quasipholon interactions. We introduce DUVET, a survey designed to investigate how galactic outflows regulate star formation. Our strategy involves identifying a sample of star-forming disk galaxies with prominent outflows and conducting high-resolution observations of their near-UV emission to map star formation activity. We present initial findings from this effort, specifically a study of the galaxy NGC 253, which exhibits a star formation efficiency of $\sim$1.5 Gyr$^{-1}$ and a mass outflow rate of $\sim$10 M$_{\odot}$ yr$^{-1}$. By analyzing the spatial distribution of star formation and its correlation with outflows, we aim to elucidate the feedback mechanisms controlling star formation. Our results indicate that star formation is highly clumpy, with 80% of the total rate occurring in regions smaller than 1 kpc. Furthermore, we observe that the outflow is not uniform; it is driven by star-forming clumps, with the most intense clumps generating the strongest outflow. This work introduces the Synchronous Robotic Framework (SRF), a method designed to facilitate the development of synchronous robotic systems. SRF enables the creation of system components, including state machines, signal processing modules, and timers, alongside their interconnections. The framework utilizes a two-tier architecture: an upper level that manages system behavior through state machines and signal processing, and a lower level that executes these designs by synchronizing state transitions and signal propagation. We demonstrate SRF's utility through a case study of a mobile robot equipped with a manipulator, which was developed using the framework and subsequently deployed on real hardware. Furthermore, we provide an analysis of SRF's design principles, evaluation results, and a discussion of the lessons learned. The source code for SRF is accessible at https://github.com/robocup-germany/srf. This code includes a mobile robot implementation featuring a manipulator, an object recognition system, and a soccer field localization system, all of which were built using SRF. Additionally, the robot's implementation on a Jetson TX2 board was achieved using a custom CUDA implementation of SRF. The corresponding paper can be found at https://arxiv.org/abs/2006.03200. Pre-training deep neural networks on large-scale datasets is a common strategy to enhance performance on downstream tasks. While recent studies have explored various pre-training approaches for semantic segmentation, their findings remain limited. This paper investigates whether pre-training on a monocular depth estimation task yields superior results compared to a standard classification task. We evaluate several representative architectures using the KITTI depth dataset as a pre-training source before testing on the Cityscapes semantic segmentation dataset. Our results indicate that this specific pre-training method does not outperform pre-training on the CoCo classification task. Additionally, we explore a few extensions to the pre-training process, such as including a second model output and applying non-maximum suppression, which lead to marginal improvements. Overall, our study underscores the necessity of further research in large-scale self-supervised pre-training to effectively train semantic segmentation models. Kendall's tau serves as a nonparametric metric for correlation, offering robustness against outliers and applicability to unordered data. However, its primary limitation is the lack of a closed-form expression, which results in a sample complexity of $O(n^2)$ for calculating the statistic. This paper introduces a method to perform statistical inference on Kendall's tau with linear time complexity relative to the number of observations. The proposed framework encompasses tests for significance, confidence interval estimation, and hypothesis testing. Furthermore, the method is extended to handle clustered data, enabling valid inference that accounts for correlation structures. Extensive simulations and a real-world case study demonstrate that the proposed approach achieves comparable statistical power while significantly reducing computation time. The code is accessible at https://github.com/robinlambert/Efficient-inference-for-Kendalls-tau.

The rise of the Internet of Vehicles (IoV) has created a demand for intelligent, intelligent decision-making at the edge, with distributed edge intelligence offering a solution to the computational and storage limitations of individual vehicles. However, these vehicles often lack robust security and privacy safeguards. To address this, we introduce a unified framework for privacy-preserving distributed edge intelligence, integrating federated learning, secure aggregation, and differential privacy. This framework enables vehicles to collaboratively train a global model while safeguarding individual privacy. Our theoretical analysis examines the trade-off between model accuracy and privacy leakage, quantified by privacy loss. We evaluate the impact of varying numbers of participating vehicles and different privacy loss thresholds on the efficiency of distributed edge intelligence. Furthermore, we propose a novel algorithm to enhance the efficiency of distributed learning, specifically targeting the reduction of communication rounds. Simulation results demonstrate that our proposed algorithm significantly improves distributed edge intelligence by up to 40% in terms of time consumption. Additionally, we observe that increasing the number of vehicles in each communication round further boosts efficiency, though it may result in a slight decrease in model accuracy. Finally, we assess the privacy leakage of the proposed framework under various conditions, including different privacy loss levels and varying vehicle participation counts. Our findings indicate that the framework effectively protects user privacy, with model accuracy remaining above 90%. We conclude that this framework is highly effective for distributed edge intelligence in IoV scenarios. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first study to propose such a framework. We believe our work will provide valuable insights for future research in privacy-preserving distributed edge intelligence. The source code is available at: https://github.com/ChenYi1999/PP-DL. Recent studies indicate that vision transformers (ViTs) are highly effective for image recognition tasks. This paper investigates their potential within the domain of face anti-spoofing. Although ViTs demonstrate strong generalization capabilities, there is currently no research exploring zero-shot ViT applications for face anti-spoofing. We introduce a straightforward yet efficient framework designed for zero-shot face anti spoofing using ViTs. Our approach is straightforward: we fine-tune a pre-trained ViT model on a training dataset and subsequently deploy it on a target dataset without requiring any samples from that target dataset. To evaluate our method's efficacy, we conducted experiments across three distinct datasets: two training on MS1RP and three testing on LFW, CelebA, and CelebA-HQ. Our results demonstrate that the proposed framework is effective, achieving an AUC of 99.90% on the LFW dataset, 99.85% on CelebA, and 99.84% on CelebA-HQ. Furthermore, our approach surpasses state-of-the-art methods on the CelebA and CelebA-HQ datasets while maintaining the same number of parameters and computational cost. To address these limitations, we introduce a novel DRL framework designed to facilitate the development of autonomous driving systems. This framework employs a two-stage training methodology: first, it utilizes a data-driven approach to train a policy network capable of handling basic maneuvers; second, it integrates a handcrafted model to refine the network for complex scenarios. We validate this proposed framework by retraining an existing model to enhance performance on the Baidu Apollo benchmark. Our results indicate that the framework effectively simplifies the development process and enhances the robustness of the trained policy network. Parallel evolutionary algorithms (PEAs) leverage parallel computing to enhance the efficiency of evolutionary computation. Among these, asynchronous PEAs (APEAs) are particularly favored for multi-objective optimization because they eliminate the complexities associated with synchronization. However, APEAs often fail to fully utilize available processing resources, resulting in suboptimal performance. To address this, this paper introduces a novel parent selection mechanism designed to maximize computational resource usage in APEAs. This mechanism operates on the insight that the optimal strategy for parent selection depends on the algorithm's current operational frequency. Additionally, the approach is easily adaptable to various existing APEA implementations. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed method significantly boosts the performance of three standard APEA algorithms across multiple test instances. Furthermore, the method exhibits robustness against variations in the number of available processing units. The study also confirms that this mechanism is readily applicable to other APEA algorithms. Finally, the research investigates the impact of the evaluation time distribution on the method's effectiveness. The code for the proposed algorithms is publicly accessible at https://github.com/SebastianKraemer1999/FrequencyBasedParentSelection.

This work investigates the $\varepsilon$-expansion of the spectrum and eigenprojectors of a time-periodic Lindblad superoperator, where the driving frequency scales as $\varepsilon^{-1}$. We demonstrate that an appropriate rescaling of the time scale yields an asymptotic series for both the eigenvalues and eigenprojectors. Central to this expansion is a non-autonomous problem termed the "slow" Lindblad equation, which is derived from the original "fast" Lindblad equation. We establish that the solution to this slow equation generates a valid asymptotic series for the original superoperator. Furthermore, we prove that these asymptotic expansions can be rigorously resolved, thereby ensuring that the resulting asymptotic series are also rigorous. As an application, we derive a high-frequency expansion for the spectrum of a periodically driven two-level system. Additionally, we apply these findings to analyze the spectrum of a driven harmonic oscillator, specifically addressing the dynamical Stark shift. In this context, we show that the asymptotic expansion for eigenvalues converges for all sufficiently high frequencies. Finally, we discuss the implications of these findings for periodically driven quantum many-body systems. Notably, we establish that the high-frequency expansion for the Lindblad spectrum of a two-level system remains applicable to quantum many-body systems, provided the Hamiltonian and Lindblad operators are quadratic in creation and annihilation operators. This finding contrasts with the case of a time-periodic harmonic oscillator, where the high-frequency expansion fails to exist. These findings are consistent with recent results by the authors and others regarding the high-frequency expansion of the effective Hamiltonian for a harmonic oscillator. Our findings also align with recent work by other authors concerning the Floquet spectrum of the generalized Rabi model. In this specific case, we show that the high-frequency expansion for the Lindblad spectrum can be derived from the high-frequency expansion of the effective Floquet Hamiltonian. This result stands in contrast to the harmonic oscillator scenario, where the high-frequency expansion for the Floquet spectrum does not exist. We attribute this discrepancy to the presence of a non-trivial Floquet spectrum in the driven two-level system, whereas the Floquet spectrum for the harmonic oscillator is empty. This distinction arises because the driven two-level system possesses a non-zero energy gap, whereas the harmonic oscillator's spectrum is unbounded. We conclude by discussing the implications of these findings for periodically driven quantum many-body systems. We conducted a 21-cm neutral hydrogen (HI) survey targeting the high-mass star-forming region G176.51+00.20 using the Green Bank Telescope. This area is renowned for hosting the massive O-type star G176.51+00.20 IR1, which drives a molecular outflow and a large HI shell. Our analysis identified 13 HI self-absorption features (HI-SAFs) with velocities ranging from -10 to 10 km/s relative to the Local Standard of Rest (LSR). The HI absorption profile aligns with the molecular gas distribution, indicating that the probed molecular cloud lies between the observer and the G176.51+00.20 star-forming region. The majority of the HI-SAFs exhibit low optical depths, suggesting they are not caused by the HI shell. We propose that the HI-SAFs with the lowest optical depths and the highest column densities are linked to the molecular outflow, while those with higher optical depths and lower column densities likely originate from molecular clouds closer to the observer. Furthermore, the HI-SAFs with the lowest column densities and highest optical depths may be associated with the HI shell. This study represents the first detection of HI self-absorption features toward G176.51+00.20. Our findings suggest that HI self-absorption observations can effectively probe the HI shell and molecular outflow surrounding high-mass star-forming regions. Additionally, the HI-SAFs with the lowest optical depths and highest column densities could serve as a new method for detecting molecular outflows. These results offer a novel perspective on the HI shell and molecular outflow around G176.51+00.20. Future research should focus on observing the HI absorption profile of G176.51+00.20 with higher resolution and sensitivity. We demonstrate that a strongly intermediate $\beta$-shift is topologically conjugate to a greedy $\beta$-shift featuring a hole. This finding offers an alternative characterization for strongly intermediate $\beta$-shifts and establishes a non-trivial instance where removing a point from one topological space results in a space conjugate to another. Furthermore, this result characterizes strongly intermediate $\beta$-shifts based on the specific nature of the hole in the greedy $\beta$-shift. Our proof relies on analyzing the symbolic dynamics of the hole and the combinatorial properties of special factors. Additionally, we provide a characterization of strongly intermediate $\beta$-shifts with constant combinatorial type, which includes the golden mean shift as a primary example. This resolves a question posed by Feng and Ye in their study of intermediate $\beta$-shifts with constant combinatorial type. The characterization is derived as a consequence of our primary result. Finally, we examine the implications of these findings for the topological entropy of intermediate $\beta$-shifts. Specifically, we confirm a conjecture by Feng and Ye regarding the entropy of the golden mean shift and characterize the entropy of intermediate $\beta$-shifts through the lens of the hole in the corresponding greedy $\beta$-shift. This latter contribution is the result of a joint effort with Feng. The paper concludes with several open problems. The first addresses the existence of a $\beta$-mixing interval within the set of strongly intermediate $\beta$-shifts, while the second concerns the continuity of the entropy map for these shifts. Both inquiries are motivated by the implications of our findings. The final section also explores the applicability of our approach to other symbolic dynamical systems, such as Sturmian shifts and their generalizations. We outline the necessary conditions for this method to succeed in those contexts, noting that these conditions are closely linked to the behavior of the associated cutting and stacking transformations. The appendix contains a detailed examination of the specific case of Sturmian shifts. This wordless proof establishes the formula $T_n = \frac{n(n+1)}{2}$ for the $n$th triangular number by comparing the total count of upright triangles to that of inverted triangles within a grid of side length $n$. The number of upright triangles corresponds exactly to the value of the $n$th triangular number, $T_n$. To determine the count of inverted triangles, we observe that for any row $k$ (where $1 \leq k \leq n$), the number of upright triangles in the $k$ rows above it equals $T_k$. Consequently, the number of inverted triangles with their top vertex in row $k$ is $T_{k-1}$. Summing these counts yields $T_{n-1} + T_{n-2} + \dots + T_0$. This sum represents the total number of triangles in a grid of side length $n-1$, which is defined as $T_{n-1}$. Therefore, the total number of triangles in a grid of side length $n$ is $T_n + T_{n-1}$. Since the problem states this total equals $n^2$, we have the equation $T_n + T_{n-1} = n^2$. Substituting $T_{n-1} = T_n - n$ into this equation yields $2T_n - n = n^2$, which simplifies to $T_n = \frac{n(n+1)}{2}$. This derivation confirms the formula for the $n$th triangular number. Additionally, this approach demonstrates that the sum of the first $n$ odd numbers equals $n^2$. By the same logic, the sum of the first $n$ even numbers is $n(n+1)$. Subtracting the sum of the first $n$ even numbers from the sum of the first $n$ odd numbers results in $n^2 - n(n+1) = n^2 - n^2 - n = -n$. Thus, the sum of the first $n$ odd numbers minus the sum of the first $n$ even numbers equals $-n$. This algebraic relationship is visualized geometrically by the difference between the number of upright and inverted triangles, which is $T_n - T_{n-1} = n$. Although Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have demonstrated remarkable success in learning from graph-structured data, their internal decision-making processes remain opaque. To address this lack of interpretability, we introduce PGExplainer, a parameterized model designed to explain GNN predictions. By training a global model on a dataset, PGExplainer can generate explanations for any test instance without requiring additional training. Our approach employs a novel explainability parameterization that enables the global model to assess the significance of input node neighbors regarding a specific prediction. We evaluate PGExplainer across six node classification datasets, assessing both its predictive performance and the quality of its interpretations. Our results indicate that PGExplainer achieves competitive accuracy while delivering more informative predictions compared to existing methods. Substructure analysis is a critical method for investigating the formation and evolution of galaxy clusters. This study utilizes X-ray data from the Chandra X-ray Observatory and optical data from the VISTA Hemisphere Survey to examine the RXCJ0232.2-4420 cluster. The Legendre memory unit (LMU) is a recurrent neural network capable of modeling high-order dynamics, making it effective for both linear and nonlinear control applications. While LMUs can be trained using standard back-propagation, this approach is computationally intensive and time-consuming. This paper introduces a parallel training method designed to enhance computational efficiency. Our method employs a novel parameterization of LMU weights that enables the simultaneous training of multiple units. We demonstrate the method's efficacy through simulations on a nonlinear pendulum system. The results show that training two units concurrently achieves performance comparable to sequential training but reduces the required computation time by 40%. Furthermore, the proposed method is applicable to LMUs utilizing various recurrent architectures, including the gated LMU. Consequently, this approach can significantly accelerate the training of LMUs for control tasks within model predictive control (MPC) frameworks. Finally, we outline the extension of our method to support the parallel training of memory units with varying numbers of states. To our knowledge, this represents the first application of parallelization techniques to LMU training. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/ControlTheoryGroup/LMU-Parallel-Training. Language evolution is frequently modeled as a co-evolutionary system involving both communicative interactions and the movement of agents. This study investigates how a specific model, the naming game, changes when agents migrate between two distinct regions. Our findings indicate that, under specific conditions, this setup leads to the emergence of two separate linguistic systems, each characterized by a unique level of semantic efficiency. Furthermore, we demonstrate that this scenario can be analyzed using a simple mean-field approach, which captures the essential dynamics of naming game co-evolution under varying migration rates. Finally, we show that these mean-field equations offer a straightforward explanation for the development of linguistic systems with different degrees of coherence. These results provide a foundation for modeling the development of multiple linguistic systems with diverse semantic efficiencies and coherences. Additionally, our mean-field analysis offers a clear explanation for the existence of linguistic systems with varying levels of coherence. This analysis relies on a new metric for semantic efficiency, which we argue is a more appropriate measure for evolving languages than the count of meaningful expressions. We also present a method to estimate this metric's value at a specific time step using the concept of entropy. Finally, we validate the accuracy of our mean-field equations by comparing their predictions against results from computer simulations. Physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) have recently gained significant traction for modeling physical systems. However, their practical application is often hindered by slow convergence and the inability to reach global optima. This study investigates how momentum techniques influence the spectral characteristics of PINNs during training. Through comprehensive experiments on both synthetic and real-world datasets, we show that incorporating momentum into PINNs leads to faster convergence and superior performance compared to methods without momentum. Furthermore, we confirm that these benefits are robust across various PINN architectures, including those utilizing different network widths, depths, and activation functions. This paper investigates the stability of a coupled wave system featuring partially Kelvin-Voigt damping, where the coupled wave lacks direct damping and propagates through an undamped region. We establish exponential stability for the coupled wave system and bounded polynomial stability for the observation region by employing a frequency approach combined with the three-lines lemma. Furthermore, we derive an explicit formula for the exponential stability constant and produce additional results concerning coupled regions and damping types. Model-based reinforcement learning (RL) offers a promising avenue for developing sample-efficient agents capable of mastering complex tasks within large environments. However, the inherent complexity of these models often hinders interpretability, making it difficult to discern the specific behaviors the agent exhibits. This paper introduces a hierarchical RL framework designed to enhance sample efficiency while simultaneously improving the interpretability of the agent's learned content. Our approach employs inductive logic programming (ILP) to induce symbolic rules from the learned dynamics, thereby revealing the agent's reasoning process. We successfully applied this method to two continuous control tasks, demonstrating that the induced rules are both informative and accurate. Furthermore, we show that the symbolic representation of the agent's behavior can be effectively transferred across different environments. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/akshaykumar1998/Interpretable-HRL. Our implementation utilizes PyTorch for model-based RL and the InductiveLogicProgramming package for ILP. This framework is easily adaptable to other model-based RL algorithms, such as MBPO and F4, as well as to various ILP methods, including those based on Markov logic networks. We have also included an implementation of the ILPO algorithm, which is available on our GitHub repository. The ILPO package can be installed via pip using the command: pip install InductiveLogicProgramming. Additional details regarding the ILPO implementation can be found in our technical report. Our codebase is also compatible with the OpenAI Gym. For further information, please visit our project website at https://akshaykumar1998.github.io/ILPO/. Nonreciprocity is a fundamental concept in photonics, describing the direction-dependent behavior of light transport. While most traditional nonreciprocal optical devices rely on external modulation or magneto-optical effects, this study presents a quantum approach to achieving all-pass nonreciprocity in a passive system by utilizing quantum squeezing as a driving force. The proposed scheme is implemented in a photonic crystal waveguide featuring coupled $\Lambda$-type atoms, where the presence of squeezed light induces a phase shift in the transmitted signal. This quantum method offers a more efficient pathway for developing nonreciprocal photonic components and holds potential applications in the field of quantum information. Furthermore, we examine the impact of decoherence on the system's performance, demonstrating that the decoherence-free subspace (DFS) technique can effectively mitigate these effects. Finally, we outline the experimental requirements necessary to validate this proposal. Our findings establish a viable framework for the design and implementation of nonreciprocal devices driven by quantum squeezing. Additionally, the work explores the application of DFS within the context of nonreciprocal devices, thereby opening new avenues for research in quantum optics. Specifically, we analyze minimax problems involving functionals of sum-of-translates type, which are expressed as integrals dependent on a continuous function $f$, its derivatives up to order $k$, and a nondecreasing convex function $\varphi$. We introduce a novel method for investigating spin-dependent dark matter interactions by utilizing the nuclear form factors of $^6$Li. This approach is particularly advantageous for solid-state experiments employing $\alpha$-emitting impurities like $^6$Li implanted in NaI detectors. We anticipate that our findings will facilitate a comprehensive analysis of spin-dependent dark matter interactions within the near future. Blind image deblurring aims to recover blurred images into their sharp counterparts without prior knowledge of the blur kernel. This paper introduces a novel blind deblurring framework utilizing a kernel mixture model. The proposed method first estimates multiple kernel components from the input image and subsequently estimates the blending weights for these components. To achieve this, a new loss function is developed to simultaneously estimate both the kernel components and their mixing weights. Furthermore, a multi-kernel deblurring model is designed to restore the image under this kernel mixture. Extensive experiments on benchmark datasets demonstrate that the proposed model outperforms state-of-the-art methods. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/ChenYi-1998/Kernel-Mixture-Blind-Deblurring. The results will be published in IEEE Transactions on Image Processing. This paper introduces natural Hoare logic, a formal system designed for verifying the correctness of imperative programs using natural language specifications. By integrating formal semantics for natural language with Hoare logic, this approach enables the formal validation of arguments traditionally made by programmers and facilitates the automatic inference of program properties. The study provides the syntax and semantics for a fragment of natural language containing the necessary components for correct assertions, alongside a syntax for formulas that capture standard proofs of this semantics. Within this framework, valid formulas correspond exactly to programs that satisfy a given semantics, and the syntax for specification and reasoning formulas aligns with the familiar syntax of Hoare logic. Furthermore, the authors present a formalization of this system in Coq and demonstrate its application to verify the correctness of imperative programs. This methodology successfully infers familiar properties of imperative programs and validates the correctness of natural language arguments. The paper concludes with a discussion of the system's limitations and potential future research directions. Keywords: formal verification, natural language, formal semantics, formal methods, Coq.

We measured the bending modulus of both DOPC and cholesterol-doped DOPC/DOPG lipid bilayers using the buckling of a thin elastic plate model. Our results indicate that the modulus for cholesterol-containing bilayers is 2.5 times greater than that of pure DOPC. Furthermore, we observed that the buckling modulus increases linearly with cholesterol concentration up to 20 mol%, after which it begins to plateau. These findings align with previous studies. Additionally, we demonstrate that cholesterol enhances the bending modulus of the bilayer. Finally, we propose that the buckling of a thin elastic plate method serves as a viable alternative to existing techniques for determining the elastic properties of lipid bilayers. Deep object detectors are widely used across numerous computer vision applications, yet their inability to provide uncertainty estimates hinders their deployment in safety-critical environments. To address this, we introduce BayesOD, the first Bayesian framework designed for uncertainty estimation in deep object detectors. This approach utilizes Monte Carlo (MC) dropout to approximate Bayesian inference, enabling the quantification of uncertainty in both localization and classification. By employing MC dropout, BayesOD can also leverage multiple detection predictions to enhance performance through ensemble voting. We evaluate the framework's effectiveness on the COCO and AI Cityscapes datasets, demonstrating that it surpasses existing methods in both accuracy and uncertainty estimation. Furthermore, we show that BayesOD improves the performance of pre-trained detectors YOLOv3 and YOLOv4 by 1.5% and 2.1% mAP, respectively, when tested on the AI Cityscapes dataset. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/ashishkumar1999/BayesOD. Our findings indicate that MC dropout is a highly effective method for inferring variational models, making it a valuable tool for developing practical Bayesian object detectors. Additionally, we find that running 50 MC samples is sufficient to achieve stable performance. We hope this work inspires the research community to explore Bayesian models for deep object detectors. Our implementation is available at https://github.com/ashishkumar1999/BayesOD. Accurate short-term traffic prediction is essential for efficient traffic management. However, current models struggle to effectively capture the complex patterns inherent in traffic data. To address this, we introduce a new dataset for short-term traffic forecasting, comprising 24-hourly speed recordings from 1,000 sensors in London, UK. We partition this data into 10-second clips and utilize them to train a Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) network. Our results demonstrate that a model trained on these snippets outperforms one trained on traditional time-series data. We attribute this improvement to the snippets' ability to encode both spatial and temporal correlations, thereby providing richer information for forecasting. Additionally, we propose a novel data augmentation technique that generates further snippets by combining existing ones, which further enhances forecasting accuracy. The dataset is accessible at https://github.com/abhishekkumar2000/TMST.

In a 2-category, every morphism possesses a unique factorization into a bijective-on-the-nose span followed by a Gray-fibration span; this result serves as a primary tool for managing strict 2-cells that are only up-to-mate. We demonstrate that this factorization extends to any bicategory of fractions. As an application, we establish a strengthened version of Finster and Uustime's coherence theorem, which ensures that any diagrammatic decomposition of a 2-cell is universally computationally universal. Additionally, we provide a characterization of bijective-on-the-nose and Gray-fibration spans through specific coherence conditions and derive several corresponding coherence results. Leveraging these findings, we construct an alternative method for generating computationally universal diagrams, which we have applied to derive the standard coherence theorem for bicategories of fractions and the coherence theorem for 2-functor-stable bicategories of fractions. We contend that this novel approach offers a more natural and flexible framework for achieving coherence across diverse mathematical domains. Furthermore, we apply these techniques to derive the coherence theorem and diagrammatic decompositions—such as those by Finster, Lack, and Soboroda—within the specific contexts of bicategories of fractions and 2-functor-stable bicategories of fractions. Finally, we discuss the relationship between our methodology and that of Finster and Uustime, as well as potential extensions to n-categorical settings. To facilitate these applications, we have developed a novel, highly general framework for factorizations that encompasses the 2-categorical case. We believe this framework will be of independent interest. All results are presented in an up-to-mate language, and we utilize a comprehensive collection of weak structures, including bi-categories, bi-functors, and bi-natural transformations. We also provide a characterization of bi-Gray-transformation stability and establish a coherence theorem for bi-Gray-categories. We believe that the bi-Gray-category structure and the associated coherence theorem will serve as valuable tools for future research. This study introduces a multiple convolutional neural network (CNN) approach designed to segment the hippocampus in 3D T1-weighted MRI scans from patients with Alzheimer's disease (AD) and epilepsy. We trained and assessed the model on the ADNI dataset, which includes both AD and control cases, and subsequently evaluated it using the International School of Epilepsy Surgery (ISES) dataset, comprising epilepsy patients and controls. The proposed method was benchmarked against two other techniques: a deep learning-based approach and a traditional level-set method. Quantitative results demonstrate that the proposed method achieves performance comparable to the level-set approach in both AD and control groups, while surpassing the deep learning method across all metrics. Furthermore, the method exhibits robustness when applied to epilepsy data. Finally, we discuss the advantages and potential limitations of this proposed approach. We examine the interferometric and diffraction components of the quantum enhanced pigeonhole effect, demonstrating that transversal modes can significantly boost the pigeonhole factor. This approach is particularly advantageous when operating near the half-pigeon limit, where it achieves performance comparable to methods relying on higher-order derivatives. Furthermore, we outline the experimental requirements necessary to observe this quantum phenomenon. Our findings indicate that reviewing the pigeonhole effect through the lens of transversal modes offers new avenues for sensitivity enhancements. Additionally, this perspective may facilitate the discovery of novel effects within interferometric frameworks. Finally, we suggest that our methodology could be applied to investigate the weak value amplification effect. These conclusions are derived from the sensitivity analysis of a specific model, which we believe captures the essential characteristics of various schemes aimed at detecting this effect. We also address certain misconceptions regarding quantum pigeonhole sensitivity. Our research was conducted within the framework of linear optical quantum mechanics. The proposed schemes are compatible with current experimental capabilities and do not demand non-classical light sources. Consequently, we believe this work provides a fresh perspective on the quantum nature of interferometric and diffraction pigeonhole effects. We anticipate that this study will inspire further investigations into the fundamental principles of optical diffraction and their potential applications in precision measurements. This study simulates the temporal evolution of trapped protons at low Earth orbits (LEO) using the CRAND model, which incorporates proton production, loss, and transport mechanisms. The simulation results align well with existing in-situ proton flux data from LEO satellites. Additionally, the simulated proton fluxes are applied to assess radiation damage in Low Earth Orbit. The analysis indicates that proton total ionizing dose (TID) and displacement damage dose (DDD) are negligible for LEO satellites, with the exception of those orbiting below 400 km. However, for satellites below this altitude, proton-induced TID and DDD can be comparable to or even exceed electron-induced doses. This finding is particularly significant for future low-altitude LEO constellations, such as Starlink, which operate beneath the 400 km threshold. Consequently, the CRAND model is deemed suitable for predicting trapped proton fluxes and their corresponding radiation effects in future low-orbit LEO satellites. Furthermore, the model offers a valuable tool for evaluating radiation effects on Low Earth Orbit space systems. A user-friendly interface for CRAND is accessible at http://crand.lamost.org. The model is designed to simulate the temporal evolution of proton fluxes and effects across the entire LEO region, with a specific focus on the International Space Station (ISS) orbit. Users can input their own satellite orbit parameters to generate proton flux and radiation effect predictions for their specific missions. The simulation outputs include time-dependent energy spectra of trapped protons and the cumulative doses of total ionizing dose (TID) and displacement damage dose (DDD) over a specified duration. This capability enables users to assess the radiation effects of trapped protons on their specific missions. The paper concludes with several examples demonstrating the application of CRAND to predict proton fluxes and their radiation effects for the ISS and other LEO satellites. These examples illustrate how to input satellite orbital parameters and select radiation effect models for the simulation. The paper also provides guidance on interpreting the simulation results. Ultimately, CRAND serves as a practical tool for evaluating the radiation effects of trapped protons on LEO satellites. The model is publicly available at http://crand.lamost.org, and this article details the inputs and outputs of the model. Users are encouraged to utilize CRAND to predict proton fluxes and their associated radiation effects for their missions. The paper also discusses the advantages and limitations of the model. This paper introduces a novel architecture for node representation learning on graphs, featuring a pyramid-like shrinkage skeleton at the global level and rewiring of local topology links. The global skeleton aims to capture multi-scale graph information, while the local rewiring mechanism is designed to uncover hidden relationships within the data. The study evaluates various configurations of the Local Topology Link Rewiring (LTLR) module, demonstrating that a single layer proves most effective. Furthermore, experiments across several real-world datasets reveal that the optimal performance is achieved when the LTLR module is placed at the final layer of the model. The authors also investigate the impact of different shrinkage skeletons within the Global Pyramid-like Shrinkage Skeleton (GPSS) module, finding that a three-level skeleton yields the best results. Additionally, the paper analyzes the influence of various pooling strategies on the GPSS module, indicating that adaptive pooling outperforms other methods. Finally, a comprehensive ablation study confirms the efficacy of the proposed GPSS and LTLR modules. Extensive experiments across multiple real-world datasets validate that the proposed Deep Graph Neural Network (DGNN) architecture surpasses state-of-the-art methods. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/ChenYi2019/DGNN. The results can be reproduced at https://github.com/ChenYi2019/DGNN/tree/master/Results. The paper itself is available at https://github.com/ChenYi2019/DGNN/tree/master/Paper. This study investigates the application of the differentially private (DP) Huber mechanism to low-rank matrix completion. We demonstrate that, under both pure and approximate differential privacy constraints, the mechanism produces $\epsilon$-sensitive outputs. By leveraging these properties, we establish that the true values generated by the Huber mechanism, when combined with the R\'{e}nyi divergence metric, follow the $\alpha$-order Renyi DP distribution. Furthermore, we propose a novel algorithm integrating the Huber mechanism with subsampling, which utilizes the Huber estimator to estimate the complete set of matrix entries. We provide a comprehensive analysis of the Huber mechanism's performance in this completion setting, demonstrating that it achieves superior accuracy compared to the Laplace mechanism. Additionally, we develop a new algorithm that combines the Huber mechanism with exponential subsampling, which also outperforms the Laplace mechanism in terms of accuracy. Finally, we empirically validate our theoretical findings through numerical experiments. The code supporting this research is available at: https://github.com/Amirhossein-Taghavi/DP-Matrix-Completion. Our results indicate that the proposed methods are effective for completing large-scale matrices. The authors thank the anonymous reviewers for their constructive feedback. We introduce a unified model that describes the extinction, emission, and polarization properties of diffuse interstellar matter (ISM). This framework relies on a single component of astrodust grains, which are amorphous silicate grains coated with a mixture of amorphous carbon and hydrogen. The grain size distribution is defined by a single size parameter, $s$, which scales the grain radius, $a_s = s \times 0.02\,\mu$m. Polarization is modeled using a single component of aligned, prolate astrodust grains, with the grain aspect ratio, $f = a/b$, serving as the sole parameter. The emission from carbonaceous and hydrogen molecules adsorbed on the grain surface is represented by a single component of polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs), characterized by an average size, $N = 60$. The extinction curve is described by the ratio $R_V = A_V/\kappa(0.55\,\mu m)$, where $\kappa$ denotes the extinction efficiency. The model's parameters are constrained using the latest data from the Sloan Digital Sky Survey (SDSS) regarding extinction, emission, and polarization. We determine that the best-fit parameters are $s = 1.0$, $f = 0.6$, and $N = 60$. The model yields a mean value of $R_V = 3.09 \pm 0.01$, which aligns with the average $R_V$ derived from the SDSS dataset. Furthermore, the model accurately reproduces the average shapes of the wavelength-dependent curves for extinction, emission, and polarization across the diffuse ISM. We conclude that astrodust grains, alongside PAHs and magnetic fields, are the primary contributors to the diffuse ISM's extinction, emission, and polarization. Additionally, we demonstrate that the astrodust grain size distribution follows a power law with a slope of $-2.0 \pm 0.1$, a finding consistent with the average slope observed in the Galactic disk. Finally, we show that astrodust grains are the dominant source of extinction in the diffuse ISM, contributing approximately 80% of the total extinction. This model is publicly accessible at http://www.astro.ucla.edu/~wright/astrodust.html. The data used to constrain the model can be found at http://www.astro.ucla.edu/~wright/SDSS/Extinction.html. We report the detection of a giant planet within the protoplanetary disk of CIDA 1, a young, low-mass star. This system was identified as a candidate for hosting a massive planet due to a prominent gap in its disk structure, which was initially observed in ALMA continuum data. By analyzing the disk's morphology, we infer the presence of a massive planet with a minimum mass of 0.8 Jupiter masses ($M_{\rm Jup}$) located at a semi-major axis of 10 astronomical units (AU). This system represents the second known very low-mass star to host a giant planet, following G29-20, and marks the first instance where the planet's mass was determined through disk structure analysis rather than direct imaging. Our findings suggest that the conditions for forming massive planets are not restricted to high-mass stars and may be achievable in the disks of low-mass stars. Furthermore, the early formation of this planet, indicated by the system's young age, aligns with predictions from core accretion models. The system also exhibits a highly inclined disk, a feature that may be linked to the migration history of the planet. Additionally, we identified a compact source at the system's center, which we attribute to a jet rather than a second planet, based on its morphology and spectral characteristics. Finally, we discuss the implications of these results for the low mass function of giant planets.

This paper introduces the Most Clicks Problem, which seeks to determine the maximum number of clicks required to reach the all-zero configuration from any initial board state. We establish a necessary and sufficient condition for a state to yield this maximum, demonstrating that the number of clicks for any other state is at least the distance to the all-zero state under this criterion minus one. Leveraging this condition, we derive a closed-form expression for the most clicks problem across all possible Lights Out games. Additionally, we examine the reverse scenario: the Fewest Clicks Problem, proving that the fewest clicks needed for any state correspond precisely to the distance from the initial state to the all-zero state using the click-count condition as the metric. Finally, we explore the relationship between the fewest and most clicks problems, deriving an upper bound for the difference between their minimum click counts. These findings hold for both standard and generalized versions of the game. As a practical application, we utilize the derived formula for the most clicks problem to generate examples of boards requiring the maximum number of clicks. Furthermore, we extend the analysis to the weighted Lights Out game, where each click incurs a specific cost, formulating the problems as integer linear programming problems and providing a solution for a specific instance. This study offers a novel perspective on Lights Out that diverges from traditional approaches. Our results offer new insights and tools for analyzing the game's complexity and contribute to a deeper understanding of its underlying mathematical structure. The paper includes a Python program that implements the solution for the weighted version, available at: https://github.com/yy12345678901234567890/MostClicks. This paper introduces a new vari-based image segmentation framework that integrates image restoration techniques. The proposed model incorporates a total variation (TV) regularizer alongside a data fidelity term that integrates both a data-driven edge-preserving filter and a deep convolutional neural network (CNN) regularizer. To facilitate a more precise and robust segmentation process, the deep convolutional encoder is trained using a supervised approach. The optimization of the resulting non-convex model is achieved through a customized alternating direction method of multipliers (ADMM). Numerical experiments conducted on both synthetic and real-world images demonstrate that the proposed method yields superior and more accurate segmentation results compared to various state-of-the-art techniques. Furthermore, the method exhibits strong robustness against noise, as evidenced by its high performance across diverse noise types and intensities. Abstract interpretation is a static analysis method that operates in two phases: the computation of an initial over-approximation of program states and the construction of an over-approximation of state transitions. This paper introduces a novel technique to decouple these phases, enabling the application of distinct domain operators for each. We demonstrate the method's efficacy through a case study on pointer aliasing, where decoupling facilitates the use of a more precise domain for state transitions. Furthermore, we show that the technique can dynamically adjust analysis precision by varying the domain used in the transition phase. Our experimental results indicate that this approach yields a 2.5x improvement in precision compared to methods that employ a single domain for both phases. Topological phonons have recently been identified in oxide perovskites, and their characteristics can be significantly altered through laser illumination. We introduce a theoretical framework that extends the tight-binding model for topological phonons to include the effects of photoexcitation. Our analysis demonstrates that the band structure of these excited states differs markedly from that of the ground state, particularly in the behavior of band gaps, which can be externally regulated by adjusting the intensity and frequency of the pumping laser. Furthermore, we examine the topological nature of these excited states, revealing that nontrivial configurations can persist even after the pumping laser is switched off. These findings offer new avenues for manipulating the properties of topological phonons and highlight exciting prospects within the field of topological excitations.

Identifying outliers within high-dimensional data is a critical step for numerous data mining tasks. This paper introduces a novel, efficient, and precise method for outlier detection in metric spaces, leveraging data structures based on proximity graphs. We propose a new metric proximity graph framework that enables the rapid and exact computation of specific distance-based criteria, such as those used in KNN and LKNN outlier detection. Furthermore, we demonstrate how this framework can be adapted to support other approaches, including density-based and statistical methods. Our proposed solution outperforms existing state-of-the-art solutions by orders of magnitude in both time and space complexity. Additionally, we present a suite of experiments that validate the effectiveness of our method. The source code is publicly accessible at https://github.com/SebastianSchulz1990/pgod. We investigate the excitation dynamics and emitted radiation from a quantum dipole atom positioned before a thin, perfectly conducting mirror. We compare two distinct theoretical frameworks: one modeling the atom as a point-like two-level system interacting with a single quantized electromagnetic mode, and another treating it as an extended entity with an electromagnetic form factor. We demonstrate that both approaches yield identical results regarding atomic population dynamics and emitted photon spectra. Specifically, we find that excitation driven by vacuum fluctuations occurs in both scenarios, with the atom acting as a transducer that converts electromagnetic energy from higher frequencies into that of lower frequencies. Furthermore, we show that this motion-induced excitation mechanism is contingent upon the atom's distance from the mirror. Additionally, we establish that the atom can be driven into a highly populated state, from which it emits a single photon upon decaying to the ground state. Finally, we analyze how the atom's spatial extension influences these phenomena, revealing that while the primary effects remain qualitatively unchanged, they are modulated by the specific dimensions of the atom. These findings may be experimentally verified using current technology, such as Rydberg atoms and planar mirrors. Our study also sheds light on the interplay between quantum and classical effects in confined geometries. Notably, we observe that within a classical framework, a dipole situated in front of a mirror would not experience such vacuum-induced excitation. This suggests that the interaction between an atom and a mirror is a fundamentally quantum effect, as it arises from the nonlocal characteristics inherent in quantum electrodynamics. Our results also offer a potential explanation for the recently observed radiation from an atom near a mirror, which contradicts standard quantum electrodiction predictions for local point-like dipoles. We propose that this phenomenon can be accurately described by the extended-atom model. Finally, we show that the quantum nature of this atom-mirror interaction can be investigated by examining the correlation between atomic transients and emitted photons. This correlation can be controlled by adjusting the atom's size and its distance from the mirror. Our proposed method for studying quantum effects in confined spaces may be tested using an atom with an extended electromagnetic form factor and a three-dimensional cavity. Such an experiment would allow for the observation of the quantum effect's dependence on the atom's size and its separation from the mirror. This could be achieved using Rydberg atoms and cavities with dimensions comparable to the atom's size. This paper addresses fair graph representation learning, a critical yet underexplored area where traditional machine learning fairness methods are insufficient due to the discrete and irregular nature of graph data. To address this, we introduce a unified framework for fairness on graphs, offering a comprehensive view of various graph fairness problems and their associated methodological solutions. We propose a novel fairness metric called Localized Neighborhood Fairness (LNF), which ensures that nodes with similar local neighborhoods exhibit similar demographic compositions. Furthermore, we develop a unified graph neural network model designed to learn fair representations under the LNF metric. Experimental results demonstrate that our method effectively produces fair graph representations and significantly enhances classification performance. This study examines kinetic models for reversible enzyme reactions, specifically comparing the Michaelis-Menten and Ping Pong mechanisms. We demonstrate the application of the Picard and successive approximations methods to solve the associated rate equations. The success of these methods in yielding convergent solutions is evaluated, and the kinetic parameters are constrained to ensure convergence. Furthermore, we derive a novel kinetic equation for a reversible bisubstrate reaction following a sequential bi-bi mechanism, and its associated rate equation is solved using the successive approximations method. This approach yields a four-term power series solution for the enzyme-substrate complex concentration, which is verified to be convergent. Additionally, we illustrate how this series solution can be employed to fit experimental data. Finally, we compare these series solutions with those obtained via the Picard method. Across all derived kinetic equations, the Picard method fails to produce a convergent solution. In contrast, the successive approximations method consistently generates a rapidly convergent series for the concentration of the enzyme-substrate complex. These findings are supported by numerical examples. The source code for the computations is available at: https://github.com/abdelrahimhassan/Enzyme-Reactions. Abdelrahim.Hassan@ucl.ac.uk. This study investigates supersymmetry (SUSY) within final states characterized by jets and missing transverse momentum. The analysis utilizes proton-proton collision data collected by the CMS detector at the LHC, corresponding to an integrated luminosity of 35.9 fb$^{-1}$ at a center-of-mass energy of $\sqrt{s} = 13$ TeV. The search targets the sequential three-body decay of heavy gluinos into light charginos, which subsequently decay into the lightest neutralino. Results are interpreted using simplified models to establish limits on SUSY particle masses for various scenarios. Additionally, the investigation examines SUSY models featuring a natural mass scale and a compressed mass spectrum between the heavy gluino and the light chargino. In this specific scenario, a compressed mass splitting of $\Delta m \lesssim 10$ GeV is examined through a dedicated analysis utilizing the CMS phase-II detector configuration. No significant excess over the standard model background was observed in either analysis. Consequently, for the final decay step gluino $\to$ chargino $\to$ neutralino, gluino masses up to 1.5 TeV are excluded at 95% confidence level for a neutralino mass of 125 GeV. For the final decay step gluino $\to$ chargino $\to$ neutralino $\to$ jet + $E_T^{\rm miss}$, gluino masses up to 1.2 TeV are excluded at 95% confidence level for a neutralino mass of 125 GeV. Furthermore, for the final decay chain gluino $\to$ chargino $\to$ neutralino $\to$ $E_T^{\rm miss}$, gluino masses up to 1.0 TeV are ruled out at 95% confidence level for a neutralino mass of 125 GeV. This paper investigates the dynamics of rational expectation financial bubbles, specifically focusing on their durations. The authors establish a new class of models characterized by stochastic, mean-reverting termination times. To analyze these models, the study develops a set of partial differential equations (PDEs) that capture the deterministic evolution of moments and provide a partial characterization of the termination time's density function. Additionally, the authors propose a suite of statistical tests to detect the presence of bubble models and estimate their parameters. These diagnostic tools are validated through simulations and by analyzing historical data on the S&P 500. The results indicate that bubble models align well with the observed data, and the estimated parameters fall within theoretically valid ranges. Furthermore, the study demonstrates that these bubble models effectively capture the empirical stylized facts of financial time series. Consequently, the proposed class of bubble models offers a valuable framework for understanding the dynamics of financial time series. This insight is particularly relevant for financial practitioners, as it underscores the necessity of accounting for the high risk of bubble formation when making investment decisions. The paper concludes by outlining several promising avenues for future research. Specifically, the authors suggest extending the current framework to include non-linear parameter estimation and exploring the implications of bubble models for financial regulation and policy. Furthermore, the authors note that their current work does not address the issue of structural breaks, an area that warrants further investigation. Finally, the authors emphasize the need to generalize their framework to allow for multiple simultaneous bubbles, a topic that remains to be explored. Overall, this work represents a significant step towards a more comprehensive understanding of financial bubbles and their impact on financial markets. By providing a more nuanced understanding of bubble dynamics, this research has the potential to inform more effective financial regulation and policy decisions. Ultimately, the authors believe that their work will contribute to a more robust and resilient financial system. Specifically, the proposed bubble models can be used to develop early warning systems for emerging bubbles, which could help prevent future financial crises. We investigate a quantum harmonic oscillator subjected to a driving force by employing the Feynman-Kac formula and evaluating the associated path integral through a Metropolis algorithm. Our results demonstrate that the oscillator's position and momentum distributions align with analytical predictions when the path integral is computed using a sufficiently large number of discrete time steps. Furthermore, we illustrate that the oscillator's wavefunction evolves in accordance with the Feynman-Kac formula. This methodology is easily extensible to other quantum systems, such as the anharmonic oscillator. Additionally, our findings indicate that the quantum-to-classical transition in a driven harmonic oscillator can be observed by analyzing the evolution of its position and momentum distributions. Ultimately, this approach offers a straightforward means of numerically simulating quantum systems and calculating their path integrals. The accompanying Python code is available at https://github.com/abhishekdeshmukh123/QHO_Python. Keywords: Quantum Mechanics, Quantum Dynamics, Path Integral, Monte Carlo Methods. Item recommendation is a fundamental component of online shopping experiences. While traditional recommendation systems primarily rely on user behavior data, they often overlook the value of user reviews. To address this, we introduce the Sentiment-aware Interactive Fusion Network (SIFN), a deep neural network designed to enhance review-based recommendation by effectively capturing the richness of review data. Our approach involves two key innovations: first, we employ a multi-level review representation to capture both individual review details and collective sentiment within review clusters; second, we utilize a multi-level sentiment-aware interactive fusion mechanism to integrate diverse sentiment signals, thereby enriching the overall review representation. Extensive experiments conducted on two real-world review datasets demonstrate that the proposed method significantly outperforms several state-of-the-art baselines. Furthermore, the model is available for download as a Pytorch pretrained model at https://github.com/ChenYi1997/SIFN/tree/master/Models. Data sparsity remains a significant hurdle in code-switching research, particularly for languages with limited corpora like Arabic. To address this, we explore data augmentation techniques for an Arabic-English code-switched dataset. Our approach involves replacing lexical items with synonyms from either language, utilizing a bilingual thesaurus and the Google Translate API. We evaluated four specific strategies: (1) substituting Arabic code-switched words with English synonyms, (2) substituting English code-switched words with Arabic synonyms, (3) substituting both Arabic and English code-switched words with synonyms, and (4) substituting the entire sentence with synonyms from both languages. These augmented datasets were evaluated across four machine learning tasks: part-of-speech tagging, named entity recognition, sentiment classification, and text classification. Results indicate that while our augmentation methods do not surpass the performance of existing techniques for Arabic code-switching, they successfully enhance performance in specific domains. Furthermore, our findings demonstrate that data augmentation is a viable strategy for improving performance in various code-switching contexts. This research offers valuable insights for future studies on Arabic code-switching and other bilingual phenomena. The code and data are accessible at https://github.com/abdulrahman-ahmed/Arabic-Code-Switching-Augmentation. This work builds upon our earlier study: Abdulrahman Ahmed, "Investigating Data Augmentation Techniques for Arabic-English Code-Switching," arXiv preprint arXiv:2101.01001, 2021. [2101.01001]. The authors' previous paper, "Investigating Data Augmentation Techniques for Arabic-English Code-Switching," was published in arXiv preprint arXiv:2101.01001 in 2021.

We demonstrate that no subgroup of the homeomorphism group of a compact surface, which fixes the boundary and acts with sufficient transitivity on the interior, can be Roelcke precompact when equipped with the topology inherited from the compact-open topology. Consequently, the question of whether the group $\mathrm{Homeo}^{+}(S_{g})$—the set of orientation-preserving automorphisms of a genus-$g$ surface—is Roelcke precompact remains unresolved for genera $g \geq 2$. Furthermore, this result extends to broader contexts, applying to the homeomorphism groups of compact manifolds and to subgroups of $\mathrm{Homeo}^{+}(S_{g})$ that are not necessarily compact. This work represents an extension of our prior research concerning the precompactness properties of these groups under the Roelcke uniformity. A detailed examination of the $\mathrm{SO}(2,n)$ isomorphism is also included. The paper concludes with an open-ended discussion on the general problem of Roelcke precompactness within the context of homeomorphism groups. The primary motivation for this research stems from the study of non-discrete topological group actions. We introduce a new algorithm for automatically untangling invalid elements within hex meshes. These elements, which include both hex and tetrahedrons, are transformed into a canonical form featuring octants and are subsequently partitioned into a collection of tets. The core of our method is a graph algorithm that generates a planar map of these tets, which is then processed by a tets-to-volumes algorithm to produce an untangled mesh. This approach successfully resolves severely distorted elements in various hex meshes, achieving a performance of 58 tets per second on a single CPU core. Relation extraction (RE) is a critical NLP task focused on identifying the relationship between a subject and an object within a given sentence. While many state-of-the-art RE models utilize knowledge graphs (KGs) as external resources to enhance performance, their reliance on specific RE training data often leads to suboptimal results when applied to different domains. This study investigates the potential of integrating pre-trained language models with a knowledge graph link prediction task to improve RE. By employing the pre-trained language model BERT, we formulate RE as a link prediction problem, thereby eliminating the need for domain-specific training data. Furthermore, we introduce a novel data augmentation technique that generates synthetic training samples by connecting entities across various sentences. Experimental results demonstrate that our approach achieves state-of-the-art performance on two RE benchmarks, specifically the RE-WN8358 and Cherenkov datasets. Additionally, our method yields promising outcomes on zero-shot RE tasks. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/ChenYi-1999/KPLP. Finally, we have released a new Chinese knowledge graph, CKBG15K, which features a larger scale and greater diversity compared to existing Chinese knowledge graph resources. The dataset can be downloaded from https://github.com/ChenYi-1999/CKBG15K. We anticipate that this work will offer valuable insights for future research in relation extraction. This study introduces a novel analytical delay model for CMOS inverters that utilizes a hyperbolic tangent function to characterize inverter delay across the entire range of input signal rise and fall times. By employing Matlab's Curve Fitting Toolbox, the model's parameters are determined from SPICE simulation data. When validated against HSPICE simulations, the proposed model demonstrates an exceptional fit, achieving a maximum relative error of 0.01%. Furthermore, the model accurately captures the impact of supply voltage fluctuations and transistor width variations on inverter delay. Its high precision and straightforward implementation make it particularly suitable for integration into larger circuit delay models and optimization frameworks. The model is implemented in Matlab and is available for download. Additionally, the accompanying Matlab file includes a utility for automatically extracting inverter delay values from SPICE simulations.
