We introduce a new method for achieving anonymous transaction privacy utilizing RingCT technology. Our approach relies on a novel commitment scheme that allows for the rapid verification of anonymous statements, such as signed transactions. This scheme is constructed from a new type of universal hash function, which we demonstrate is compatible with Schnorr signatures. The method is detailed in a technical report available at arXiv:2004.00277. A paper based on this report is currently under review for publication in the 2020 USENIX Security Symposium. To our knowledge, this represents the first application of universal hash functions within the fields of RingCT and digital currency privacy. We have implemented the proposed scheme and integrated it into the Monero software. Compared to the previous delegation-based RingCT implementation, our solution offers a 30% reduction in ringCT signature generation time and a 20% decrease in signature size. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the scheme can be extended to handle statements beyond simple integer values, such as sets of integers or arbitrary strings, while maintaining efficient generation and verification times. These capabilities enable new applications in the domain of digital currency privacy. Specifically, we show that universal hash functions can be applied to create stealth address technology, which facilitates the private distribution of funds. Our proposed approach is the first to achieve both stealth address generation and ringCT signature generation within the same software execution context, thereby eliminating the need for multiple transactions. Additionally, we demonstrate that stealth addresses generated via universal hash functions can be verified up to 10 times faster than those produced using elliptic curve-based methods. Our solution is available for download at https://git.io/mxct. The source code includes a new RingCT implementation, a universal hash function implementation, and a stealth address implementation. We have also provided a benchmarking suite that compares our implementation against the previous version, as well as a comparison with the first implementation of stealth addresses in Monero. The benchmarking suite can be found at https://git.io/mxct-bench. The paper describing the solution is currently being reviewed for publication in the 2020 USENIX Security Symposium. Driven by the growing demand for interpretable and accurate models in fields like life sciences, there is increasing interest in integrating traditional knowledge-based modeling with data-driven approaches. This survey examines recent advancements in modeling that leverages both experimental data and existing domain knowledge. It begins by outlining two primary categories of knowledge used to enhance data-driven methods: mechanistic models and expert heuristic rules. This review serves as a comprehensive guide to the synergy between prior knowledge and data in modeling, particularly for readers new to the topic. This paper introduces AskewSGD, a novel algorithm designed to train deep neural networks using quantized weights and activations. By employing a non-convex interval-constrained optimization approach, AskewSGD utilizes a constrained optimization framework to minimize the average loss of individual samples. The training process involves solving a sequence of prox-convex problems, where the objective function comprises the average sample loss plus a total variation regularizer. This regularizer encourages the training process to produce weight intervals with low total variation. Theoretically, the paper demonstrates that the sequence of optimal solutions generated by AskSGD converges to a stationary point of the unconstrained problem. Numerical experiments confirm that the test error produced by AskSGD is comparable to that of state-of-the-art unconstrained optimization methods. Furthermore, AskewSGD is applicable to a broad range of architectures and datasets, including but not limited to LeNet, AlexNet, VGGNet, and CIFAR10, MNIST, and ImageNet. The source code is publicly available at https://github.com/abhishekkumar12/askewsgd. Additionally, the authors have released a new open-source Python package, askew, which facilitates the easy training of quantized neural networks via AskewSGD. This paper revisits the definition of the real Jacobi group by viewing it as the normalizer of a specific maximal compact subgroup within the general linear group of a specific vector space. We establish an Iwasawa decomposition for the group and provide an explicit formula for the multiplication law. Furthermore, we derive a Cartan decomposition, which includes a characterization of the extreme rays of the associated Weyl chamber. We also examine the subgroups corresponding to each component of the Iwasawa decomposition, characterizing the latter as a maximal parabolic subgroup. Additionally, we analyze the symmetric space formed by quotienting the real Jacobi group by its maximal compact subgroup, presenting a diffeomorphism between this space and the quotient of the symmetric space of the general linear group by the maximal compact subgroup. We investigate the geometric structure induced on this symmetric space, including an analysis of its curvature tensor and its rank. Finally, we demonstrate that this space is isometric to the quotient of the curvature-dimension space by a specific affine action. We conclude by exploring certain unitary representations of the real Jacobi group, which are constructed from those of the general linear group via induction. Specifically, we show that the restriction of these induced representations to the maximal compact subgroup decomposes into a countable direct sum of irreducible representations, each with finite multiplicity. We further characterize these irreducible representations of the maximal compact subgroup as belonging to the principal series and explore their relationship with the irreducible representations of the real Jacobi group. We also address the multiplicity-one property and provide an explicit realization of these representations on a specific function space. In the final section, we consider holomorphic discrete series representations of the real Jacobi group, proving that their restriction to the maximal compact subgroup similarly decomposes into a countable direct sum of finite multiplicity, where the components belong to the discrete series of the maximal compact subgroup. We also characterize these irreducible representations of the maximal compact subgroup and their relationship with the holomorphic discrete series of the real Jacobi group. Finally, we establish that the holomorphic discrete series of the real Jacobi group possess the multiplicity-one property. This approach to constructing and analyzing representations of the real Jacobi group is expected to be valuable for future research. Additionally, we explore the connection between our findings and those of other researchers. Verifying facts using tables is a difficult challenge, particularly due to the diverse formats of table queries and the vast array of information contained within tables. This study proposes decomposing table-based fact verification into three sequential stages: query reformulation, retrieval, and verification. We introduce a novel end-to-end framework that integrates a query reformulator, a retrieval module, and a verification model. To train the retrieval component, we develop a new dataset, TabQA-R, which pairs relevant tables with questions. Furthermore, we incorporate a ranking loss to enhance the model's ability to distinguish between relevant and irrelevant tables. Experimental outcomes demonstrate that our framework surpasses current state-of-the-art methods in both query reformulation and fact verification tasks. The code and datasets are accessible at https://github.com/1000099999/TabFact. Additionally, we release a new dataset, TabQA-R, for the query-relevant retrieval task. Generative adversarial networks (GANs) are a type of generative model capable of producing synthetic data that mirrors the statistical characteristics of real datasets. While GANs have proven effective for generating images, videos, and audio, they often suffer from unstable training processes. This challenge is particularly acute in style-transfer tasks, where the goal is to generate synthetic data matching both the statistical properties and the stylistic attributes of a specific input. This paper introduces a novel method for conditionally training GANs by embedding a specific style within the latent space of generated samples. Our approach is versatile and can be applied to various input modalities, including images, videos, and text. We demonstrate the method's efficacy across these diverse domains and highlight its potential applications in areas such as data augmentation and data anonymization. Furthermore, we present a new application in the field of data privacy, where the technique generates synthetic data to facilitate the analysis of sensitive information. To our knowledge, this represents the first instance of utilizing generative adversarial networks for this specific purpose. We have made our code publicly available to support this application. Bayesian nested sampling serves as a method for model comparison and parameter estimation. It utilizes importance sampling to navigate complex likelihood surfaces, accumulating data points that are increasingly unlikely. However, this process can result in data being sampled from distributions that are excessively concentrated, causing the algorithm to terminate prematurely. To address this, various resampling techniques have been developed to enhance the exploration of unlikely regions. We introduce a method utilizing two-time correlations to investigate two-particle momentum distributions in driven-dissipative Bose-Hubbard systems. This approach is demonstrated through two-particle correlations at first harmonic frequencies, which correspond to the momentum distributions of the steady state under counterpropagating two-beam driving conditions. The technique proves effective for both the dissipatively driven steady state and the associated frequency-domain response state. Furthermore, we demonstrate that this method can detect the superfluid-Mott insulator phase transition by identifying the critical ratio of hopping interaction strength to hopping frequency. Finally, we show that the method remains applicable even when the system is far from any driving-induced response. These findings establish a robust framework for experimentally measuring momentum distributions in non-equilibrium quantum many-body systems. Additionally, we anticipate that this approach will facilitate the study of phase transitions and topological properties in periodically driven (Floquet) and dissipatively driven quantum systems. The coefficients associated with the principal part belong to $C^1(\mathbb{R}^d)$, while the drifts are elements of $L^2(\mathbb{R}^d)$. The study focuses on establishing the existence and uniqueness of weak solutions within $L^p(\mathbb{R}^d)$, as well as the existence of unique solutions in $\text{BMO}(\mathbb{R}^d)$, for both inhomogeneous homogeneous problems. Furthermore, we analyze the behavior of the solution operator as a function of the ellipticity constant. These findings are subsequently applied to investigate the uniqueness of the representation problem for the Riesz potential. Additionally, we explore the implications of our results regarding the existence of Green functions. Finally, we address the existence of fundamental solutions for a specific class of operators. This paper introduces the distributional Gaussian process layer, a neural network component designed to enable deep neural networks to perform out-of-distribution detection. Functionally, this layer operates similarly to a Gaussian process by learning the conditional distribution of a multivariate Gaussian distribution over a latent space, conditioned on the network's activations and an empty prior dataset. We provide an analytical proof demonstrating that the layer's posterior distribution converges to a multivariate Gaussian distribution as the size of the prior dataset increases. Furthermore, we utilize this layer on a synthetic dataset to show its capacity for effective out-of-distribution detection. Finally, we evaluate the layer's performance in detecting corrupted inputs and identifying out-of-distribution images using both synthetic and real-world datasets. Our results indicate that the distributional Gaussian process layer can achieve out-of-distribution detection accuracy comparable to state-of-the-art methods while maintaining high generalization performance. The code is available at https://github.com/aleksandar-novakovic/DGP-layer. Our contributions are twofold: first, we propose a distributional Gaussian process layer capable of detecting out-of-distribution data; second, we provide a theoretical analysis of the layer's behavior as the prior dataset grows. We believe this layer will be valuable for enhancing the robustness of deep neural networks against adversarial attacks and out-of-distribution inputs. Our experimental results demonstrate that the layer can identify up to 90% of adversarial examples and out-of-distribution images without degrading accuracy on in-distribution data. Additionally, we show that incorporating a small prior dataset allows the layer to generalize to new datasets, enabling the detection of novel out-of-distribution classes. We also highlight the layer's effectiveness in detecting out-of-distribution inputs, such as MNIST digits rotated by 90 degrees, which are significantly more difficult than standard out-of-distribution classes. Finally, we demonstrate that the layer can detect input transformations, including rotations and color changes, that are not present in the training data. The source code can be found at https://github.com/aleksandar-novakovic/DGP-layer.

This study establishes a Strengthened Alexandrov Maximum Principle (SAMP) for the Monge–Ampère equation defined on a convex domain $\Omega \subset \mathbb{R}^n$ ($n \ge 2$) involving a bounded right-hand side. The proof relies on the theory of uniformly elliptic divergence-form equations with a right-hand side in $L^\infty(\Omega)$, specifically utilizing established $C^{0,1-\varepsilon}(\Omega)$ estimates. This work represents the first derivation of the SAMP for the Monge–Ampère equation with a bounded right-hand side, thereby extending the Alexandrov maximum principle originally formulated by Caffarelli, Li, and Nirenberg (1990) and later refined by Trudinger and Wang (2009) to cases where the right-hand side belongs to $L^p(\Omega)$ with $p > n/2$. Furthermore, the paper demonstrates the uniform Hölder continuity of $C^0$-bounded solutions to the specified Monge–Ampère equation, advancing upon the findings of Caffarelli, Nirenberg, and Johnson (1983) and Li and Wang (1990). These results are applicable to the study of the Dirichlet problem, the inhomogeneous Monge–Ampère equation, and the prescribed curvature problem. The primary contribution is a novel proof technique that leverages the SAMP of uniformly elliptic divergence-form equations with bounded right-hand sides to derive the uniform Hölder continuity of $C^0$-bounded solutions for the specified Monge–Ampère equation. This approach offers a significant simplification compared to the methods employed by Caffarelli, Nirenberg, and Johnson (1983) and Li and Wang (1990). The paper concludes with an outline of the proof strategy and a discussion of open questions. Keywords: Alexandrov maximum principle, Monge–Ampère equation, uniformly elliptic divergence-form equation, Hölder continuity, bounded right-hand side. We introduce a new holographic error correction code built upon a pyramid-shaped graph. This graph is divided into polygonal units linked by a central edge, mirroring the structure of a triangulation within a hyperbolic disk. Each edge connects to the three nearest edges in the disk and is associated with a unit that implements a three-qubit unitary gate. By setting all units to a specific corner solution, the resulting code corresponds to a perfect tensor network. We then analyze a family of approximate holographic codes derived from the hyper-invariant MERA network, which arises as the fixed point of a renormalization group flow on a $\mathbb{Z}_2$ Ising model with long-range interactions. These models are characterized by a power-law correlation decay and a negative temperature. The holographic codes are defined by a negative temperature parameter and an additional parameter that controls the deviation from the corner solution. We demonstrate that these networks maintain robust, constant-distance codes capable of correcting arbitrary errors. Furthermore, we establish that the fault tolerance of these codes scales with the temperature, reaching its peak at the critical point. Finally, we show that these networks can implement a non-trivial, non-local logical operator, thereby providing a concrete example of a code with non-trivial holographic geometry. This work extends the family of holographic error correction codes by incorporating power-law correlations and non-zero temperatures. The code's fault tolerance is enhanced by long-range interactions, which suppress the propagation of errors. Additionally, we show that the codes achieve optimal distance by operating at the critical point. This result is supported by the presence of a non-analyticity in the free energy of the model at the critical point. We also examine the behavior of the model in the low-temperature regime, where the model exhibits a phase transition to a ferromagnetic state. We find that the codes perform optimally at a temperature that decreases as the deviation from the corner solution increases. We discuss the potential for generalizing these models to higher dimensions and their applications in quantum simulation. Our findings suggest that these models can be engineered using Rydberg atom arrays, which are capable of simulating long-range interactions and operating near the critical point. This capability offers a pathway to creating a quantum computer with a large number of qubits. This study introduces a distributed control strategy designed to implement Conservation Voltage Reduction (CVR) across both primary and secondary distribution networks. The primary goal is to lower voltage levels to decrease real power losses and suppress real power demand, all while adhering to specific voltage constraints. To achieve this, an optimal control framework is developed, which is subsequently converted into a distributed form. This distributed approach relies on two essential components: distributed gradient updates for each distributed optimal control variable and distributed consensus updates for auxiliary variables. The efficacy of the proposed distributed CVR scheme is validated through simulations utilizing a real-world test system. Results demonstrate that the distributed method performs comparably to the centralized approach, successfully achieving the desired optimal CVR outcomes across the entire test system. Furthermore, this distributed solution offers a significant advantage by eliminating the need for extensive communication between the distribution utility and individual distribution transformers. This ensures that the distributed distributed CVR scheme can be readily deployed in practical settings. Finally, the algorithm's performance is evaluated under various scenarios, such as the outage of specific agents, to verify its robustness and reliability. These evaluations confirm that the distributed distributed CVR scheme can reliably achieve optimal voltage reduction throughout the entire test system. This research investigates nonstochastic bandits and experts within a framework characterized by arm-dependent delays. In this setting, an algorithm selects an arm, potentially encountering a delay of varying length, during which no reward or feedback is received. We introduce a novel framework where delay durations are governed by a function of the selected arm and the accumulated regret of an imaginary algorithm. We demonstrate that, under a specific condition on this function, a quasi-no-regret algorithm exists whose regret grows at a rate of $O(\sqrt{T})$. Furthermore, we establish that this condition is tight by proving that for any function exceeding this threshold, at least one instance can be constructed where the best achievable regret is $\omega(T)$. Our framework encompasses several prior models as special cases, including the expert problem, the full information expert problem, and a specific delayed bandit scenario previously analyzed. Additionally, we present a new framework for delayed experts that is also tight. Finally, we introduce a new tight condition for the delayed expert problem, which was previously an open question. These conditions are expressed in terms of the properties of a matrix derived from the instance, a method that unifies the analysis of both bandits and experts. We also provide a unified analysis for both bandits and experts. Notably, we demonstrate that a no-regret algorithm exists for delayed bandits even when the condition is not tight, provided the number of arms is small relative to the function's growth rate. This result is tight, as we show that if the arm count is large, no such algorithm exists. Crucially, these findings apply to both the full information and partial information bandit problems. Our analysis relies on a new technique that avoids the need to construct specific instances to demonstrate tightness. Instead, we utilize a continuous relaxation of the problem and apply tools from control theory to prove tightness. This approach is broadly applicable and can be adapted to other tightness analyses. Finally, we discuss the relationship between our condition and the concept of "connectivity" found in existing literature. We show that while connectivity is tight for uniform growth functions, it is not tight in general. We also introduce a new condition based on a matrix that is tight for all functions and provide a simple proof for this result. Our condition is also tight, and we extend this analysis to both bandits and experts. The paper is structured as follows: Section 2 presents the problem formulation; Section 3 covers the main results; Section 4 addresses tightness; and Section 5 offers a discussion. This study introduces a novel probabilistic surrogate model designed to estimate the stochastic response of an offshore wind turbine under stochastic wave and wind loading. The surrogate, built on a chained architecture, utilizes Gaussian processes to represent the joint probability density function of the system response. It is trained using a limited dataset of simulations generated by a high-fidelity, time-domain, time-history-based numerical model. The methodology is validated using the NREL 5MW offshore wind turbine, with results compared against the numerical model and a commercial probabilistic reliability software. The study demonstrates that the chained Gaussian process surrogate can accurately and efficiently model the joint probability density function of significant response variables, including tower-top displacement, tower-top rotation, and the 3rd and 1st blade-root bending moments. Furthermore, the surrogate proves capable of identifying the dominant failure modes governing system reliability. Finally, the approach is shown to enable rapid, on-demand probabilistic assessments, allowing for the swift evaluation of various scenarios and the analysis of how response statistics and reliability vary with changes in environmental conditions and design parameters. These capabilities are essential for optimizing the design and operation of offshore wind farms. The paper concludes by outlining future research directions, such as extending the method to model the joint probability density function of a larger set of response variables. This expansion would facilitate the analysis of response non-stationarity and the identification of non-stationary periods, which is crucial for assessing the accuracy of stationary assumptions in design and operation. Additionally, modeling a broader set of responses would support the analysis of response correlation, a key factor in assessing the potential for load and power-sharing strategies to mitigate extreme loads. Such analysis is particularly relevant for scenarios involving multiple turbines operating in close proximity. Overall, the proposed chained Gaussian process framework offers a highly efficient and accurate solution for analyzing the stochastic behavior of offshore wind turbines, with potential applications in various other engineering fields. The method is implemented in an open-source Python library available at https://github.com/aboukilla/gp_surrogate. This library can be easily adapted to model the stochastic behavior of other engineering systems, provided that a numerical model capable of generating the required stochastic input-output data is available. The paper also provides a tutorial on using the library. The availability of an open-source implementation of the method and the associated library will facilitate further research and foster collaboration among researchers and practitioners. The paper also includes a discussion of potential future research opportunities. Finally, the paper includes a discussion of the limitations of the proposed method. Social media platforms have become integral to social media data analysis, a field that has gained significant traction in recent years. This paper examines the impact of the May 6, 2022, earthquake in Turkey and Syria, specifically focusing on Twitter data from the Turkish city of Izmir. The study employs a novel approach to analyze social sentiment and monitor the evolution of trending topics. Furthermore, it introduces a new method for detecting trend changes within topic clusters. The findings indicate that, following the initial shock, public interest in the event gradually diminished, and topic clusters exhibited distinct characteristics. The results also demonstrate that the proposed method is effective for tracking the progression of trending topics. Additionally, the methodology is adaptable for monitoring various events, such as elections, and the code is publicly accessible. Ultimately, the paper underscores the potential of social media data analysis for disaster management. The source code can be found at: https://github.com/ozlemkose/TopicClustering. This study introduces a new framework for reconstructing time-resolved data, specifically addressing the inversion of time-resolved x-ray computed tomography. The proposed method employs a forward-optimization strategy that integrates a physics-informed prior with a physics-based prior. To address the under-determined nature of the inverse problem, a forward-optimization process is utilized to minimize the data misfit by adhering to a suitable entropy measure of the inverse problem's solutions. This prior is constructed by embedding a prior on a set of time-evolution trajectories within a chosen basis. The framework is validated using a time-evolution dataset of a single crystal undergoing phase transformation, demonstrating that the method successfully recovers the sequence of crystal orientations and slip planes. Furthermore, the approach is robust to noise in time-evolution data and effectively mitigates the issue of data misfit stagnation. Boundary conformal field theory (BCFT) and interface conformal field theory (ICFT) have garnered significant interest due to their roles in the holographic framework, specifically describing the dynamics of holographic quantum field theories near black hole horizons. This paper extends the concept of reflected entropy to these lower-dimensional conformal field theories. By employing the HKL method, we calculate the reflected entropy for arbitrary regions within pure and single-interval BCFTs across two dimensions. Furthermore, we derive the reflected entropy for a double-interval region in an interface conformal field theory (ICFT). Additionally, we determine the reflected entropy for arbitrary regions in 2D BCFTs when they are dual to anti-de Sitter spaces with a boundary (AdS_3 with a boundary), utilizing the RTZ formula. Finally, we illustrate the connection between reflected entropy and the correlation between boundary operators. Our findings demonstrate that reflected entropy remains non-monotonic in these lower-dimensional settings. These results offer a valuable foundation for investigating the lower-dimensional holographic duality between quantum field theories and black hole horizons. Additionally, we identify a new information quantity within holographic quantum field theories that exhibits non-monotonic behavior. This work paves the way for exploring reflected entropy in higher dimensions and may facilitate the investigation of its holographic complexity. Finally, we anticipate that the methods developed here will assist in calculating reflected entropy in other contexts. The calculations presented herein were performed using the Xenia software. The source code is accessible at: https://github.com/ChenYi1999/ReflectedEntropy. Future research will extend these results to higher dimensions. This paper introduces a novel channel estimation framework designed for RF reconfigurable intelligent surface (RIS)-aided orthogonal frequency division multiplexing (OFDM) systems operating under hardware imperfections and reduced cyclic prefix (CP) durations. The proposed method utilizes a single pilot symbol, an extended learning model, and a two-stage enhanced learning map to achieve high-precision channel state information (CSI) recovery. Specifically, the extended learning model addresses the under-determined nature of the system by mapping the received signal to an intermediate variable, while the enhanced learning map further refines this by incorporating the estimated channel into the mapping process to produce the final channel estimate. The study evaluates the performance across three distinct hardware scenarios: perfect, imperfect phase shifters, and imperfect phase/amplitude shifts. Simulation results demonstrate that the proposed scheme significantly outperforms existing methods, achieving a 1 dB gain over the enhanced learning map and a 2 dB gain over the extended learning model. Furthermore, the scheme exhibits robustness against estimation errors caused by insufficient CP, phase noise, and amplitude quantization errors. Finally, the computational complexity of the proposed approach is lower than that of other existing techniques. Keywords: Channel estimation, RIS, OFDM, Extended learning model, Deep learning.

This work examines the deformation theory of $\mathrm{G}_2$-instantons on nearly $\mathrm{G}_2$ manifolds. We demonstrate that the obstructions to integrating a tangent vector from the moduli space into a full instanton deformation map lie within the kernel of the operator $\psi \wedge \cdot : \Omega^1 \to \Omega^2$. This finding extends a result by Ferenc Szabó, who established that the operator possesses no kernel for genuine $\mathrm{G}_2$-instantons. Furthermore, this insight offers an explanation for why certain non-flat instantons on nearly $\mathrm{G}_2$ manifolds exhibit infinite-dimensional deformation spaces. Finally, we present examples of curvature components that prevent self-dual connections on nearly $\mathrm{G}_2$ manifolds from being instantons. These findings contrast with those on nearly Kähler manifolds, where it has been proven that all non-Abelian instantons are flat. The COVID-19 pandemic has spurred numerous countries to implement contact tracing applications as part of their strategies to curb the virus's spread. However, these applications face significant privacy challenges, prompting the need for rigorous and effective privacy assessments. This study introduces a privacy analysis framework that integrates information theory with probabilistic modeling to evaluate the privacy risks inherent in contact tracing systems. This approach enables the quantification of information and correlations within such systems. In this Letter, we investigate a model of a finite, closed chain of interacting qubits to identify the emergence of quantum information. We demonstrate that, for a specific set of initial conditions, the system transitions from a highly entangled state to one marked by significant quantum mutual information. Furthermore, we show that these information metrics can be estimated using only local observables. These findings hold potential applications in the study of quantum simulators and the development of efficient experimental protocols for measuring quantum information in complex systems. Additionally, we outline a method for designing experimental setups to test these quantum information measures in real-world systems. Our proposed approach is validated through data collected from a quantum circuit experiment. Finally, we discuss the relevance of these results to artificial neural networks. Specifically, we find that the relationship between mutual information and the distance between neurons in a real-world artificial neural network trained to recognize handwritten digits mirrors the behavior observed in our qubit chain model. This suggests that the mechanisms governing the information flow in our qubit chain model may also be present in artificial neural networks. We conclude that our model provides a valuable tool for investigating quantum information in both artificial and biological neural systems. This paper introduces a C code generator for ACL2 that identifies ACL2 representations of C constructs based on a shallow embedding of C within ACL2 and translates them back into their corresponding C forms. Furthermore, this work represents an early stage in a broader research initiative aimed at developing a general code generator for any shallow embedding of a source language into a formal logic. This study examines the application of machine learning to solve initial value problems in cosmology. We demonstrate that a neural network can efficiently learn the map between initial and final conditions for the Klein-Gordon field, a task that is analytically intractable. This capability enables the rapid prediction of future cosmological states and the swift inversion of the problem. Furthermore, we show that a neural network can identify the symmetries of a physical system without prior knowledge, allowing for the reconstruction of the system's equations of motion. We also explore the use of graph neural networks to represent cosmological perturbations, proving their ability to predict future states of these perturbations. Finally, we investigate the generation of synthetic datasets for training neural networks using generative adversarial networks. These tools offer a novel approach to analyzing cosmological initial value problems and hold potential for uncovering new physics. Our findings suggest that machine learning is poised to become an essential instrument in cosmology. Our code is publicly accessible at https://github.com/akshaykumar2000/CosmoML.

This paper presents a next-to-leading-order (NLO) investigation into the production of $J/\psi$, $\chi_{c0}$, and $\chi_{c2}$ in the process $e^{e}^{+} \to J/\psi + \eta_c,\chi_{cJ}$ at $\sqrt{s} \approx 10.6$ GeV. We calculate the cross sections and the longitudinal and transverse polarization components for these processes at both leading order (LO) and NLO using the color-singlet model. Our NLO findings reveal a substantial increase in the cross sections for $e^{+}e^{-} \to J/\psi + \eta_c,\chi_{cJ}$, whereas the production of $J/\psi + \chi_{c1}$ remains unchanged. Furthermore, the polarization of the $J/\psi$ and $\chi_{cJ}$ states is determined through the spin density matrix elements. This study examines how Signal users perceive and utilize the PIN security feature. We surveyed 100 Signal users and interviewed 20 of them to explore their beliefs, definitions, and usage of the PIN. Our findings indicate that user perceptions of the PIN's purpose vary significantly, with many users unaware of its specific role. Furthermore, users hold diverse views on the PIN's characteristics, including its length, complexity, and recovery methods. These insights into user perceptions can assist Signal developers in refining the feature's design and communication. Solar irradiance, which varies with the sun's position, is frequently utilized in numerical simulations across diverse fields. This paper introduces a general framework for computing irradiance integrals using a quadrature rule. We derive a set of optimal abscissae and weights for solar-weighted integrals, enabling high-accuracy approximations with a minimal number of evaluations. Additionally, we provide a computational method to generate these optimal points and weights for any given degree of quadrature. The approach is validated through numerical experiments, demonstrating its accuracy and efficiency. The resulting solar-weighted abscissae and weights are made available for public use. Furthermore, we illustrate a broad application of this framework by developing a highly accurate and efficient solver for the radiative transfer equation. The radiative transfer weights and corresponding solvers are also released for public access. This paper serves as a comprehensive guide for accurately and efficiently evaluating irradiance and solving the radiative transfer equation. All code is open-source and accessible via GitHub. The accompanying supplementary material includes routines for calculating solar-weighted quadrature points and weights, as well as a radiative transfer solver. The primary reference [1] details the derivation of the quadrature points and weights, while [2] describes the derivation of the radiative transfer solver. This work expands upon the findings presented in [1-2].

Keywords: solar irradiance, quadrature rule, radiative transfer equation, numerical integration, numerical simulation.

The curvature information of a deep neural network (DNN) is essential for numerous applications, including robustness analysis, model compression, and training. This paper introduces a curvature access method based on the generalized Gauss-Newton (GGN) matrix, leveraging its low-rank structure. By employing a curvature-based metric for evaluating model quality, we demonstrate that GGN's low-rank property stems from the model's high quality. Furthermore, we develop a curvature access technique that approximates GGN using its dominant eigenvectors, with a complexity comparable to that of a standard DNN. This approach is validated through experiments on MNIST and CIFAR10. Our results indicate that the proposed method can efficiently extract the GGN's low-rank structure, achieving performance equivalent to full-rank GGN. Additionally, we show that this curvature-based metric effectively identifies the most challenging samples for a given DNN. Finally, we illustrate the method's effectiveness in downstream tasks, including model pruning, compression, and robustness analysis. Notably, the curvature access model demonstrates superior performance in these applications compared to a DNN trained with the same number of parameters. This study investigates how grammatical gender influences word representations in language models trained on a gender-rich language. By analyzing the embeddings of German models (BERT and ELMo) across various tasks, the research examines how the model treats nouns of different genders and whether these gendered patterns are utilized during training. Results indicate that models generate distinct grammatical gender representations, which are leveraged for tasks requiring gender knowledge, such as predicting agreement morphemes or identifying gender primes. However, these representations fail to predict semantic gender or gender stereotypes. Furthermore, the study reveals that models tend to associate masculine nouns with concrete concepts and feminine nouns with abstract ones, a bias that contributes to gender bias within the models. Finally, the authors explore how specific training tasks impact these gender-related biases. The code for this study is accessible at \url{https://github.com/linguistics-and-ai/gender-in-german-bert}. The findings are also replicated for English BERT models. This work represents the first large-scale investigation into grammatical gender in gender-marking languages, offering a novel perspective on the gender dimensions within neural representations. It underscores the need for further research into gender biases in NLP, particularly regarding the distinction between grammatical and semantic gender. Additionally, the study highlights the challenges inherent in measuring gender and proposes a new methodology for assessing gender bias in NLP. The data and methods employed can be adapted for other languages and gender types. Accurate short-term traffic prediction is essential for intelligent transportation systems, yet it remains difficult due to the scarcity of historical data and the diverse nature of traffic patterns across different road segments. To address this challenge, we introduce a similarity-driven approach that leverages historical data to enhance forecasting accuracy. Our method relies on the observation that roads with similar daily traffic volume patterns can share historical data to improve prediction. We demonstrate that extracting a low-dimensional feature space based on these patterns facilitates efficient similarity matching. Furthermore, this feature space enables a sparse linear model for prediction. Experimental results show that our approach significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods in both accuracy and computational efficiency. This paper introduces VACA, a new class of variational graph autoencoders designed for causal inference. Unlike existing generative models that struggle to represent causal structures or answer interventional and counterfactual questions, VACA is built to learn causal graphs and support valid causal reasoning. Cyber-physical systems (CPS) are anticipated to become increasingly ubiquitous in the near future, with the concept of systems of systems (SoS) gaining prominence as a primary means to manage these complex environments. This paper introduces the concept of an intelligent SoS, which leverages the inherent intelligence of its constituent CPS to achieve a holistic, system-level understanding. We examine the challenges associated with developing such intelligent SoS architectures and propose a foundational framework that utilizes the concept of "intelligent reflection" to generate high-level abstractions of individual CPS. This framework enables the SoS to maintain a comprehensive view of its composition, thereby supporting high-level reasoning and the dynamic, on-the-fly reconfiguration of the SoS itself. The efficacy of this framework is demonstrated through an initial case study involving a smart home setting. Ultimately, we argue that the intelligent SoS framework presented here offers a novel and promising approach for the design and deployment of intelligent cyber-physical systems. Additionally, we outline several avenues for future research, including the need for new theoretical foundations, innovative algorithms, and advanced tools to facilitate the realization of these systems. Finally, we identify the Internet of Things (IoT) as a significant future application domain for intelligent SoS. By leveraging the intelligence of IoT devices, we can enhance the overall system's cognitive capabilities, leading to improved decision-making and the ability to autonomously adapt to evolving contexts. This advancement will enable the creation of more intelligent, self-aware, and self-healing IoT ecosystems. This study introduces MAPPIES, a novel Monte-Carlo code designed to simulate the origin of the ultraviolet (UV) and soft X-ray excess observed in the spectra of blazars. The model incorporates a relativistic jet with a power-law electron energy distribution subjected to a power-law photon field, both of which are external to the jet. This external Compton scattering framework is particularly well-suited for radio-quiet active galactic nuclei (AGN), where the jet is hypothesized to be in a hadronic state. The code accounts for electron energy loss via synchrotron radiation and inverse Compton scattering, as well as photon absorption through pair production and the photon field. Furthermore, the model includes the radiative cooling of the electron population and its polarization induced by the anisotropy of the photon field. We applied this approach to the radio-quiet AGN 3C 273, successfully reproducing the UV/X-ray excess in its spectrum. The analysis indicates that a power-law photon field with an index of $\alpha_f = 1.5$ and a density of $n_f = 10^4$ cm$^{-3}$, combined with an electron distribution of $n_e = 10^{20}$ cm$^{-3}$ and a Lorentz factor of $\gamma_e = 10^4$, can explain the emission. The resulting polarization degree is estimated at $P_e = 0.001$. These findings suggest that the UV/soft X-ray excess in 3C 273 may arise from external Compton scattering of polarized photons by relativistic electrons within a radio-quiet jet. Additionally, the study demonstrates that the MAPPIES model can replicate the observed spectra of radio-loud AGN, such as Mrk 421 and Mrk 501, as well as the X-ray emission from the black hole X-ray binary Cyg X-1. Finally, we outline the potential of the MAPPIES model to constrain the physical properties of AGN jets and black hole X-ray binaries. We examine the analytic properties of the partition function in theories featuring complex scalar potentials. We demonstrate that, under specific conditions, the partition function can be analytically continued to a holomorphic function defined over the space of complexified couplings. This analytical property holds particular significance for investigating the spectral characteristics of the Hamiltonian. We examine the relevant analytic structure in an explicit, yet non-trivial, example: a quantum mechanical system with a double-well potential. Furthermore, we explore the implications of this finding for the swampland program. Specifically, we argue that the analytic continuation of the partition function around complexified couplings imposes novel constraints on the spectrum of quantum gravity theories. We illustrate these constraints with a non-trivial example: the spectrum of four-dimensional $\mathcal{N}=2$ theories. Additionally, we examine the analytic structure of the partition function in the presence of a background electric field, revealing that the resulting function is multi-valued and characterized by branch cuts. We elucidate the origin of this multi-valuedness and its connection to the WKB approximation. Finally, we discuss the implications of this structure for the conjectured analytic continuation of the partition function over complex couplings. In conclusion, we contend that the analytic structure of the partition function in quantum theories with complex scalar potentials remains an underexplored domain, one that may yield significant insights into the fundamental characteristics of quantum gravity. This paper serves as a preliminary investigation into this subject. A more comprehensive study will be presented in a forthcoming publication. Finally, we note that several of the concepts explored herein were previously examined in the context of Yang-Mills theories with complex couplings. This work addresses the quantum state identification problem, specifically focusing on the online context where the unknown state is selected from a known set of mutually orthogonal states. While a straightforward strategy exists for identifying the full set of $d$ mutually orthogonal qubit states, the efficient online identification of two or more symmetric states in higher dimensions remains an unresolved question. We demonstrate that two symmetric states can be identified with $n+1$ measurements using $n+1$ distinct observables, each requiring only a single measurement. Furthermore, we propose that $k$ symmetric states can be identified using $n + k - 1$ measurements. Finally, we examine the strategy for identifying three symmetric states, offering a partial solution. Our findings are applicable to quantum key distribution, quantum random access codes, and the identification of unnormalized pure states. Additionally, the proposed measurement strategy can be implemented using a single photon across $d$ modes. Baryon production is investigated through the quantized fragmentation of a helical string, which models color flux between a diquark and a quark. By analyzing the string's decay into hadrons, we calculate baryon production rates and their momentum distributions. The resulting yields align with the $\sim 1/27$ ratio of meson production, while the momentum distributions match the observed $p^2$ scaling. Furthermore, this quantized fragmentation framework offers a natural explanation for the diquark-quark enhancement observed in the fragmentation functions of baryons relative to mesons. These findings are derived from the analytic solution to the string decay problem, which incorporates realistic baryon masses and decay widths. Additionally, the model predicts a $\sim 1/9$ yield for hidden charm baryons, a value that can be tested in future experiments. The study also addresses the potential for baryon-antibaryon correlations, a feature that could be investigated in future studies of back-to-back hadron production. Finally, the work discusses the relationship between the helical string model and the tunneling model of baryon production. The Sun's internal rotation is influenced by flows surrounding active regions (ARs). This study investigates the potential impact of these flows on north-south helioseismic travel-time measurements. We developed a method to quantify the contribution of AR-related flows to helioseismic data. By applying this method to 17.5 years of SDO/HMI data, we identified 1,000 ARs and calculated their contributions to travel-time measurements. Our results indicate that the average AR affects the mean north-south helioseismic travel time by approximately 0.02 seconds, while the maximum contribution reaches about 0.06 seconds. We further analyzed the temporal evolution of these contributions and their correlation with sunspot number data. Finally, we compared the observed impact of ARs on helioseismic travel times with the magnitude of low-latitude meridional flow anomalies. This analysis suggests that ARs may account for up to 50% of the observed low-latitude meridional flow anomalies. These findings have significant implications for understanding the solar dynamo. Additionally, we have made our code available for others to apply to their own data. [abridged] (Cite as: Sol. Pulsar Timing Array (PTA) experiments are currently searching for a stochastic gravitational wave background (SGWB) within the nanohertz frequency band. This study demonstrates that the background generated by a turbulent, stochastic primordial magnetic field (PMF) can be detected by PTA facilities, including the International Pulsar Timing Array (IPTA), NANOGrav, EPTA, and PPTA. We establish that the PMF-induced SGWB exhibits a nearly flat spectral energy density across the PTA frequency range, with a detectable signal contingent upon the PMF's helicity and the turbulence injection scale. Specifically, signal detection is feasible when the PMF helicity is small and the injection scale is large. Furthermore, we show that the characteristic amplitude of the PMF-induced SGWB can reach the minimum detectable level for PTA instruments, particularly when the injection scale is large and the PMF amplitude is minimal. Consequently, PTA observations may identify the SGWB origin as PMF-induced, thereby offering a novel method to investigate the physics of the early universe. Additionally, we provide a formula for the SGWB amplitude, which can be utilized to constrain the properties of PMFs. Finally, we conclude that the PMF-induced SGWB is potentially detectable by PTA instruments in the near future. This detection would enable researchers to determine the PMF amplitude and turbulence injection scale, while also constraining the PMF decay rate and the PMF generation mechanism. These findings could significantly advance our understanding of the early universe. Future work will explore the detectability of the PMF-induced SGWB by third-generation space-based gravitational wave detectors. This paper introduces a learning-based disparity model designed for the compression of light field (LF) images. Unlike conventional approaches that rely on computationally intensive methods to estimate disparities, our model leverages the capabilities of convolutional neural networks (CNNs) to predict disparity values directly from raw LF data. The estimated disparities are then utilized to reorganize the LF into a plane-based format, which serves as input for subsequent compression stages. We also detail the implementation of these compression stages, which include a CNN-based encoder and decoder paired with an entropy model for compressing the plane-based LFs. Extensive experiments were conducted to evaluate the proposed model's performance. Results demonstrate that our approach achieves superior compression efficiency compared to other methods, particularly in scenarios where disparity estimation is challenging. Furthermore, we show that the model generalizes effectively to LF datasets beyond the one used for training. Small-area estimation (SAE) is a statistical framework designed to derive reliable estimates for small populations, such as specific geographic regions or demographic groups. This methodology is particularly valuable for generating estimates of health indicators like HIV prevalence and fertility rates in developing nations, where data are often scarce and expensive to collect. The primary objective of SAE is to leverage large-scale surveys to produce robust estimates for areas where no survey data exist. This study evaluates various SAE methodologies, including model-based and design-based techniques, to estimate HIV prevalence and fertility rates within the context of the Malawi National Demographic and Health Survey (MDHS 2015/16). The analysis utilizes data from 288 districts across the Malawi Central Statistical Office's District Statistical Area (DSA) framework. Findings indicate that model-based methods outperform design-based approaches in estimating HIV prevalence and fertility rates for small areas, offering superior accuracy and reliability. Consequently, the study recommends the adoption of model-based SAE for small-area estimation in low- and middle-income countries. Additionally, a novel model is introduced to enhance the precision of HIV prevalence and fertility rate estimates for small areas. This new model incorporates auxiliary variables related to socio-economic status, education, and health, alongside key HIV drivers such as age, marital status, and urbanization. The results demonstrate that integrating these variables significantly improves estimation accuracy. The study concludes that integrating relevant auxiliary variables into model-based SAE frameworks can substantially boost the precision of estimates for HIV prevalence and fertility rates in low- and middle-income countries. The accompanying R package, `smallarea`, is available at https://github.com/abakker/smallarea. The package includes the `saemethods` function, which implements the proposed model-based SAE approach, and the `saeexamples` function, which provides the datasets and code used in this analysis. Furthermore, the package offers a suite of additional functions to calculate estimates, assess model fit, and generate output reports. The package also features a suite of design-based SAE methods, including `svy2sae`, which utilizes the `survey` package to apply Taylor series linearization for SAE. The `svy2sae` function supports both model-based and design-based estimation, allowing users to select the most appropriate method for their specific analysis. This study examines a generalized quantum version of the classic Kelly Betting problem, distinguishing it from prior research by incorporating a continuous variable approach. We demonstrate that the optimal betting strategy involves preparing a specific class of entangled states across multiple betting channels. Furthermore, the analysis reveals a non-trivial connection between the optimal betting strategy and the von Neumann entropy of the underlying quantum states. Finally, we illustrate that the proposed scheme enables non-trivial wagering on events that would remain impossible to bet upon in the classical framework. These findings have significant implications for quantum financial modeling and offer a potential avenue for experimental verification. Additionally, we discuss the problem's relevance within the broader context of quantum game theory. Our results are supported by supplementary material available at [1]. Keywords: Quantum Finance, Quantum Game Theory, Quantum Information Theory.

We present a three-dimensional simulation of the gravitational collapse of a prestellar core to create a protostar and its surrounding protoplanetary disk. Our model incorporates a novel implementation of the SPH algorithm that enables the self-consistent formation of a disk from the collapse of a spherical cloud. The initial prestellar core, characterized by a mass of 0.5 solar masses and a radius of 0.05 parsecs, was modeled as a uniform sphere with a temperature of 10 Kelvin and a mean density of $10^4$ particles per cubic centimeter. The simulation was advanced until the central object's mass reached 0.2 solar masses. Results indicate that the prestellar core contracts into a star-disk system where the disk comprises 90% of the central mass. The disk's outer edge settles at a radius of 100 astronomical units, while the central star stabilizes at a mass of 0.2 solar masses. The final system consists of a central star with a mass of 0.2 solar masses, a disk of identical mass, and a central density of $10^{10}$ particles per cubic centimeter. The disk's outer boundary is defined by a density of $10^{-2}$ particles per cubic centimeter, with a scale height of 10 astronomical units. The star-disk temperature is 100 Kelvin, and the temperature gradient follows a $T \propto r^{-0.5}$ profile. The disk's surface density is described by $\Sigma \propto r^{-1.5}$, while the midplane density follows $\rho \propto r^{-2}$. The disk's viscosity is governed by the temperature profile, resulting in a kinematic viscosity of $\nu = 10^{17} r^2$ cm$^2$/s. Finally, the disk's angular velocity is determined by the viscosity profile, yielding an angular velocity of $\Omega = 10^{-10}$ s$^{-1}$. These findings offer a viable framework for simulating disk formation from the collapse of prestellar cores. Furthermore, the derived disk parameters align with observations of young stellar objects, suggesting that the proposed model can be applied to study the formation of young stellar objects. Additionally, the disk parameters provide a foundation for investigating planet formation. This work serves as a precursor to our subsequent study, which will examine planet formation within the disk generated in this simulation. The simulation code is accessible at https://github.com/

Atmospheric dispersion correctors (ADCs) are essential instruments in modern ground-based telescopes, designed to eliminate the impact of atmospheric dispersion on astronomical observations. This study introduces a novel methodology for measuring on-sky atmospheric dispersion and applies it to data collected using the ESO 3.6m telescope's Fast-Windows Spectrograph (FWS). By analyzing over 100 on-sky ADC measurements, we developed a global atmospheric dispersion model that incorporates both a statistical description of atmospheric conditions and a set of extreme values. This comprehensive modeling approach enables the determination of ADC parameters required to satisfy the European Southern Observatory's (ESO) service level agreement. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the statistical properties of atmospheric dispersion can be quantified using a single spectroscopic measurement, thereby reducing the time and financial resources needed for these measurements. The paper concludes with a discussion of the advantages and limitations of this new modeling approach. The resulting atmospheric dispersion model is accessible via the ESO Public Archive. (Abridged)

We present Pontryagin duality for locally compact abelian groups within the framework of continuous first-order logic. Specifically, for any topological abelian group $A$, we define a topological group $B$ such that the category of continuous maps from $A$ to the circle group $S^1$, equipped with the uniform topology, is isomorphic via Pontryagin duality to the category of homeomorphisms from $B$ to itself, also under the uniform topology, when viewed through continuous logic. This construction yields the novel result that the group of circle-valued continuous homomorphisms from the circle group to itself, endowed with the uniform topology, is not locally compact in the Euclidean topology. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the uniform topology on these homomorphisms is metrizable if and only if $A$ is either discrete or compact. Additionally, we establish that the uniform topology on these homomorphisms coincides with the topology generated by the continuous logic formulas of $A$. Finally, utilizing the language of continuous logic for $A$, we provide a first-order definition for the subgroup of homomorphisms that are continuous with respect to the original topology of $A$. These findings offer a continuous logic interpretation of various properties of the space of such homomorphisms. Notably, we characterize the local compactness of this space via continuous logic formulas and determine that the type space of $A$ remains unchanged when equipped with the uniform topology. We also investigate the continuity of the map $A \mapsto B$ relative to the uniform topology. While this map is generally discontinuous, we identify a class of groups where it becomes continuous under the uniform topology, including all compact groups and those possessing a finite number of irreducible subgroups up to conjugacy. For groups within this class, we explicitly characterize the topology of $B$ using continuous logic formulas. The paper concludes with an appendix detailing the continuous logic formulation of the Peter-Weyl theorem. This work extends the methodology introduced in [10] to the setting of continuous logic. This study addresses two critical challenges in federated learning: ensuring fairness and maintaining privacy. To achieve these goals, we introduce a novel federated privacy fair stochastic gradient descent (FPFSGD) algorithm. By integrating differential privacy with fair stochastic gradient descent, the method ensures that sensitive user data remains protected while simultaneously guaranteeing fair model performance across different user groups. We provide a theoretical analysis of the proposed approach, demonstrating that it offers differential privacy guarantees and achieves optimal convergence rates for both global and local loss functions. Furthermore, we empirically evaluate the technique using two standard datasets, comparing its efficacy against existing federated learning methods. The results indicate that our proposed method outperforms current alternatives in terms of both fairness and privacy preservation. Additionally, we offer a comprehensive comparison with differential privacy-based fair stochastic gradient descent, highlighting the superior privacy guarantees of our approach. Finally, we explore how varying numbers of clients influence the method's performance. Overall, our findings suggest that FPFSGD is a promising solution for enhancing fairness and privacy in federated learning environments. We introduce a supersymmetric framework extending the Standard Model with a $U(1)_X$ gauge symmetry, where the gauge boson acquires a 1 TeV mass through a vacuum expectation value of a scalar field. This model incorporates a right-handed neutrino for each generation to ensure anomaly cancellation. The $U(1)_X$ charge assignments are derived from a $Z_4^Y$ symmetry, which assigns a charge of $-2$ to the right-handed neutrino. We demonstrate that the neutrino oscillation data can be accommodated via see-saw mechanisms operating at both tree and one-loop levels. Furthermore, we show that a significant portion of the parameter space allows the one-loop right-handed Majorana neutrino to account for dark matter. In this scenario, we examine the collider signatures of the model and its detectability within current and upcoming experiments. Our findings indicate that the proposed parameter space is accessible to the LHC and its high-luminosity upgrade, as well as to future experiments such as XENONnT, DARWIN, and HyperKamiokande. Additionally, we discuss the implications of neutrinoless double beta decay experiments in probing this region. Finally, we establish that the model can explain the muon $g-2$ anomaly and the B meson decay discrepancies. This work serves as a foundation for investigating similar models with $U(1)_X$ charges determined by a $Z_4$ or $Z_5$ symmetry. In those variants, the right-handed neutrino carries a $Z_4^Y$ charge of $-1$ or $0$, respectively. We anticipate that these models will exhibit distinct phenomenological features compared to the $Z_4^Y$ scenario. Our analysis suggests that the parameter space where the right-handed neutrino constitutes dark matter is excluded in both $Z_4$ and $Z_5$ cases. However, the $Z_4$ model permits a viable parameter region where a Kaluza-Klein particle serves as dark matter, a possibility not present in the $Z_5$ case. This study introduces an IRS-assisted Wireless Powered Communication Network (WPCN) designed to enhance the throughput of a Time Division Multiple Access (TDMA) system operating in the presence of interference. The objective is to optimize the duration of energy harvesting and information processing intervals, alongside the design of the IRS phase-shifting pattern, to maximize the network's total throughput. To address this, an unsupervised deep learning approach is employed, which avoids the need for extensive training data. The proposed method yields significant throughput improvements compared to existing schemes, while also reducing computational complexity and eliminating the requirement for training data. Furthermore, the method demonstrates robustness against variations in the number of learning iterations and the number of hidden layers. Finally, the study confirms the method's effectiveness in scenarios where the base station lacks global channel state information. Keywords: Wireless Powered Communication Network, IRS, Deep Learning, Unsupervised Learning. (Corresponding author: M. S. Alouini)

The beta-decay characteristics of $^{186}$Hg were investigated using a high-purity germanium detector. The decay scheme was constructed, and the half-life was determined to be $T_{1/2} = 3.06(4)$ s. Additionally, beta-decay intensities, gamma-ray conversion coefficients, and beta-delayed neutron branching ratios were measured. These findings were compared with the results of shell model calculations. The study confirms that the beta-decay of $^{186}$Hg is primarily delayed by neutrons, with a significant beta-delayed neutron branching ratio of $P_n = 31(4)\%$. We introduce a unified framework that simultaneously accounts for dark matter and neutrino mass/leptogenesis. This model extends the Standard Model with three right-handed neutrinos, a dark sector comprising a fermion and a scalar, and additional particles that enable a new dark matter production mechanism. In this scenario, dark matter is generated via freeze-in through the decay of a heavy scalar, mirroring the mechanism responsible for lepton asymmetry. We analyze the parameter space capable of explaining both dark matter density and lepton asymmetry, finding that a dark sector mass scale of approximately 10 TeV is required to satisfy current constraints. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the dark sector can enhance the lepton asymmetry, thereby lowering the necessary temperature for dark matter production. This asymmetry amplification is particularly significant when the dark sector mass exceeds 100 TeV. Finally, we discuss the potential for detecting this dark matter at the High-Luminosity LHC. Specifically, we show that the dark sector can facilitate the decay of a heavy Higgs into dark matter, allowing for detection through the channel $\gamma\gamma + E_T^{miss}$. Additionally, we investigate the production of a Higgs-like resonance in association with large missing transverse energy, a signature that could be observed at the High-Luminosity LHC. Our findings indicate that the dark sector can significantly boost the production cross-section of this process. Finally, we discuss the implications of these findings for the LHC and its future upgrades. Our results suggest that the Higgs decay $H\to \gamma\gamma$ can be enhanced by up to two orders of magnitude, a feature that could be investigated in the upcoming HL-LHC era. We conclude that the proposed signatures offer a promising avenue for detecting dark matter produced through a freeze-in mechanism. This approach is especially viable when the dark sector mass is relatively low, around 10 TeV. However, we also note that this method remains applicable for much higher dark sector masses, extending well beyond 100 TeV. In such high-mass regimes, the dark sector's role is primarily to amplify the lepton asymmetry, which in turn facilitates dark matter production. This work underscores the necessity of exploring dark matter production mechanisms that rely on the same physics as lepton asymmetry generation. Such mechanisms are essential for a comprehensive understanding of dark matter and neutrino properties. Reinforcement learning (RL) has demonstrated significant potential for robot skill acquisition by enabling robots to master new capabilities with minimal human input. Nevertheless, applying RL to real-world scenarios remains difficult due to the vast state-action spaces, the need for extensive data, and the high computational costs. This study investigates whether prior knowledge of physical laws can facilitate the learning of new skills using only a small amount of data. We propose a model-based control framework that integrates learned physics models with a specialized controller to achieve this learning efficiency. Our approach was validated on a real robot, successfully executing a complex task involving a quadcopter navigating a water surface by simultaneously swimming and flying. The results indicate that the proposed method enables the robot to learn to swim and fly across a diverse range of targets in a single trial, utilizing just 100 interaction episodes. Furthermore, the method demonstrates robustness against model errors and disturbances. This work represents the first integration of physics-based models with RL for robot skill learning, offering a promising pathway for future advancements. The accompanying video can be viewed at: https://youtu.be/2222222222.

Conformal field theories (CFTs) are extensively utilized in string theory, particularly for analyzing non-critical and AdS$_2$ contexts. While conformal symmetry dictates the form of correlation functions, additional symmetries impose further constraints. This paper examines Ward identities within a specific CFT framework, focusing on the two-dimensional Toda conformal field theory associated with the Lie algebra sl$_3$. We demonstrate that these Ward identities can be derived from conformal symmetry and null vector constraints, eliminating the necessity for Ward identities involving Ward identities. Furthermore, we establish that Ward identities linked to sl$_3$ Cartan generators yield constraints that are redundant with those derived from null constraints. Consequently, we conclude that conformal symmetry and Ward identities for sl$_3$ highest weight primary fields constitute a complete and independent set of constraints. We also examine Ward identities for degenerate highest weight primaries, noting that while they generate constraints, these are not independent as they can be derived from null constraints. Finally, we show that Ward identities for non-degenerate sl$_3$ highest weight primaries do not impose additional constraints beyond conformal symmetry and null constraints. These findings are significant for understanding Ward identities in other CFTs, such as those involving AdS$_2$ symmetry. Additionally, we derive Ward identities for sl$_3$ current algebra by utilizing the connection between sl$_3$ Toda CFT and the sl$_3$ current algebra. This approach confirms that the same set of Ward identities applies to the current algebra, suggesting that the complete set of sl$_3$ current algebra Ward identities is now fully determined. We anticipate that these results will facilitate the investigation of sl$_3$ current algebra Ward identities in future research. Our methodology is also applicable to other algebras, including sl$_n$ and sp$_n$. This work serves as a sequel to our previous study, where we derived Ward identities for the sl$_2$ Toda CFT. We expect our findings to be valuable for understanding Ward identities in the sl$_2$ Toda CFT as well. Our findings are also relevant for AdS$_2$ physics, as the CFTs discussed here are dual to AdS$_2$ theories. We anticipate that our findings will aid in the study of Ward identities within AdS$_2$ theories. Relation Networks (RNs) are recognized for their ability to model complex interactions between entities within an image, making them highly effective for instance-level segmentation. However, current RN architectures rely on fixed triplet data and struggle to adapt to varying RN parameters during training. To address this, we introduce GAN Relation Networks (GAN-RN), a novel approach that adapts RN architectures to dynamic parameters by employing a GAN framework. This method utilizes fixed triplets to train the model, where the relationship between two target objects is represented by the RN, and triplet data is generated by another RN. The framework consists of two components: a generator network and a discriminator network. The generator creates a relationship map for one object pair, while the discriminator evaluates these maps to distinguish between two types of object pairs. We demonstrate the efficacy of GAN-RN across various instance segmentation tasks, including CIFAR-10, ImageNet, and PASCAL VOC. Our results show that GAN-RN significantly enhances performance, achieving a 3.5% increase in mean Average Precision (mAP) on ImageNet and a 1.5% improvement on PASCAL VOC. Furthermore, GAN-RN exhibits robustness against domain shifts, maintaining consistent performance across different training and testing domains. The source code is available at https://github.com/ChenYi2019/GAN-RN. The paper can be found at https://arxiv.org/abs/2002.01001. Finally, our findings indicate that GAN-RN substantially boosts the performance of instance segmentation models. By leveraging the strengths of both Relation Networks and Generative Adversarial Networks, our approach yields superior results compared to existing methods. The integration of GANs allows the model to learn more robust representations, while the use of triplet data ensures that the model generalizes well to unseen data. Overall, GAN-RN represents a significant advancement in the field of instance segmentation. Our work paves the way for future research in this area and provides a valuable resource for the computer vision community. We hope that our findings will inspire further research and innovation in the field of instance segmentation. Our results demonstrate that GAN-RN is a powerful tool for instance segmentation and can significantly improve the performance of existing models. We believe that GAN-RN will play a crucial role in the future of instance segmentation and will continue to drive advancements in the field. Twin-field quantum key distribution (TF-QKD) has recently become a promising solution for long-distance fiber-optic communication. However, TF-QKD typically relies on precise phase locking to maintain identical phases across the entangled twin fields. We demonstrate that TF-QKD can operate without phase locking, provided that the relative phase is measured at the end of each transmission and the data is post-selected accordingly. This approach, termed "TF-QKD without phase locking," achieves raw key rates approximately 1.5 times higher than those of TF-QKD with phase locking. Furthermore, the maximum secure distance for TF-QKD without phase locking is predicted to reach 1,000 km, surpassing the limits of conventional phase-locked implementations. These findings indicate that TF-QKD without phase locking could serve as a highly effective technology for ultra-long-distance quantum key distribution. Additionally, the methodology employed to eliminate phase noise may be applicable to other quantum protocols, such as quantum random access coding. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/ChenYi-1997/TF-QKD. The detailed analysis can be found in our supplementary material [1].

For a complex $n$-tuple of noncommutative analytic Toeplitz operators acting on the symmetric Fock space $\mathcal{F}(\mathbb{C}^n)$, we define the Toeplitz algebra $\mathcal{T}(\mathbf{u})$ as the C*-algebra generated by these operators. We characterize the ideal structure of this algebra and demonstrate that its quotient is isomorphic to the Cuntz algebra $\mathcal{O}_{|{\mathbf{u}}|}$. Furthermore, we establish an isomorphism between the C*-algebras $\mathcal{T}(\mathbf{u})$ and $\mathcal{T}(\mathbf{v})$ whenever the degree of $\mathbf{u}$ and $\mathbf{v}$ shares the same prime factors and their respective essential normal subvarieties are of equal dimension. Additionally, we provide a classification of pure states on $\mathcal{T}(\mathbf{u})$ up to unitary equivalence. Finally, we extend these findings to Toeplitz algebras defined over the Bergman space of the unit ball in $\mathbb{C}^n$.
