Although object detection has advanced significantly, most current approaches are restricted to a narrow range of categories, limiting their practical utility. To address this, researchers have developed open-vocabulary object detection methods that enable detection of novel categories absent from training data by leveraging pre-computed class-level features from vision-language models. However, these existing solutions depend on precise annotations for each category, a requirement that is often impractical or unavailable in real-world scenarios. This paper introduces a pioneering method that achieves open-vocabulary object detection using only image-level labels, eliminating the need for bounding box annotations for each category. Our approach utilizes a two-stage training framework that generates pseudo bounding-box annotations for categories within a support set. We demonstrate the efficacy of our method across various domains, including zero-shot, few-shot, and large support few-shot object detection, as well as in cross-domain settings. Experimental results indicate that our method outperforms previous state-of-the-art techniques, particularly in large support few-shot scenarios and when detecting classes from diverse domains. The code is accessible at https://github.com/visipedia/pbbox-detection.

We conducted a survey of the Rho Oph A cloud using the IRAM 30m telescope to observe the ionized gas tracers $^{12}$CO(3-2), $^{13}$CO(3-2), and $^{13}$C$^{18}$O(3-2), alongside dust emission at 850 $\mu$m. This study aims to map the spatial distribution of ionized, atomic, and photodissociation region (PDR) gas surrounding the S1 cluster. Our findings reveal that the ionized gas is not uniformly distributed around the S1 cluster but instead forms a filamentary structure. The atomic gas distribution aligns with the ionized gas, though the latter exhibits a higher column density. The PDR gas is located at the edge of the ionized gas, displaying a more extended morphology. The ionized gas structure is likely shaped by the S1 cluster's environment, including the cloud's magnetic field and density inhomogeneities. The atomic gas distribution is primarily determined by the cloud's density structure, while the PDR gas is influenced by both the density structure and the position of the cloud's edge. These results underscore the necessity of multi-wavelength observations to investigate the interaction between star formation and the interstellar medium. Furthermore, the Rho Oph A cloud serves as a valuable laboratory for studying the interplay between the interstellar medium and star formation. The remarkable success of transformers within natural language processing has spurred their adoption across diverse computer vision tasks. This survey offers a thorough review and classification of current research utilizing transformers in computer vision. We begin by examining the foundational transformer architecture and its two primary variants designed for vision. Subsequently, we detail the comprehensive structure of this survey, covering low- and mid-level vision tasks (such as classification, object detection, and segmentation), high-level tasks (including image generation and synthesis), as well as 3D vision and vision-language interfaces. Furthermore, we present a survey of large-scale vision foundation models built on transformer architectures. Finally, we outline key challenges and future research directions. Our aim is to provide a well-organized reference that highlights both the achievements and unresolved issues in vision transformers, thereby inspiring further advancements in this field. The survey can be accessed at https://arxiv.org/abs/2101.00337. The corresponding source code is available at https://github.com/ashkumar1999/Transformers-in-Vision-Survey. The survey's website is located at https://ashkumar1999.github.io/Transformers-in-Vision-Survey/. Additionally, the survey video is available at https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=4222222222. Keywords: Computer Vision, Transformers, Survey. Citation: Kumar, A., & Gupta, S. B. (2021). Transformers in Vision: A Survey. arXiv preprint arXiv:2101.00337.

This study evaluates the performance of time-varying versus time-invariant factor loadings within factor models for mortality forecasting. We introduce a straightforward yet effective method for determining time-invariant loadings and compare its utility against standard chain-ladder and Lee-Carter models. Our analysis utilizes data from the Human Mortality Database covering ages 30 to 89. Results indicate that while time-varying loadings offer superior out-of-sample fits, they do not necessarily lead to better forecasts. Furthermore, we find that factor loadings estimated via the time-invariant approach remain relatively stable over time, exhibiting only minor fluctuations. Finally, we demonstrate that the time-invariant factor loading model produces forecasts comparable to both the chain-ladder model and the Lee-Carter model. These findings are validated through case studies of Japan, the United States, and the United Kingdom. The associated R package, `mortality_forecasting`, is available at https://github.com/hiroki-ito/mortality_forecasting. Additionally, the R code is provided in https://github.com/hiroki-ito/mortality_forecasting/tree/master/code. The supplementary materials are located at https://github.com/hiroki-ito/mortality_forecasting/tree/master/supplementary_materials. Keywords: Mortality forecasting, Factor model, Factor loading, Time-varying, Time-invariant.

Neural Architecture Search (NAS) has demonstrated remarkable success in creating high-performing models for computer vision tasks. However, the extensive search space and superior performance of robust architectures result in significant overfitting, causing the validation error to drop nearly to the training error. This issue, known as the generalization gap, is particularly problematic for robust models, which typically demand higher accuracy and greater computational resources. To address this, we propose a novel approach that mitigates interference by leveraging a regularization technique to lower training error. Our method, called Interference-aware Architecture Search (IARAS), integrates this regularization into a reinforcement learning-based search framework. IARAS successfully identifies architectures that balance strong generalization with high accuracy. Experimental results on the CIFAR-100 dataset confirm the efficacy of IARAS, showing it outperforms state-of-the-art methods in both accuracy and computational efficiency. Furthermore, IARAS surpasses existing techniques for narrowing the generalization gap, such as early stopping and generalization-aware search, on CIFAR-100 and ImageNet-1K datasets. The code is accessible at https://github.com/ChenchenChen1997/IARAS.

We provide specific, "infinitesimal" criteria ensuring that a proper geodesically complete CAT(0) space possesses a semistable fundamental group at infinity. These conditions are met by a wide range of spaces, notably those featuring uniform negative curvature or exhibiting tangential curvature bounded from below. Additionally, we demonstrate that certain examples illustrate the necessity of these hypotheses. Our approach relies on a novel local-to-global technique for CAT(0) spaces, which we believe holds independent significance. As an application, we establish new examples of proper geodesically complete CAT(0) groups with semistable fundamental group at infinity, including a family of nonamenable groups where the fundamental group at infinity is trivial. We further present a construction of examples with nontrivial but amenable fundamental groups at infinity, and we conjecture that every example we produce actually has a trivial fundamental group at infinity. Along the way, we offer a characterization of CAT(0) spaces exhibiting uniform negative curvature and investigate the relationship between this property and nonpositive curvature. We also examine a question originally proposed by Cornulier regarding groups with semistable fundamental groups at infinity. Finally, we address a question by Cornulier concerning the relationship between groups with amenable fundamental groups at infinity and groups where every geodesic triangle is infinitesimally thin. Our analysis reveals that the former property is strictly stronger than the latter. In the final section, we explore the connections between fundamental groups at infinity and coarse geometry, specifically coarse amenability and coarsestability. We demonstrate that for a class of spaces encompassing all those with uniform negative curvature, the fundamental group at infinity is amenable if and only if the space is coarsely amenably embedded in a Hilbert space. We conclude by outlining an open problem regarding the coarse geometry of such spaces. This work extends our earlier paper, \emph{Isoperimetric inequalities and at infinity geometry of CAT(0) spaces}, to the broader context of CAT(0) spaces. Our methods are inspired by the foundational work of Cornulier, Dranishnikov, and Tessera. This paper introduces a Bayesian methodology for evaluating translator reliability. We begin by defining a translator's reliability as a binary indicator of whether they correctly identify all segments within a dataset. We then outline a Bayesian framework designed to estimate a translator's reliability probability, specifically determining the likelihood that a translator correctly translates every segment in a dataset. Furthermore, we develop a method to calculate the uncertainty surrounding this estimated probability. Our approach relies on observing a translator's output across multiple datasets and assumes that reliability events follow a Bernoulli process. We also present a simulation study to validate the proposed methodology. The results indicate that our Bayesian approach yields accurate estimates of translator reliability probability and produces reliable uncertainty assessments. Additionally, we demonstrate that the method is computationally efficient, capable of processing thousands of sentences within a few seconds. Finally, we illustrate the method's utility through a case study involving the translation of COVID-19 related content. The code required to replicate our methodology and findings is accessible at https://github.com/abhishekbhagwat/TranslatorReliability.

Sum rules are essential for characterizing the integrated properties of systems across physics, chemistry, and engineering. This work derives sum rules for energy deposition in open quantum systems by leveraging the complete set of eigenchannels for a two-body collision operator. We demonstrate that total and partial cross sections for energy transfer can be expressed through these eigenchannels, offering a fresh perspective on the well-established relationship between the moments of the collision operator's spectrum and these same cross sections. Furthermore, we derive sum rules regarding the transfer of energy, angular momentum, and parity, alongside sum rules for the collision operator's spectrum itself. The methodology is demonstrated using two models of atom-diatom systems, where we explicitly calculate the eigenchannels of the collision operator. These findings offer a new framework for analyzing energy transfer in scattering processes and provide a rigorous mathematical basis for understanding the statistical and dynamical attributes of such collisions. Additionally, the approach is applicable to a broad range of quantum scattering problems. Finally, we discuss the extension of this method to classical scattering scenarios. The code used to generate the results is publicly accessible at https://github.com/andrewjg1990/Sum-rules-for-energy-deposition-in-scattering-systems. Convolutional networks excel at extracting and utilizing features, a capability that fully connected networks lack. We hypothesize that this advantage stems from the fact that convolutions can easily discard uninformative features, whereas fully connected architectures struggle to do so. To test this, we introduced a straightforward pruning method that removes neurons with minimal impact on performance. Our findings indicate that convolutions can prune a significantly higher proportion of features with minimal accuracy loss compared to fully connected networks. Furthermore, the remaining features in convolutions are more abundant and diverse. These results support our hypothesis and demonstrate that the ability to effectively prune features is a key factor in the superiority of convolutional architectures. Additionally, this insight could be valuable for developing efficient models across various domains. Finally, we show that the proposed pruning technique can be applied to other feature selection methods, such as saliency-based approaches. This is particularly useful for creating lightweight models and enhancing the interpretability of deep networks. To our knowledge, this is the first demonstration that convolutions possess a superior feature selection mechanism compared to fully connected networks. This study examines maximizing expected returns in lotteries by determining the optimal timing for purchases and the best locations to sell unsold tickets. We develop a general framework for pricing lottery tickets and derive explicit solutions for scenarios involving a single buyer or a large group of buyers. Our findings indicate that to maximize expected value, tickets should be sold prior to the draw and in states with a lower population of winners. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the standard ticket price is not optimal; instead, a higher price yields a greater expected return. We also explore the impact of illegal lottery operations, revealing that such activity reduces the optimal selling price and increases the optimal time to purchase. Finally, we present numerical results for major US lotteries, which confirm that the selling strategies proposed here significantly boost a seller's expected return. These strategies are particularly effective when the seller possesses private information regarding the winning numbers. We conclude that these optimal selling strategies are most applicable to large-scale illegal lottery operations. Additionally, we note that a buyer can increase their expected return by purchasing tickets after draw times are announced in different states, specifically by waiting for states where the draw has already concluded. This approach is especially beneficial when the buyer possesses private information about the winning numbers. We illustrate that these strategies are especially effective when the buyer holds a high-precision prediction of the winning numbers. Finally, we observe that the optimal selling strategies remain robust even when the buyer's information is noisy. Our framework is also relevant to other games of chance, such as casino games and card games. In those contexts, the draw corresponds to the end of the game, and the buyer represents a casino or a skilled player. We show that the optimal selling strategies identified here are particularly effective when the player possesses a high-precision strategy for predicting the outcome. This paper is the first to address the pricing and timing of lottery ticket sales. It is the first to derive explicit solutions for pricing and timing when there is a single buyer or a large group of buyers. Additionally, this work is the first to examine the effect of skilled players on lottery operations. Our results are derived using the law of iterated expectations, a fundamental concept in probability theory. This methodology is also applicable to other games of chance, where the draw represents the end of the game and the buyer represents either a casino or a skilled player. Our work is the first to analyze the impact of skilled players on casino games. We have computed the $g^6$ term in the large-$N$ anom dimension of the $\phi^Q$ operator within the $O(N)$ symmetric $\lambda\phi^4$ theory in $d=6-\epsilon$ dimensions, where $Q=N,2N$. This result yields a total of six loop orders. Additionally, we calculated the $g^4$ and $g^5$ contributions for the $Q=N$ case, bringing the overall perturbation theory for the anomalous dimension to five-loop accuracy. Our approach relies on the method of nested sectors, utilizing Feynman integrals evaluated by network theory, along with various techniques to reduce the computational workload. The final expressions for the anomalous dimensions are presented in a compact form through multiple zeta values. Furthermore, we have verified all results through independent checks. These findings are relevant for the investigation of the critical behavior of the $O(N)$ model in the vicinity of the Berezinskii-Kosterlitz-Thouless transition. Specifically, the five-loop accuracy achieved here represents the highest order of perturbation theory available for the $\phi^4$ theory with a $Q=2N$ operator. This precision is essential for analyzing the critical behavior of the $O(2)$ model in $d=5$ dimensions, which is believed to exhibit a nontrivial critical point characterized by the appearance of a massless $Q=4N$ operator. Our results provide the necessary data to determine the critical exponents of this transition up to five-loop order. Finally, we have determined the five-loop coefficient of the $\beta$-function for the $Q=N$ operator, which is required for the analysis of the critical behavior of the $O(2)$ model in $d=5$ dimensions. The valley degree of freedom in two-dimensional materials has garnered significant interest due to its potential for valleytronics. This study investigates how various electron-phonon coupling mechanisms influence valley physics, specifically examining how different valley-phonon coupling channels affect the valley Hall effect and valley polarization. We identify that certain phonon modes can induce scattering events leading to valley-phonon degeneracy breaking, which diminishes the valley Hall effect. Furthermore, we demonstrate that electron-phonon coupling can drive rapid depolarization of a valley polarization state. These findings offer a deeper understanding of electron-phonon interactions and their critical role in valley-based transport phenomena. Additionally, the methodologies employed are applicable to the investigation of electron-phonon interactions in other two-dimensional materials. This paper presents our technical solution for the Visual Domain Adaptation (VDA) challenge, where we achieved first place across all three tasks. Our approach leverages a straightforward yet effective domain adaptation framework built upon a state-of-the-art vision transformer. Specifically, we demonstrate that a simple self-supervised pre-training strategy yields substantial performance gains in this domain. Additionally, we explore various techniques to enhance the robustness of our model against domain shifts, including a novel method for training with multiple pseudo-labels. Our results underscore the critical role of self-supervised pre-training in visual domain adaptation and highlight the potential of self-supervised learning to develop more robust domain adaptation models. The code is accessible at https://github.com/robinstrudel/vda-challenge-solutions. The paper is available in English at https://arxiv.org/abs/2210.01021 and in German at https://arxiv.org/abs/2210.01021. These resources can be found at: https://arxiv.org/abs/2210.01021.

t-SNE is a widely adopted method for visualizing high-dimensional data in low-dimensional spaces. However, its universal applicability is limited, as it fails to account for the intrinsic geometric characteristics of specific datasets. This paper introduces SNEVF, a novel spherical embedding technique that integrates t-SNE with von Mises-Fisher projection. By leveraging the von Mises-Fisher distribution, our approach enhances the visualization of spherical data. We validate the efficacy of this method through various experiments, demonstrating its effectiveness. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/ChenYi-1999/SNEVF. Furthermore, we have established a new benchmark for spherical data embedding, which can be found at https://github.com/ChenYi-1999/Spherical-Data-Embedding. This benchmark includes multiple datasets and evaluation metrics designed to facilitate future research in the field. The comprehensive evaluation results are available at https://github.com/ChenYi-1999/Spherical-Data-Embedding/tree/main/results. The paper itself is hosted at https://github.com/ChenYi-1999/Spherical-Data-Embedding/tree/main/paper. We hope this work inspires further advancements in spherical data embedding. This research investigates the two-dimensional Fermi polaron, consisting of a mobile impurity interacting with a Fermi sea of opposite-charge carriers via a contact potential. We develop and implement a diagrammatic Monte Carlo algorithm capable of sampling perturbation theory series to high orders. By averaging over an extensive collection of diagrams, our method yields robust results even at relatively low coupling strengths. We examine the polaron's ground state energy and wave function, as well as the energy of the excited state with opposite momentum. Furthermore, we analyze the polaron's residue and the energy of the molecule-like bound state formed by the impurity and a quasi-particle from the Fermi sea. These findings are compared with existing theoretical predictions and numerical simulations from the literature. Our results indicate that the polaron's residue is significantly smaller than previously believed, while the molecule-like state's energy is notably lower than earlier estimates. Finally, we discuss the method's applicability to more complex polaron variants. The accompanying repository includes a user-friendly implementation of the algorithm for the 2D Fermi polaron. This code is designed to be easily adaptable for studying other many-body problems via diagrammatic expansions, serving as a valuable resource for both researchers and educators. The implementation is open-source and released under the MIT license. Additionally, we provide a detailed user manual and a tutorial for pedagogical purposes. These resources can be utilized in advanced quantum mechanics or many-body physics courses to illustrate diagrammatic expansions and diagrammatic Monte Carlo techniques. The tutorial is also suitable for introductory quantum mechanics courses or as an advanced laboratory exercise. We believe this implementation will be a valuable asset for students and educators in quantum mechanics and many-body physics. Keywords: Fermi polaron, diagrammatic Monte Carlo, impurity problem. Hybrid digital-analog quantum computing represents a promising new paradigm that leverages the inherent strengths of both digital and analog computational methods. This work outlines a protocol for simulating fermionic systems within the Jordan-Wigner framework, utilizing a hybrid architecture. We demonstrate that the proposed algorithm can be implemented on existing noisy intermediate-scale quantum hardware. Furthermore, we show that key physical properties of the simulated systems can be accurately extracted with high precision by performing both digital and analog components of the algorithm on the device. The study includes detailed numerical simulations of the hybrid algorithm applied to fermionic systems, specifically the 1D transverse-field Ising model and the Su-Schrieffer-Heeger model. Our results indicate that the method achieves high accuracy in estimating physical observables, such as the ground state energy, even under realistic noise conditions. Additionally, we demonstrate that the algorithm can determine the ground state wave function with high precision. These findings suggest that the hybrid digital-analog approach offers a viable pathway for quantum simulation using near-term hardware. Finally, we discuss the potential for extending this method to a broader range of fermionic systems. Our results hold significant promise for advancing quantum computing research and for developing new algorithms capable of simulating complex physical systems. We establish a lower bound for graph polynomials defined by non-negative weights, utilizing the count of induced subgraphs. Furthermore, we apply this finding to investigate the unimodality and log-concavity characteristics of these polynomials. Specifically, our findings offer novel proofs for the unimodality of chromatic and flow polynomials, confirm the recently conjectured log-concavity of the chromatic polynomial, and extend these results to weighted scenarios. Additionally, we demonstrate the strong sign-pattern property and real-rootedness of a broad class of polynomials linked to the chromatic polynomial, a finding that resolves a conjecture by Brändén and Kim. The study also encompasses numerous examples and counterexamples. Notably, we identify an infinite family of weighted polynomials that adhere to unimodality and strong sign-pattern properties despite not being real-rooted, thereby contrasting with established conjectures. Finally, we present a polynomial related to the chromatic polynomial that is unimodal but fails to be sign-symmetric. This work provides an explicit formula for the pullback of the Hitchin connection to a specific geodesic curve within the moduli space of holomorphic quadratic differentials, known as the Veech curve. This curve traces a sequence of strata encountered by the geodesic $\lambda^\infty(t)=e^{it}(1+i)$ as $t$ varies. We demonstrate that pullbacks of both the connection form and the curvature of the Hitchin connection are expressed as iterated integrals of specific meromorphic 1-forms defined on the curve. Furthermore, we establish that these forms are analytic and can be represented as power series, enabling their computation to any desired order. The study also examines symmetries of the forms and their relationship to the monodromy of the Hitchin connection. Finally, we present numerical results and explore applications to multiple zeta values. The methods employed here are also applicable to other algebraic curves. Additionally, we investigate the connection between the Hitchin connection and the connection on the space of holomorphic quadratic differentials, which remains flat under the Weil-Petersson geodesic flow. We compute the connection forms and curvature for a specific family of geodesic curves in the Teichmüller space of $\mathbb{C}P^1$ that project to the Veech curve. This family consists of geodesics connecting the cusp to the cusp of the Teichmüller space of a genus 2 surface with a symmetric waist. We calculate the connection forms and curvature up to the third order and highlight applications to isomonodromic deformations of a differential equation featuring a Fuchsian singularity at the origin and a regular singularity at infinity. We also examine the link to the connection on the space of holomorphic quadratic differentials and its relation to the Gauss-Manin connection. Finally, we address the problem of computing the connection form of the Gauss-Manin connection on the moduli space of genus 2 cubic curves with a symmetric waist. This form is expressed using iterated integrals of meromorphic 1-forms on the Veech curve, and we prove that these forms are analytic, providing an explicit formula for their Taylor series. We further examine the connection's invariance under a specific group action and its relation to the monodromy of the Fuchsian differential equation. The paper concludes with an appendix detailing the connection between iterated integrals and multiple zeta values. The computational results were generated using the Sage package

This study examines how remote work influences Scrum project outcomes. Utilizing a mixed-methods approach, we analyzed data from 112 questionnaires completed by software developers and interviewed 12 project managers. Our findings indicate that while the remote environment negatively impacts team communication, it can enhance self-management. Consequently, teams must adapt their communication strategies to mitigate these challenges. We conclude that the remote work environment does not inherently favor or hinder Scrum success; instead, its impact is neutral and contingent upon specific contextual factors. To address the communication deficits identified, we propose three targeted solutions. Furthermore, we offer additional insights into the nuances of remote work and Scrum success, supported by 112 case studies. The paper concludes with a set of recommendations for project managers overseeing remote Scrum initiatives. Additionally, we have developed a web-based tool to assist managers in assessing the potential impact of remote work on their specific teams. The source code and data for this tool are available at: https://github.com/RemoteScruTool. The tool's details can be found at: https://remutescrutool.com/. The concept of the Gau-Wu number, originally introduced by C.-L. Gau and J.-L. Wu in 1991, is a combinatorial tool used to determine the sign of the signature for specific symmetric matrices, most notably diagonal-plus-arrow (DPA) matrices. This paper aims to broaden the application of the Gau-Wu number within a broader combinatorial framework. We present a combinatorial model linking the Gau-Wu number to perfect matchings in graph theory and to the sign of the determinant, with the latter connection being particularly significant for arrowhead matrices. Leveraging these connections, we derive closed-form expressions for the Gau-Wu numbers associated with classes of DPA matrices, including $4\times 4$ arrow matrices and symmetric arrowhead matrices featuring a constant main diagonal. These findings offer a combinatorial perspective on the Gau-Wu number, thereby enhancing its utility in matrix theory. Furthermore, our results provide a combinatorial proof for the signature of DPA matrices, validating the original findings of Gau and Wu. The study concludes with an exploration of potential future research directions. This work serves as a foundation for the theses of both the first and second authors. Specifically, the first author's thesis focuses on the general properties of the Gau-Wu number, while the second author's thesis details the derivations of closed-form expressions for the Gau-Wu numbers of DPA matrices. The collaboration between the two authors was essential in unifying the thesis into a single cohesive research paper. Additionally, the first author's thesis incorporates a combinatorial proof for the signature of DPA matrices, a contribution that was not included in the second author's thesis. The inclusion of this combinatorial proof significantly enriches the thesis by demonstrating the versatility of the combinatorial model for DPA matrices. Ultimately, the thesis of the first author represents a more comprehensive and integrated body of research, whereas the thesis of the second author provides a more detailed and specific exploration of the combinatorial model's applications. We present an algorithm utilizing persistent homology to analyze the chromatic patterns of lattice gases, which are defined as maps from a lattice to chromatic colors. Our findings indicate that the homology of the resulting chromatic complexes offers a more refined description of the gas's microstructure than the persistent homology of the raw lattice. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the latter can be derived from the former by disregarding the specific chromatic colors. These results hold significant implications for the field of topological data analysis. Specifically, our examples illustrate that chromatic complexes can exhibit non-trivial homology in arbitrarily high dimensions, even when the gas occupies a bounded region within the lattice. Additionally, we provide a counterexample to a conjecture by Carlsson and Morozov, which suggested that the persistent homology of chromatic complexes would be concentrated in dimensions up to the dimension of the color complex. Finally, we show that the persistent homology of the chromatic complexes associated with inverse temperature maps on the lattice encodes the convergence behavior of the corresponding lattice system as the gas approaches thermodynamic equilibrium. These outcomes are achieved through the development of new combinatorial and geometric techniques. Our work introduces a novel class of simplicial complexes, which we term chromatic complexes, and establishes the first comprehensive theory for their persistent homology. We also provide a combinatorial interpretation of the persistent homology of chromatic complexes, revealing that their persistent homology groups are isomorphic to the direct sum of the persistent homology groups of specific simplicial complexes that represent the gas's macrostructure. This insight yields a constructive method for generating examples of chromatic complexes with non-trivial persistent homology. Finally, we propose a conjecture regarding the persistent homology of chromatic complexes, which posits that this homology is entirely determined by the connected components of the gas. We verify this conjecture for a specific class of lattice gases, thereby providing strong evidence for its validity. For instance, we establish a new conjecture concerning the homology of chromatic complexes, which generalizes a conjecture by Carlsson and Morozov to higher dimensions. We also demonstrate that the persistent homology of chromatic complexes can be computed in linear time relative to the size of the gas. This study examines the Generalized Degrees of Freedom (GDoF) performance improvement achieved by optimal power control (OPC) over binary power control (BPC) in interference networks. In a $K$-user interference network, BPC restricts each transmitter to a binary power spectrum, whereas OPC permits each transmitter to utilize any interference-exponent spectrum. We demonstrate that the extremal GDoF gain of OPC over BPC in a $K$-user interference network scales as $\Theta(\sqrt{K})$. This finding indicates that the previously established $\Theta(\log K)$ upper bound on this gain is tight only when $K$ is constant. Furthermore, we note that the extremal GDoF gain in specific suboptimal networks, such as the Z-interference channel, is $\Theta(\log K)$, which contrasts with the gain observed in the general $K$-user interference network. Additionally, we prove that the extremal GDoF gain of network coding over BPC in a $K$-user interference network is $\Theta(\log K)$. This result implies that the earlier $\Theta(\log \log K)$ upper bound on this gain is loose. The primary technical contribution of this work lies in the development of a general framework for analyzing the extremal GDoF gain of BPSK network coding and OPC in $K$-user interference networks. This framework relies on the concept of "effective" users, defined as those users whose desired signals are the most sensitive to interference. We show that the extremal GDoF gain of BPSK network coding over BPC is bounded by the gain of network coding over BPC in a specific subnetwork involving only the effective users. Similarly, we establish that the extremal GDoF gain of OPC over BPC is upper-bounded by the gain achieved by network coding over BPC in a particular subnetwork containing the effective users. Consequently, the analysis of the OPC gain over BPC in the full network can be reduced to analyzing the network coding gain over BPC in the relevant subnetwork. The paper concludes with a discussion on the tightness of this upper bound. Our findings are applicable to various interference network models, including X-networks, and can be extended to other power control schemes. Finally, we discuss the implications of these results for the design of practical interference management strategies. This paper introduces a categorization method designed to handle uncertain data within the Dempster-Shafer framework, specifically to enhance the auditability of machine learning models. The process begins by applying formal concept analysis to derive accurate and plausible labels for uncertain instances. Subsequently, Dempster-Shafer evidence theory is employed to fuse the results from multiple categorization steps, yielding a final result for each uncertain instance accompanied by a confidence level. The study demonstrates the method's efficacy through a case study on the CIFAR-10 dataset, which confirms its effectiveness in improving the auditability of machine learning models. The methodology is also illustrated using a classification task on the Fashion MNIST dataset. The authors conclude that the proposed approach offers a valuable alternative for categorizing uncertain data and successfully address the inherent challenges in auditing machine learning models. Future research will explore extensions to other decision-making frameworks, such as Bayesian theory. Keywords: Auditability, Dempster-Shafer, Fashion MNIST, CIFAR-10, Machine Learning, Formal Concept Analysis.

The STRAUSS process is a widely utilized inhomogeneous point process model, valued for its flexibility and capacity to represent both repulsive and attractive interactions among points. However, current state-of-the-art methods for drawing samples from its distribution are limited to specific scenarios, such as low particle counts or attractive interactions involving only pairs of particles. This paper introduces a novel, general-purpose algorithm capable of efficient sampling for any Strauss process. The method operates by decomposing a general Strauss process into a mixture of models featuring disjoint stitching processes, which are significantly simpler to sample from. Furthermore, the proposed algorithm is validated through various point process modeling applications, including the analysis of neuronal spike trains, protein structures, and tree branching patterns. The code is accessible at https://github.com/andreas-klauer/stitching. Additionally, the authors have released a user-friendly, open-source Python package, Stitching, which implements the algorithm and provides a user interface for sampling from any Strauss process. The package can be installed via pip using the command: pip install stitching. The package documentation is available at https://stiching.readthedocs.io/. The authors acknowledge funding from the Austrian Science Fund (FWF) under grant number P32000. Finally, the authors express gratitude to the anonymous reviewers for their constructive feedback. This study examines the impact of the generalized uncertainty principle on Galilean and Lorentz transformations. We demonstrate that both transformations remain invariant under GUP, provided a specific condition is met. Furthermore, we derive the GUP-modified energy-momentum relation for a free particle within both frameworks. Our findings indicate that the GUP-altered energy and momentum for a free particle are not invariant under either transformation, although they satisfy a consistent condition. Additionally, we calculate the GUP-modified dispersion relation for a particle interacting with a field, showing that it also fails invariance under both Galilean and Lorentz transformations while adhering to a similar condition. Finally, we explore the link between the GUP-invariant Lorentz transformation and the deformed special relativity (DSR) framework. We observe that the GUP-invariant Lorentz transformation aligns with the DSR transformation when the noncommutative scale $\lambda$ is identified with the Planck energy scale. Consequently, we conclude that DSR can be derived from GUP-invariant mechanics. Finally, we examine the relationship between the GUP-invariant principle and the DSR principle. We establish that the DSR principle is a specific instance of the GUP-invariant principle, contingent upon a particular relationship between the parameters $\lambda$ and $\hbar$. This relationship is precisely the one that connects the Planck mass and Planck length. Thus, the GUP-invariant principle serves as a more general foundation for DSR. We argue that this broader principle is essential for developing a unified theory that integrates quantum mechanics, special relativity, and spacetime noncommutativity. Furthermore, we note that the GUP-invariant principle is a necessary condition for the quantum gravity regime. Therefore, it is crucial to investigate the physical consequences of this principle within the context of quantum gravity. In this regard, we suggest that the GUP-invariant Lorentz transformation, which we have derived, may hold significant physical relevance. We anticipate that this research will contribute to the ongoing quest to unify quantum mechanics and general relativity. Finally, we acknowledge that this paper is a preliminary report, and we intend to expand upon these findings in future work. Specifically, we plan to explore the implications of the GUP-invariant Lorentz transformation for quantum mechanics and quantum field theory. Multitasking is a ubiquitous computing phenomenon where multiple applications and services are managed concurrently, often sharing a single processor. This shared processing capability allows for significant energy savings by reducing the total number of required processors. We introduce a multitasking scheduling framework that permits the partial sharing of a single processor among multiple tasks. We demonstrate that a specific work conservation property is both necessary and sufficient for optimality in multitasking scheduling. Building on this, we propose an optimal schedule generation algorithm for the scenario where tasks are available at the beginning of the planning horizon. Furthermore, we extend this approach to a more complex scenario where task availability is dynamic, proving that a work conservation property incorporating discounted completion times remains both necessary and sufficient for optimality in that context as well. Finally, we present computational results that validate the practicality of our methodology. (This work was partially presented at the 2019 IEEE International Conference on Big Data). This paper introduces a model for monopod dynamics on deformable ground, alongside its corresponding simulators and an optimizer. The deformable ground model defines the ground reaction force as a function of the indentation depth at the contact point. The dynamics model accounts for both the kinematics of the monopod's flight phase and the dynamics of the ground contact phase. The simulators developed in this work include a single monopod simulator and a multi-monopod simulator capable of simulating the behavior of a swarm. The optimizer presented here utilizes a multi-monopod simulator to optimize the behavior of a swarm within a specified area. The results obtained from the simulators demonstrate that the proposed optimizer can successfully generate cooperative behaviors among the monopods. Furthermore, the optimizer is able to adapt the behavior of the monopods to variations in the terrain. The paper concludes by outlining potential future work. Specifically, the method for determining ground reaction force as a function of indentation depth requires experimental validation. Additionally, the optimization process is computationally intensive, and the current approach does not account for the dynamics of the monopod's arms. Finally, the optimizer could be extended to optimize the behavior of other types of robots. For instance, a similar method could be applied to optimize the behavior of multi-legged robots, where arm dynamics would be incorporated into the model. The robustness of the optimizer could also be enhanced by including a model of the monopod's sensor measurements. Furthermore, the optimizer could be utilized to optimize the behavior of a group of monopods in an unstructured environment. Finally, the concept of using an optimizer that relies on a simulator could be applied to other areas of research. For example, an optimizer based on a simulator could be employed to optimize the behavior of a group of vehicles in an unknown environment. The vehicle behavior could be optimized using a vehicle simulator, and the optimizer could be tuned to account for uncertainties in the vehicle dynamics. The robustness of such an optimizer could be improved by including a model of the vehicle's sensor measurements. Additionally, the concept could be applied to the field of digital twins, where an optimizer based on a digital twin simulator could be used to optimize the behavior of a group of digital twins. The vehicle behavior could be optimized using the digital twin simulator, and the optimizer could be calibrated to reflect uncertainties in the vehicle dynamics. The robustness of this approach could be further improved by incorporating a model of the vehicle's sensor measurements. Internet of Things (IoT) systems are expanding rapidly, with the projected count of connected devices surpassing that of personal computers by 2020. This growth is driven by the need to enhance the reliability of existing devices and to introduce new, more capable ones. However, the widespread adoption of IoT introduces significant security risks, particularly from firmware vulnerabilities. Consequently, regular firmware updates are essential for maintaining security, yet this process is challenging within large-scale IoT networks. This difficulty stems from the need to ensure that updates are applied reliably and that devices can resume normal operation immediately if the process fails. This paper examines the performance of a specific firmware update mechanism, analyzing its behavior across various network conditions and comparing it against a theoretical baseline. Our findings indicate that the current mechanism is highly susceptible to network failures, resulting in a substantial number of devices failing to update. We also identify specific scenarios where the mechanism performs optimally, offering guidance for implementing updates in real-world networks. Furthermore, we outline several promising directions for future research. The code and datasets supporting this research are accessible at https://github.com/andreamaria/2020-iot-firmware-update. We investigate the multifractal characteristics of many-body localized systems by analyzing the spectral properties of Fock-space dynamical matrices. Specifically, we examine the spectral density of eigenvalues for the $k$-th return to the origin over time, denoted as $\rho_k(E_k)$, where $k$ represents the excitation level and $E_k$ is the corresponding eigenvalue. In one-dimensional (1D) systems, the spectral density of the Fock-space Hamiltonian $H$ follows a Gaussian distribution, with its variance scaling as $\langle E_k^2\rangle \sim k^{2\tau_1}$. We demonstrate that the scaling exponent $\tau_1$ remains independent of the interaction strength $V$ in the 1D ferromagnetic Heisenberg spin model. Furthermore, we establish that the spectral density of the Fock-space Hamiltonian exhibits a fractal structure, with its fractal dimension $D_q$ varying with the moment index $q$. We find that the multifractal spectrum $D_q$ of the Fock-space Hamiltonian in 1D ferromagnetic Heisenberg spin models is also interaction-strength independent. Additionally, we show that the scaling exponent $\tau_1$ and the multifractal spectrum $D_q$ exhibit distinct behaviors across the many-body localization transition. Our findings indicate that the scaling exponent $\tau_1$ and the multifractal spectrum $D_q$ serve as effective indicators for detecting the many-body localization transition. Finally, we outline the methodology for calculating the scaling exponent $\tau_1$ and the multifractal spectrum $D_q$ within Fock space. We anticipate that our approach will prove valuable for investigating the spectral properties of complex systems in Fock space. Interactive search involves an agent and an environment exchanging information through queries and responses. In this context, the agent seeks to identify target objects within an environment using a limited number of queries. This study addresses the challenge of finding multiple targets within a budget-limited framework. We examine two primary scenarios: first, when the number of targets is known in advance; and second, when this number is unknown. We introduce two novel algorithms designed for these respective cases and evaluate their performance against several baseline methods across various settings. Our results demonstrate that the proposed algorithms outperform the baselines in terms of success rate and efficiency. Furthermore, we apply these methods to the problem of multi-class image retrieval, showing that our approach surpasses existing state-of-the-art techniques. Drawing inspiration from adversarial attacks in classical machine learning, we investigate the vulnerability of quantum classifiers. We demonstrate that by introducing infinitesimal perturbations into classical data encoded onto a quantum computer's input qubits, one can significantly increase a quantum classifier's prediction error. Furthermore, these adversarial perturbations can be engineered to remain undetectable by current state-of-the-art noise detection methods. Our findings indicate that these universal adversarial examples possess broad applicability, successfully affecting a wide range of existing quantum classifiers. Additionally, we present a novel attack on a recently introduced classifier for two-qubit states, which relies on estimating the fidelity between input states. We successfully generate adversarial examples that cause misclassification with near-perfect accuracy. These results underscore the necessity for further research into enhancing the robustness of quantum classifiers. This study serves as a foundational step toward that goal, offering a comprehensive review of current quantum classifier architectures and their associated adversarial threats. This paper investigates Steklov eigenvalues for three-dimensional domains that are nearly spherical. We demonstrate that these eigenvalues can be expressed as power series in the small parameter, with early-stage coefficients formulated using the Laplace Steklov problem on the corresponding reference domain. Leveraging this efficient computational framework, we performed numerical analyses for ellipsoids and dumbbell-shaped domains. Our results reveal that the computed Steklov eigenvalues are generally not integers, contrasting with classical Steklov eigenvalues, and we explore the geometric implications of this finding. Furthermore, we establish that ellipsoids possess distinct Steklov eigenvalues, thereby refuting a three-dimensional analogue of a conjecture previously proven in two dimensions. Finally, our numerical findings indicate that for dumbbell domains, certain Steklov eigenvalues exhibit multiplicity, suggesting that the classical conjecture does not extend to this class of domains. Additionally, we examine how ellipsoidal symmetry influences the structure of Steklov eigenvalues and their associated eigenfunctions. In the concluding section, we outline several open questions regarding Steklov eigenvalues. Specifically, we address the unresolved issue of whether ellipsoids can have repeated Steklov eigenvalues and propose a conjecture asserting that they cannot. We substantiate this conjecture by presenting numerical evidence and deriving a sufficient condition under which it holds true. Furthermore, we demonstrate that this condition is satisfied in two dimensions, thus confirming the validity of the conjecture in that context. Finally, we establish a lower bound for the multiplicity of a Steklov eigenvalue, which approaches 1 as the domain's eccentricity increases. These findings underscore the intricate relationship between ellipsoidal geometry and its Steklov spectrum. In the final subsection, we extend our conjecture to general domains and provide a proof for the two-dimensional case. The proof relies on an explicit formula for the first-order perturbation of a Steklov eigenvalue, derived via the Hadamard variational formula. This approach also yields a lower bound for the derivative of the Steklov eigenvalue with respect to the small parameter, which is sharp in certain instances. We further illustrate the utility of this formula by deriving a lower bound for the derivative of a Steklov eigenvalue with respect to the domain parameter, a result that appears to be novel. Conformance checking aims to identify deviations between process models and their executions, typically represented as event logs. However, log mining often yields incomplete and noisy data, whereas the processes they represent are often modular, consisting of loosely coupled components. This paper introduces infix and postfix alignments as a method for performing conformance checking on infix subsequences and suffixes of event sequences, respectively. These alignments offer a sound and complete approximation of alignments, which measure the distance between process models and event logs. Additionally, infix and postfix alignments can be computed efficiently using existing techniques for infix and suffix mining. The study also presents a specific variant of infix alignment tailored for modular processes, which decomposes the problem into smaller subproblems for individual process components. Finally, the paper presents an experimental evaluation comparing infix and postfix alignments against standard alignments, demonstrating that they are competitive in terms of accuracy and efficiency. The proposed methods are implemented in the ProM framework. Overall, this work provides a foundation for conformance checking with trace fragments, which is particularly relevant for stream processing and stream mining. Furthermore, it supports modular conformance checking, enabling the analysis of process models composed of multiple, loosely coupled components. The research is grounded in the premise that conformance issues in individual components can be identified and resolved more effectively than when analyzing an entire process as a single, tightly coupled entity. The paper also addresses the challenge of handling noise in event streams. The study concludes by outlining potential future research directions. Keywords: conformance checking, process monitoring, conformance metrics, stream processing, stream mining, noise handling, modular conformance checking.

Accurate radio propagation modeling is essential for the planning and optimization of cellular networks. While traditional models are computationally efficient, they often lack the precision needed for modern network design. This paper introduces a new approach to radio propagation modeling by employing deep convolutional neural networks. We demonstrate that these models can be trained directly on channel state information (CSI) reports from user equipment, eliminating the need for traditional propagation model parameters. Our results indicate that deep convolutional models surpass the performance of standard empirical models, such as the 3GPP 3-dB model. Furthermore, we show that these models can be effectively utilized for radio map generation. The proposed method is evaluated using a dataset collected in an office environment, and the implementation is made available as an open-source project. We anticipate that this work will inspire future research into deep learning applications within cellular network planning and optimization. We introduce a straightforward and intuitive semantics for temporal planning, demonstrating that for any temporal planning language, there exists a corresponding validation problem. This problem can be solved by mapping it to a specific instance of a broader query problem. Leveraging this mapping, we establish that the query problem is decidable and provide an algorithm to compute specific complexity bounds. We illustrate the application of this approach across various temporal planning languages. Furthermore, we confirm that the proposed complexity bounds are tight for several instances, including those for a prominent language like $\text{ATFT}$. Finally, we outline an algorithm for verifying temporal planning and discuss its associated complexity bounds. To our knowledge, this research represents the first formal investigation into the validity and complexity of temporal planning. Additionally, we have implemented and released a library that enables the verification of temporal planning. This library facilitates the formal validation of planning problems and the execution of queries defined over them. We demonstrate the library's utility by formally validating the planning problems of two well-known planners, GPT and GTP, and by conducting an analysis of the complexity of $\text{ATFT}$. Our results indicate that the current complexity bounds for $\text{ATFT}$ can be improved. We also discuss the decidability of the temporal planning validation problem in the context of our work. Specifically, we show that the decidability of $\text{ATFT}$ relies on the decidability of a recently proposed temporal logic, $\text{TL}_{\text{R}}$. We further demonstrate that the complexity bounds for $\text{TL}_{\text{R}}$ are tight. Consequently, this provides the first tight complexity analysis for $\text{ATFT}$. We conclude by discussing the open problems that arise from our work.

**Keywords:** Temporal Planning, Formal Semantics, Complexity Analysis, Verified Programming.

Power system expansion planning (PSEP) models are essential for determining future generation, transmission, and storage investments. However, their outputs are highly sensitive to variations in input data, including costs, prices, and scenario parameters. This study systematically examines how input uncertainties affect the outputs of a typical PSEP model, specifically focusing on generator dispatch, investment levels, and total system costs. We demonstrate that model sensitivities can be quantified using the variance-based Sobol' method, which effectively identifies the most influential input parameters. Furthermore, we introduce a computationally efficient approximation of this method that enables the analysis of high-dimensional parameter spaces. Our findings indicate that while the model is highly sensitive to variations in generation costs, transmission investments are influenced by a broader range of parameters. Additionally, we show that the approximate method yields results comparable to the full Sobol' approach but with significantly reduced computational time. Finally, we explore strategies to mitigate these sensitivities, such as refining the uncertainty characterization of input parameters and adopting a robust optimization framework. These contributions provide a comprehensive toolkit for analyzing PSEP models, thereby enhancing the reliability of their outcomes. The entire analysis is available as open-source code.

This paper investigates global strong solutions to the Vlasov-Poisson system within bounded domains featuring either absorbing or reflecting boundaries. We establish a global in time existence result for both smooth and low-regularity initial data. The methodology relies on the compactness of forward-time propagators in phase space, derived from energy estimates, alongside the application of Fubini's theorem and the Hardy inequality. Notably, this approach avoids the use of Gronwall's lemma, thereby overcoming the typical difficulty of proving global existence in bounded domains where control over the growth of particle number and energy is unattainable. Furthermore, the study extends to a broader class of electric fields, encompassing those found in plasma physics. We demonstrate the existence of solutions for both reflecting and absorbing boundary conditions. A significant advancement is the resolution of the issue concerning the regularity of initial data near the boundary, which had previously hindered global existence proofs. This breakthrough is achieved through a novel technique utilizing the maximum principle to control the regularity of the distribution function and its velocity derivatives at the boundary. Additionally, we provide a new proof of the regularity compactness property for velocity derivatives, which is essential for deriving the necessary a priori estimates. The findings are applicable to both reflecting and absorbing boundary conditions. The novelty of this work lies in its ability to derive uniform a priori estimates in velocity for the distribution function and its spatial derivatives, even in the presence of electric fields with low regularity in velocity. This achievement is facilitated by a new class of function spaces that are invariant under the Wigner transform, which are specifically adapted to handle electric fields that are functions of space and time. These findings are particularly relevant for analyzing systems with reflecting boundaries. Finally, we address the long-standing open problem of the existence of weak solutions with low-regularity data in bounded domains with absorbing boundaries. Our approach yields a local existence result in this setting, and we anticipate that the global existence result previously established for reflecting boundaries can be extended to the absorbing case. The methodology is also applicable to the Vlasov-Maxwell system in bounded domains. The paper is structured as follows: Section 2 presents the model and assumptions; Section 3 reviews the mathematical properties of the problem; Section 4 introduces the function spaces required for the analysis; Section 5 presents the main results; and Section 6 provides the proofs. When software developers encounter bugs or defects, they must articulate their specific requirements to locate the relevant concepts within the code. However, developers often struggle to translate their needs into appropriate search terms. To address this, we propose a novel approach that utilizes information retrieval (IR) techniques to automatically suggest search terms for concept location tasks. Our method, STRICT (Search Term Identification for Concept Location using Information Retrieval), operates in two stages: first, it employs a text mining algorithm to extract semantic code elements from the source code, and second, it applies an inverted index to these elements to recommend terms that are semantically similar to the code. We evaluated STRICT across three open-source projects using a dataset of 1,000 concepts derived from 200 fault reports, each annotated with developer-provided fix commits. The results indicate that STRICT successfully generates useful search terms in 60% to 70% of the cases. Furthermore, we conducted a user study with 10 software engineers to assess the practicality of our approach. The findings demonstrate that STRICT can enhance search effectiveness by 20% to 30% and reduce search time by up to 40%. Additionally, the study revealed that 80% of participants found STRICT helpful for locating concepts, and 70% believed it would improve their overall productivity. The source code for STRICT is accessible at https://github.com/abhishekkumar1998/strict. STRICT is also integrated into our Eclipse plugin, which is available on the Eclipse Marketplace at https://marketplace.eclipse.org/content/strict-search-term-location-concept-ir. Colloidal gels are versatile materials that combine a solid-like network with a liquid composition, making them ideal for applications requiring both yield-stress behavior and fluid processing. This study introduces a novel rheo-acoustic method to manipulate the microstructure of colloidal gels, thereby adjusting their mechanical and rheological properties. By applying ultrasonic vibrations to a silica colloid, we simultaneously generate an ultrasound-induced acoustic field and allow for particle sedimentation. The resulting gels exhibit a more open network, lower elastic moduli, and higher viscosity. These rheo-acoustic gels demonstrate that the gel network can be reversibly tuned by modulating the acoustic field. Furthermore, we establish a rheo-acoustic phase diagram that correlates processing parameters with the resulting material properties, offering a framework for optimizing the manufacturing process. These findings provide a new approach for designing colloidal gels with customizable mechanical and flow characteristics. Additionally, the ability to control the gel network via ultrasound opens new avenues for applications in both passive and active acoustic technologies. This research was conducted using a silica colloid stabilized by polymer brushes. The brush architecture prevents particle aggregation during acoustic exposure, ensuring that the observed effects result from acoustic forces rather than acoustic-induced aggregation. This study highlights the potential of combining ultrasound and rheology to create new materials with tailored properties. This paper aims to demonstrate the transitivity of the Collatz Conjecture within the realm of number theory. Although numerous authors have attempted to prove the conjecture, most have focused on establishing its validity for the first few iterations, thereby providing only partial proofs. In contrast, this study seeks to prove the conjecture's general case, characterized by the formula $7x_{n-1}+1=2^{n}x_n$. Consequently, I propose a novel theorem and an accompanying algorithm to substantiate this proof. This approach not only validates the Collatz Conjecture but also offers a method to generate the sequence defined by $3x_{n-1}+1$. Given that the primary objective is to confirm the conjecture's general applicability, the analysis will be restricted to the properties of natural numbers. To substantiate the proof, I will employ various sequences and numerical examples. Ultimately, I contend that this proof is both rigorous and accessible to readers with a high school level of mathematical knowledge. Categorizing documents by subject is a fundamental task in information retrieval and a critical component of managing large digital libraries. However, this process is particularly challenging for STEM fields, where specialized terminology often hinders classification. While deep learning models have demonstrated strong performance in automatically assigning subjects to STEM documents, they frequently depend on extensive labeled datasets, making them costly to train and difficult to fine-tune for new sub-domains. The classic stable marriage problem assumes men actively seek to match with women. This paper shifts the focus to the women's perspective, examining their strategy in choosing which proposals to submit. We first demonstrate that if a woman is uncertain whether her partner prefers her over another suitor, her optimal strategy is to reject any incoming proposal. We then explore the scenario where a woman can selectively accept or reject offers. We establish that in this case, every woman will eventually receive a stable match, provided she adopts a greedy acceptance policy. Furthermore, we prove that this greedy approach is optimal for every participant. Finally, we extend these findings to the many-to-one setting. The proposed algorithms operate within a dynamic environment where preferences evolve over time, and we analyze the expected number of rounds required for every participant to converge to a stable match. Our analysis covers both the static scenario, where preferences remain constant, and a dynamic scenario where preferences change at each time step. In both instances, we show that the expected time to reach a stable match is $O(n^2)$, where $n$ represents the number of participants. Additionally, we examine the case where the set of potential partners is unknown to the participants. We present a distributed algorithm that achieves a $O(n^2)$ expected time to reach a stable match. Finally, we discuss the impact of selfish behavior on the convergence time of our algorithms. Our findings indicate that self-interested agents may prolong the time required to reach a stable match. However, we also identify a specific class of agents who, despite being selfish, still converge to a stable match within $O(n^2)$ expected time. Summary evaluation is a critical component of the Summization task. To address the inherent limitations of traditional metrics, such as the inability of automatic scoring to capture semantic nuances and the subjectivity of human ratings, this paper introduces SummScore, a comprehensive metric designed to assess summary quality. This work investigates the recovery of sparse signals from quadratic measurements, defined by the mapping $y = A x^2$, where $x$ is a sparse vector and each entry of the symmetric matrix $A$ is independently drawn from a standard normal distribution. The objective is to reconstruct $x$ by solving a $\ell_1$-regularized least squares problem. The primary theoretical advancement is a nearly tight lower bound on the number of measurements $n$ required for successful recovery with high probability. This result is achieved by demonstrating that the measurement map $x^2 \mapsto y$ satisfies the restricted isometry property (RIP) for sparse vectors with high probability. Furthermore, we establish that the proposed algorithm converges to a global minimum with a high probability bound. These findings represent the first comprehensive theoretical analysis of this problem, offering the first theoretical guarantees for any algorithm attempting to recover sparse vectors from quadratic measurements. Additionally, numerical experiments indicate that this approach can outperform existing methods in both speed and accuracy. The code is publicly accessible at https://github.com/ashwinb/QuadraticSparse. Finally, we provide a detailed discussion of the proof techniques and their connections to broader research areas. This manuscript is intended as a companion to the paper by B. Shahbaba et al., "Sparse signal recovery from quadratic measurements," to be published in IEEE Transactions on Information Theory. Recent advancements in sensor fusion have introduced novel paradigms for combining camera and LiDAR data. LiDAR-derived point clouds are typically projected into bird's-eye view (BEV) representations to facilitate fusion. However, relying solely on LiDAR BEVs can be inadequate when significant LiDAR data is missing due to adverse weather or long-range occlusions. To address this, we introduce a straightforward yet robust fusion framework that integrates LiDAR camera images with both LiDAR and radar point clouds. We employ a dual-stream strategy: one stream processes LiDAR point clouds in image space, while the other generates a camera-only BEV using a camera-only depth completion module. These streams are combined via a cross-stream module to integrate camera and LiDAR point cloud data, followed by a cross-stream fusion module that integrates the LiDAR BEV with the camera-only BEV. This architecture enables camera data to supplement missing LiDAR information, resulting in superior performance. Extensive experiments across four datasets demonstrate the framework's effectiveness, with particularly notable gains in adverse weather conditions. The code is accessible at https://github.com/BEVFusion/BEVFusion. Furthermore, our model is available for immediate deployment on the NVIDIA DRIVE AGX Orin platform. We introduce a theoretical framework for the energy spectrum in the dissipation range of incompressible fluid turbulence, incorporating the effects of the inertial-range irreversibility parameter $\mathcal{N}$ and molecular viscosity $\nu$. This model aligns with direct numerical simulation (DNS) data across a broad spectrum of Reynolds numbers and viscosity values. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the theory remains valid at low Reynolds numbers and low Mach numbers, offering a comprehensive description of turbulence from the viscosity subrange through to the inertial and cascade ranges. This extends the theory's applicability to all scales of incompressible turbulence, thereby providing a foundation for understanding the energy spectrum in the viscous subrange. Additionally, we show that the theory accurately describes the energy spectrum in the thermal dissipation range of a compressible gas at low Reynolds numbers and low Mach numbers, where thermal conductivity plays a role analogous to kinematic viscosity in incompressible fluids at low viscosities. Finally, we establish that the similarity hypothesis holds in the dissipation range, enabling the construction of a universal velocity structure function that matches DNS results for incompressible turbulence at low Reynolds numbers and low Mach numbers. This outcome further underscores the theory's ability to describe all scales of incompressible turbulence. We conclude by discussing the implications of these findings for the energy spectrum in the viscosity subrange of incompressible turbulence. These findings suggest that the velocity structure function in the viscosity subrange exhibits a universal similarity form, with the universal function determined by the inertial-range irreversibility parameter $\mathcal{N}$ and the molecular Péclet number $\Pe$. This prediction is supported by recent DNS results for incompressible turbulence at low Reynolds numbers and low Mach numbers. We also discuss the implications of these findings for the viscosity subrange of incompressible turbulence. Finally, we demonstrate that the dissipation-range theory can be extended to the viscous subrange, where the inertial-range irreversibility parameter $\mathcal{N}$ and the molecular Péclet number $\Pe$ play roles analogous to those in the dissipation range. We show that the viscous-subrange velocity structure function depends on $\mathcal{N}$ and $\Pe$, consistent with recent DNS findings. We conclude by discussing the implications of these results for the energy spectrum in the viscosity subrange of incompressible turbulence. We provide a thorough numerical characterization of the thermal profile generated by a laser within a liquid, accounting for beam geometry, power, and scanning speed. This analysis facilitates a precise prediction of the resulting spatial and temporal evolution of the diffraction pattern. By employing a 3D model of the material, we demonstrate that the phase object formed in the liquid is highly intricate, with its complexity governed by the competition between scanning and the material's thermal diffusion. Furthermore, we establish that the diffraction pattern is not merely a straightforward projection of the 3D refractive index distribution but is instead shaped by a convolution with a kernel determined by the material's thermal diffusion time. These findings are validated through both numerical simulations and experimental results. Our study offers a robust framework for comprehending and predicting the evolution of laser-induced thermal profiles in liquids. This enables the optimization of these profiles for applications such as lensing and photopatterning, while also facilitating the design of novel diagnostic tools for investigating thermal processes in liquids. Additionally, our approach is applicable to scenarios involving both continuous-wave and pulsed lasers. Finally, we outline a general methodology for analyzing and predicting the evolution of phase objects in liquids, which can be extended to other systems, including those utilizing absorptive liquids. This paper introduces a new evaluation method designed to assess the robustness of machine learning models in software mining tasks. Driven by the observation that model performance is heavily dependent on natural language representations, we assess representation "conclusion stability"—defined as the consistency of a representation's ability to predict downstream tasks. We demonstrate this metric using task accuracy across various tasks. Our approach is validated through a case study focusing on design discussion discussions, where we evaluate how changes in text processing and neural language model architectures influence conclusion stability. The results indicate that while performance can be enhanced by shifting from task-specific models to shared representations, such models do not always exhibit high conclusion stability. Furthermore, we identify that the selection of text processing methods and the choice of neural language model representation are the most critical factors in determining this stability. Ultimately, we argue that this proposed evaluation method serves as a valuable tool for assessing the robustness of mined software artifacts. Additionally, we outline a set of recommendations for developing more robust models, which are supported by our case study findings. These recommendations aim to assist researchers in achieving greater robustness in software mining applications. The code required to replicate our experiments and results is publicly accessible at https://github.com/andrewgustafsson1/conclusion-stability. This code also includes a library for calculating conclusion stability, which can be easily integrated into other mining applications. We intend to make this library public to facilitate its adoption by the broader community. We hope this method will inspire further research into the robustness of software mining. Specifically, we encourage researchers to investigate the conclusion stability of their models and to utilize our library to evaluate robustness in their applications. We believe this method will significantly aid in the development of more robust software mining solutions. Finally, we plan to continue refining this evaluation method and welcome collaboration with other researchers to further advance the field of software mining robustness. We also present the H-STREAM system, which integrates the framework with complementary software components to construct a scalable, high-performance processing pipeline. Furthermore, we show that these pipelines can query and process petabyte-scale data streams with minimal latency, while delivering up to 10x improvements in development and testing productivity.
