This study investigates how the top quark mass predicted by the $\overline{\rm MS}$ scheme varies with the number of light quark flavors $n_f$ at leading and next-to-leading orders. We demonstrate that incorporating the $n_f$ dependence at next-to-leading order is essential for a percent-level precision comparison between $\overline{\rm MS}$ predictions and experimental top quark mass measurements. Applying this framework, we show that the top quark mass is approximately 1.3 GeV larger when considering one light flavor ($n_f=1$) compared to the case with six light flavors ($n_f=6$). Furthermore, we discuss the implications of these findings for the recent top quark mass determination by CDF II. Finally, we provide updated predictions for the production cross section of top quark pairs at the LHC, which now include two-loop QCD corrections and $n_f$ dependence up to next-to-leading order. These enhancements result in a total uncertainty of 2.5% for $n_f=5$ and 3.5% for $n_f=6$ at $\sqrt{s}=7$ TeV. Additionally, we note that the uncertainty associated with the top quark production cross section is comparable to the current experimental precision of the LHC $t\bar{t}$ data. Consequently, future top quark mass measurements will require precise theoretical predictions for production cross sections, necessitating the inclusion of two-loop QCD corrections. Such advancements will be crucial for determining the Standard Model top quark mass with high accuracy. Our findings also suggest that any potential discrepancy between the LHC and Tevatron experimental results for the top quark mass is unlikely to be attributed to the $n_f$ dependence. A vertex $v$ in an $r$-edge-colored graph $G$ is defined as almost regular if the counts of incident edges with distinct colors are nearly equal, specifically differing by at most 1. This paper establishes that for any integer $k \geq 2$, if $G$ possesses an almost regular vertex of degree at least $kr$, then $G$ admits a $(kr + \lfloor \sqrt{2k} \rfloor + 1)$-list coloring. Furthermore, we prove that if $G$ has an almost regular vertex of degree at least $r(r+1)$, then $G$ is $(r^2 + r + 1)$-list colorable. Both results are optimal. This paper introduces a novel approach to modeling the spatial distribution of active and inactive satellites in low-Earth orbit (LEO). We develop a non-homogeneous Poisson process that accounts for the temporal evolution of the satellite fleet and the spatial clustering of satellites driven by their orbital elements. The study details the data collection methodology and outlines the model's properties, including parameter estimation techniques and model selection criteria. When applied to in-service satellites, the proposed model demonstrates superior performance compared to a homogeneous Poisson process. Furthermore, it effectively captures the historical growth of the LEO fleet and the resulting spatial clustering. The methodology is also extended to model space debris, with initial results indicating that debris exhibits even stronger clustering than the satellite population. These findings are supported by a simulation study that replicates the evolution of active satellites using Low-Earth Orbit Traffic Information (LEO-TI) data. This paper introduces a novel approach for creating coarse quadrilateral meshes on CAD models with complex topology, a process referred to as coarse quad-mesh generation. The technique begins by producing an initial coarse quad-mesh using quad-mesh simplification, which is then refined through a new integer linear programming (ILP) framework. This framework facilitates the insertion of refinement lines and the rearrangement of existing ones to achieve a target coarse quad-mesh. The proposed method is versatile, capable of handling various constraints such as specific topological requirements, predefined line locations, and global or local symmetry. Furthermore, it supports the creation of quad-meshes with a quad-dominant topology, a feature that is difficult to address using traditional meshing techniques. The paper demonstrates the method's effectiveness through several examples, including CAD models of an airplane, a car, and a human head. The resulting coarse quad-meshes serve as a foundation for subsequent fine quad-mesh generation. The entire algorithm is implemented in C++ and is publicly accessible via the QuadMesh Creator (QMC) tool. Additionally, the code is open-source, allowing users to apply the method to their own CAD models. The QMC tool is available at http://www.cs.uafroo.com/qmc. The source code can be found at https://github.com/taekyung/QuadMeshCreator. The authors welcome inquiries and collaboration. For further details, please contact Tae-Kyung Kim at tkkim@cs.uafroo.com. Pearson's correlation coefficient is a fundamental metric widely used to quantify the strength of the linear relationship between two variables. However, interpreting the magnitude of correlation in practical applications remains challenging due to the absence of universally accepted standards. This difficulty is often compounded by the reliance on Monte Carlo simulations to determine statistical significance, which can be computationally intensive. To address these issues, we present a novel approach for calculating the distribution of the sample correlation coefficient under data permutations using analytic formulas rather than simulations. This method enables the derivation of exact, closed-form expressions for the mean, variance, and higher-order moments of the permuted sample correlation. These analytic formulas are derived via the moment generating function, which is obtained through a change of variables applied to the multivariate normal probability density function. Furthermore, we demonstrate that applying this transformation to the multivariate Student's t probability density function yields analytic solutions for its moments as well. It then emphasizes that the primary motivation for this approach is to investigate the strongly coupled regime of general relativity, specifically addressing the problem of non-perturbative gravity. The discussion begins by noting that while perturbative quantization of the Einstein-Hilbert action yields a non-renormalizable theory, a quantum description of classical gravitational two-body scattering in the strong-field regime remains an unsolved problem. Consequently, the text argues that a non-perturbative quantum framework for classical two-body scattering is necessary, with the quantum $S$-matrix providing the appropriate language. The subsequent section details the derivation of black-hole metrics as an application of this $S$-matrix approach. Finally, the concluding section explores the strong coupling problem by examining two distinct non-perturbative extensions of the Einstein-Hilbert action: first, a theory incorporating a non-linear term in the curvature scalar, and second, a theory featuring a non-linear term in the Riemann tensor. In both scenarios, the $S$-matrix approach is demonstrated to enable the derivation of black-hole metrics. The text ends by emphasizing that these findings suggest a viable path toward constructing a non-perturbative quantum theory of gravity. Additionally, an appendix is included to outline the fundamental principles of the $S$-matrix approach to classical two-body scattering. This study achieves uniform stabilization of 3D Navier-Stokes equations, defined by the critical Sobolev exponent $H^{1-\frac{3}{q}}$ where $1<q<3$, through finite-dimensional localized feedback controls. The control region is determined by a compact set $K\subset\Omega$, and the resulting control forces depend exclusively on the trace of the velocity on the boundary of this region, $u|_{\partial K}$. This methodology extends the stabilization results previously established in [10] and [11] to broader functional settings. Furthermore, the paper provides an explicit formula for the minimal dimension of the control subspace, a feature absent in the work of [10]. These findings are applicable to both bounded domains and the entire space $\mathbb{R}^3$. The stabilization is proven to be exponentially stable, with the required gain in the feedback control law being explicitly calculated. Additionally, the study demonstrates that the control subspace can be constructed using a minimal number of eigenfunctions of the Stokes operator. A key advantage of this approach is that the necessary data for designing the feedback control is gathered from an interior region rather than the entire boundary. These results are also relevant to the stabilization of the linearized Navier-Stokes equations. The methodology employed here is also utilized in [12] to derive explicit bounds for the control energy. Finally, the paper includes a detailed analysis of the case where the control region is the boundary of the domain. Notably, the authors have also addressed the stabilization of the linearized Navier-Stokes equations within critical $L^q$-based Sobolev and Besov spaces using a control subspace generated by a finite number of Laplacian eigenfunctions. The corresponding results are published in [2]. The paper also references [3], which details the stabilization of the linearized Navier-Stokes equations in critical $L^q$-based Sobolev spaces using Laplacian eigenfunction-based feedback controls. Other relevant references include [4], which discusses uniform stabilization of the Navier-Stokes equations in critical $L^q$-based Sobolev spaces via finite-dimensional localized feedback controls, and [5], which explores uniform stabilization of the Navier-Stokes equations in critical $L^q$-based Besov spaces using Laplacian eigenfunction-based feedback controls. The authors acknowledge that the control subspace can be generated by a finite number of Laplacian eigenfunctions, a detail that warrants further investigation.

To address this, we present the LitMind Dictionary, an open-source online platform that provides definitions and contextual examples for a vast array of words. Its backend is supported by the LitMind Dictionary Network, a new open-source resource comprising over 1.5 million high-quality entries. We outline the platform's features and demonstrate how its backend enhances the performance of downstream applications, including the downstream network. LIME-RS is a post-hoc, model-agnostic, and local explanation method designed for black-box recommendation models. Despite its promise, its utility is constrained by the inability of current approaches to guarantee specific properties for these explanations. This paper introduces a method to ensure four key characteristics of LIME-RS explanations: adherence, sparsity, constancy, and stability. By leveraging the concept of perturbation neighborhoods, we demonstrate that simultaneously satisfying all four properties is impossible. Consequently, we propose a strategy to enable the joint fulfillment of adherence and constancy, as well as stability and adherence, though the latter comes at the expense of sparsity. Our approach is evaluated using a recommendation dataset, and the code is publicly available at https://github.com/fernando-ruiz/lime_rs. Furthermore, we demonstrate that our method can be applied to recommender systems based on deep learning architectures. The experimental results indicate that explanations generated by our method are more interpretable and trustworthy than those produced by existing state-of-the-art techniques. Finally, we show that our method enhances the fairness of LIME-RS recommendations. The paper concludes with a discussion of potential future research directions. The source code can be found at https://github.com/fernando-ruiz/lime_rs.

This capability is realized through a straightforward adjustment of the sheet charge in an overlying capping layer. Furthermore, we show that the 2DEG gap can be fully closed in InAs by positioning the Fermi level at the bottom of the conduction band. This paper investigates the impact of local queries on the sample efficiency of robust learning. Specifically, we examine a model where the learner can query the model within a bounded region surrounding each training example. Our theoretical analysis demonstrates that local queries can significantly enhance sample efficiency, yet this advantage is constrained by the size of the queried region. We illustrate this limitation through a specific instance where local queries fail to improve sample efficiency when the region is sufficiently small. Furthermore, we establish an algorithm that achieves sample efficiency improvements by leveraging local queries within a reasonable region. We support these findings with experiments on real-world datasets that confirm the effectiveness of our approach. Finally, we extend the problem framework to incorporate local queries and prove that our proposed algorithm maintains its sample efficiency guarantees under this generalized setting. This paper introduces Fast Sinkhorn \textsc{Ii}, a new iterative algorithm designed to efficiently and accurately compute optimal transport distances between two $n$-dimensional discrete measures. The method achieves linear time complexity, $O(n)$, and linear iteration count, while maintaining exact results without the exponential error growth typical of approximate approaches. This advancement addresses a key limitation of the previously published Fast Sinkhorn \textsc{I}, which, despite its linear complexity, suffered from significant numerical errors at high precision levels. In contrast, Fast Sinkhorn \textsc{Ii} scales effectively to large problem sizes and achieves convergence within a linear number of iterations. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the proposed method can be parallelized, offering substantial performance gains on multicore architectures. Experimental results confirm that Fast Sinkhorn \textsc{Ii} is up to three orders of magnitude faster than Fast Sinkhorn \textsc{I}} while delivering more accurate solutions. The source code is publicly accessible at \url{https://github.com/andreasmertel/FastSinkhornII}. The implementation is available in the Python package \texttt{ot} (https://github.com/PythonOT/PythonOT) and the C++ package \texttt{pyot} (https://github.com/andreasmertel/pyot). Both packages support the use of Fast Sinkhorn \textsc{Ii}. The \texttt{pyot} package also includes a GPU implementation of Fast Sinkhorn \textsc{Ii}, enabling execution on graphics processing units. The AU Mic system, a young, active M-dwarf, hosts two transiting planets, AU Mic b and c. This study presents Far Ultraviolet (FUV) observations of AU Mic captured during both quiescent and flaring states, utilizing the Cosmic Explorer Explorer Satellite (CoEES) and the Imaging Ultraviolet Spectrograph (IUVS) on the Mars Polar Lander (MPL). We analyzed the CoEES data to determine the FUV flux and its variability, while IUVS data were used to measure the emission of the O VI 1032/1038 Å doublet. Our results indicate that AU Mic's quiescent FUV flux is approximately 100 times greater than that of the Sun, with a flare component roughly 10 times more intense. Furthermore, the ratio of O VI 1032 Å to 1038 Å suggests that the majority of the O VI emission originates from the stellar chromosphere rather than the corona. Finally, we estimated the mass loss rate for AU Mic b and c, finding that both planets experience extreme mass loss, with AU Mic b losing mass at a rate about 100 times higher than AU Mic c. These findings suggest that AU Mic b is likely in a late stage of evaporation, whereas AU Mic c may still retain a substantial portion of its initial mass. Collectively, these results underscore the critical role of high-energy radiation in the evolution of planets orbiting active M-dwarfs. This paper investigates the dynamics of charged particles subject to both radiation reaction and movement through a resistive medium. We demonstrate that within this framework, the classical bound state becomes unstable, yielding a fractal trajectory. The fractal dimension is determined by the ratio of the radiation reaction timescale to the characteristic timescale of the charged particle's motion in the resistive environment. These findings are corroborated by numerical simulations. Additionally, the continuous charge distribution associated with this fractal trajectory exhibits a multifractal structure. Our results suggest that the coexistence of radiation reaction and resistive material forces can generate complex dynamics, including fractal trajectories and multifractals. This phenomenon is particularly relevant for charged particles in gaseous environments, such as those found in the solar wind and other astrophysical settings. We have also provided links to the computational code used in this study. In classification tasks involving severely imbalanced datasets, where one class significantly outnumbers others, standard nearest neighbor methods often yield poor results. This study introduces a statistical approach to enhance the performance of such algorithms. The proposed method involves resampling the overrepresented classes to balance the dataset, followed by the application of a weighted nearest neighbor classifier. The weighting scheme is determined by the distance between each observation and its assigned class label. We present the theoretical underpinnings of this methodology and outline the mathematical framework for the weighted nearest neighbor classifier. Furthermore, the paper provides a comprehensive simulation analysis to evaluate the method's performance. Finally, the results of applying this approach to real-world datasets are discussed. The code required to replicate the simulations is available at: https://github.com/Ankit-1998/NN-Classifier. Keywords: Classification, Imbalanced Data, Nearest Neighbor, Resampling, Weighted KNN. We report the second installment of a series identifying the brightest quasars at high redshifts by cross-matching SkyMapper Deep Survey (SDS) data with the 2018 Cosmic Evolution Survey (COSMOS) catalog. This study presents 11 new ultra-luminous quasars (ULQs) with absolute magnitudes $M_{AB} \leq -28.5$ and redshifts $z \geq 2.5$, detected within the COSMOS field. These findings are complemented by ULQ discoveries from the first paper in this series, which utilized SDS observations of the COSMOS Extended Survey (COSMOS-XE). The combined sample comprises 21 ULQs, including 11 previously unknown objects. We analyze the properties of these newly identified ULQs and compare them to the sample from the first paper. Furthermore, we calculate the luminosity function (LF) for the combined sample and compare it with LF estimates derived from other studies. Our results indicate that the SDSC catalog contains 10 ULQs with $M_{AB} \leq -28.5$ at $z \geq 2.5$ that were not previously known. We also identify 11 ULQs that are either newly discovered or detected for the first time with $M_{AB} > -28.5$. The resulting LF at $M_{AB} \leq -28.5$ and $z \geq 2.5$ is $\Phi = 1.1^{+0.3}_{-0.1} \times 10^{-9} \text{ Mpc}^{-3}$. This value is approximately 1.5 times higher than the LF derived from the SDSC catalog in the first paper, and it is 1.5 to 2.5 times higher than LF estimates from other studies. This discrepancy suggests that the SDS survey is uncovering a population of ULQs that is more abundant than anticipated. We conclude that the SDS survey is highly effective at identifying ULQs, and the discovery of these numerous ULQs in the SDSC catalog may offer insights into the mechanisms driving the formation of supermassive black holes. Future work will focus on analyzing the physical properties of these ULQs. The data utilized in this study can be accessed via the SkyMapper Deep Survey Data Portal at https://www.skymapper.org/sds/. We introduce a gate-sensing technique to investigate charge tunneling dynamics between a quantum dot and an Al island situated on a 2D electron gas. By analyzing the time evolution of the dot's Coulomb blockade peaks, we determine tunneling rates that vary with temperature and the dot-superconductor coupling strength. Furthermore, we examine how the spectral shape of these time-evolution curves provides insights into the quantum nature of the tunneling process. These findings are compared against simple sequential tunneling models and a more sophisticated framework based on time-dependent density matrix equations. Ultimately, our results indicate that the spectral characteristics of the tunneling rates can be effectively modeled using a density matrix equation that incorporates both elastic and inelastic tunneling processes. Additionally, we explore the potential of this method for characterizing the tunneling properties of a quantum dot coupled to a phonon bath. Finally, we discuss the implications of these findings for establishing a quantum dot-qubit hybrid system. This paper introduces a data-driven approach to control networked processes by leveraging the Markov property inherent in these systems. Specifically, we develop a model-predictive framework for the control of networked processes using purely data-driven techniques. This methodology relies on estimating a transition probability matrix derived exclusively from historical state data, without requiring knowledge of the underlying process dynamics. We demonstrate the application of this framework to networked SIS epidemic models, where the network structure is unknown and the process is highly nonlinear and heterogeneous. Our results show that this data-driven approach yields superior performance compared to traditional model-based methods in terms of both cost and infection rates. Furthermore, we establish the convergence of the proposed framework to an optimal solution as the amount of data increases. Finally, we present numerical studies that validate the efficacy of this data-driven strategy. These examples illustrate that the proposed approach can achieve a near-optimal cost within a reasonable timeframe using a limited amount of historical data. Additionally, we confirm that the method remains effective even when the historical data is sparse. These findings underscore the potential of data-driven techniques for the prediction, optimization, and control of networked processes. The associated code is accessible at https://github.com/abhishekkumar12345678/Data-driven-control.

**Background:** The accuracy of automated robotic ultrasound systems for scoliosis assessment depends on the reliability of human operators. While the impact of operator experience on measurement accuracy has been established, the reproducibility of these measurements across different operators remains unverified.

**Objectives:** To evaluate the reproducibility of spinal curvature measurements performed by multiple operators using a robotic ultrasound system.

**Methods:** A total of 100 scoliosis patients were recruited. Each participant underwent 3D scoliosis assessment via robotic ultrasound, with every operator completing three scans per patient. The inter-operator reliability of these measurements was analyzed using intraclass correlation coefficients (ICC).

**Results:** The ICC values for the robotic ultrasound system ranged from 0.91 to 1.00, indicating excellent reproducibility.

**Conclusion:** The findings demonstrate that the robotic ultrasound system yields highly reproducible scoliosis measurements, regardless of the operator's experience level. This supports the system's potential for widespread clinical adoption. However, further research is necessary to confirm the accuracy of these measurements.

**Key words:** scoliosis, ultrasound, reliability, reproducibility, robotic.

This paper presents a non-parametric approach to generating synthetic speech prosody, utilizing a statistical duration model grounded in speech production theory. By integrating the theory's mathematical formulation with a statistical framework, we develop a model that produces speech duration contours based on the three primary constraints identified by the theory. To address the inherent non-linearity of the model, we propose an efficient median-based estimation method for its parameters. The resulting model is designed to generate synthetic speech with natural-sounding duration contours. We evaluate the quality of the generated duration contours through both quantitative analysis and human perceptual assessment. Our approach is implemented in Python and is available as open-source code. Furthermore, we demonstrate that this model can be effectively applied to both fixed and variable formant synthesis. Our quantitative findings indicate that the generated speech sounds natural, with human evaluations confirming that the produced duration contours are nearly indistinguishable from those of real speech. Additionally, we show that the model can synthesize speech that is intelligible to native speakers. Finally, we illustrate how this implementation can be adapted to create speech with controlled duration contours. To our knowledge, this represents the first successful application of a duration model to achieve such control. We anticipate that this implementation will facilitate further research into the application of statistical speech production theory. The Python code is accessible at https://github.com/abhishekkumar12345/Duration-Model-Implementation. This work was presented at Interspeech 2019.

This paper introduces a flatness-based control (FBC) strategy for the direct torque control of an industrial robot joint drive system that relies solely on motor position measurements. **Background:** Investigating life course health trajectories is essential for comprehending disease etiology and progression. While time-to-event data is frequently utilized to analyze these trajectories, the standard approach of averaging event times overlooks the dynamic nature of health over time. **Methods:** We introduce Multiple State Analysis (MSA), a novel multidimensional technique designed to handle multiple time-to-event data. MSA employs a two-dimensional framework where the x-axis represents time and the y-axis signifies a latent health status. By fitting a linear mixed model to observed event times, the trajectory of this latent health status is estimated. The study's primary objective is to demonstrate MSA's utility in analyzing time-to-event data and life course health trajectories, specifically using data from a Swedish cohort of myocardial infarction patients. **Results:** MSA successfully identified distinct patterns of time-to-event data, including a general decline in health, a decline followed by an increase, and an increase. Furthermore, the analysis revealed that patients with hypertension exhibited a more pronounced decline in health compared to those without hypertension. **Conclusions:** MSA offers a robust method for analyzing time-to-event data and investigating life course health trajectories. The technique is highly flexible, accommodating various data structures and enabling the simultaneous analysis of multiple time-to-event variables. Additionally, the method is straightforward to implement, requiring only standard statistical software. This article provides a detailed exposition of the method, including a user-friendly R package. We introduce a multi-center quadrature approach to evaluate the molecular continuum of atomic and atomic-like bound states. This scheme relies on a product of radial functions and angular spherical harmonics, where the radial components are expanded into a series of one-center partial wave functions centered at the quadrature points. The bound state radial wave function is represented as a product of exponential functions, while the angular part is expanded using spherical harmonics centered on the quadrature points. The angular dependence of the molecular continuum is determined via the coupled angular momentum theorem, and the bound state radial wave function is constructed using a recent method. This proposed quadrature scheme demonstrates high accuracy for both non-relativistic and relativistic molecular continua. Furthermore, we apply this scheme to compute the photoionization cross sections of the 1s2s ³S state of helium across the entire energy range, comparing our results with experimental data and other theoretical calculations. Additionally, the scheme is utilized to calculate the photoionization cross sections for the 1s2s ¹S and 1s2s ³P states of helium. Finally, we demonstrate that the scheme can be extended to handle relativistic continua within the Dirac formalism. These findings indicate that the multi-center quadrature scheme is highly effective for photoionization calculations involving molecular continua. The Fortran code implementing this scheme is publicly accessible. Keywords: Relativistic continuum bound state, photoionization cross section, multi-center quadrature scheme, molecular continuum. This paper investigates the decision problem of determining whether a graph $G$ possesses a resolving set of size at most $k$, specifically when parameterized by the size of a feedback vertex set, the number of vertices, and the genus. We demonstrate that the problem is fixed-parameter tractable (FPT) with respect to feedback vertex set and numerous natural parameters, including bounded vertex-degeneracy, bounded path-width, bounded tree-width, bounded branch-width, bounded tree-depth, and bounded Euler genus. Furthermore, we show it is FPT with respect to the number of vertices when the path-width is bounded by $O(\log n)$. Our proofs rely on the following novel concepts: (i) the application of graph embeddings to establish upper bounds for metric dimension, and (ii) the introduction of resolving depth and resolving branch-width, which extend the notions of graph depth and graph branch-width, respectively. Additionally, we prove that graph depth and graph branch-width are bounded above by the metric dimension. We also examine the problem under the parameter count of clique minors, showing it is para-NP-complete. Finally, we present a family of graphs with high genus and a large gap between their metric dimension and tree-width, thereby illustrating the tightness of our bounds. To our knowledge, this represents the first instance where graph embeddings are utilized to derive upper bounds for metric dimension. Our findings are supported by an open-access implementation available at https://github.com/akshaykumar1999/metric-dimension. This study investigates the potential for intense flooding events to occur during hothouse climates, characterized by high carbon dioxide levels and elevated global temperatures. Utilizing a high-resolution global climate model, we conducted simulations across various greenhouse gas concentrations and orbital configurations. Our findings indicate that while the atmosphere's water vapor capacity rises significantly in these extreme conditions, the likelihood of flooding does not increase proportionally. Instead, the probability of deluges is governed by the product of two factors: the total available water and the frequency of precipitation events. Consequently, the most severe flooding events are predicted to happen when the climate is warm enough to hold substantial atmospheric water, yet cool enough to maintain a relatively high frequency of precipitation. This narrow climatic window is expected to be widened by Earth-like orbital dynamics, which introduce periodic fluctuations in solar insolation that drive glacial-interglacial cycles. These orbital variations could facilitate episodic deluges during simulated hothouse climates. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the occurrence of such extreme flooding events can be identified through the analysis of hydrological time series. This approach offers a method for detecting extreme climate events in geological records, which is crucial for understanding the habitability of planets under extreme climatic conditions. This phenomenon is particularly pronounced during simulated supergreenhouse climates, where the Hurst exponent approaches 1.0. This instability is characterized by a sharp rise in the probability of extreme weather events, which could have profound implications for the habitability of such environments. The transition probability matrix for a correlated random walk (CRW) is defined by five parameters. This study introduces a novel polynomial, $P_{\lambda}(x)$, which relies on four of these parameters, to express the eigenvalues of CRW transition operators. Specifically, the eigenvalues are derived from the roots of the equation $P_{\lambda}(x) - \lambda P_{\lambda}^{*}(x) = 0$. Consequently, the eigenvalues of a CRW transition operator are bifurcated: one set consists of the fifth parameter, while the remaining set is determined by the aforementioned equation. We further establish an inequality for $P_{\lambda}(x)$ that facilitates the calculation of these eigenvalues. Additionally, we provide a formula to compute the transition probability of a CRW (CRWP) using these eigenvalues and their corresponding eigenvectors. The paper concludes by presenting an example of a graph where the transition probability is computed via the derived equation. This approach yields a graph transition matrix with a significantly reduced number of parameters compared to the original CRW transition matrix. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the transition matrix for this specific graph family adheres to the equation $P_{\lambda}(x) = 1$, implying that the transition probability for this graph family is entirely independent of the fifth parameter. This result is particularly significant for graph theory, as it simplifies graph analysis by reducing the parameter count to just one. We also examine the transition probability for another graph family, the Petersen graph, which follows the equation $P_{\lambda}(x) = 1 - \lambda$, yielding five distinct transition probabilities. These findings highlight the utility of the proposed equation in analyzing graph transition matrices and calculating associated transition probabilities. The methodology is also applicable to other graph transition matrices, such as those for the complete graph and the Petersen graph. The paper concludes with several open problems. This paper introduces a new tactic for HOL that allows users to temporarily restrict the set of available lemmas and axioms. The objective is to facilitate tactics that function without specific knowledge of the lemmas and axioms subsequently clocked in, while ensuring that any proofs generated are still verifiable using the originally available lemmas and axioms. We detail the implementation of this tactic and its underlying method, which involves creating a new type of theorem suitable for use by the user-defined restriction mechanism. Furthermore, we propose several tactics that effectively leverage this new capability. Finally, we outline a few potential future applications of both the tactic and the related methods.

We investigate the interplay between the Hofstadter regime and time-reversal symmetry breaking within a two-dimensional lattice model featuring two types of Weyl fermions. By applying a synthetic magnetic flux, the electronic band structure transitions from two sets of two Weyl nodes to a Hofstadter butterfly spectrum. At a specific flux value, the Hofstadter butterfly merges with the two original Weyl nodes, resulting in a spectrum characterized by ten new Weyl nodes. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the Berry curvature of these bands exhibits a fractal pattern known as the "Hofstadter butterfly." Finally, we illustrate the Hofstadter regime's potential to influence Weyl semimetals through a concrete example. This study aims to advance our understanding of Hofstadter physics and its applications in topological materials. Additionally, we anticipate that the Hofstadter regime could be realized in artificial systems, such as quantum Hall devices, where Hofstadter Weyl semimetals may emerge. This could be achieved by connecting quantum dots arranged in a two-dimensional square lattice, with an external magnetic field generating synthetic flux between them. We expect that the Hofstadter regime's influence on topological quantum systems will be a significant area of future research. Finally, we acknowledge the Hofstadter model's historical significance, noting that its discovery in 1954 preceded the formulation of quantum mechanics. We hope this work inspires further exploration of the Hofstadter regime's impact on topological systems. We present a hybrid dielectric-plasmonic nanoantenna designed to support a dark electric dipole mode within a quantum emitter positioned at its center. This system enables the creation of a bright, unidirectional electromagnetic dipole mode with a high Purcell factor. We demonstrate that this unidirectional emitter can be integrated into a waveguide, facilitating the efficient coupling of light into the waveguide's propagating mode. Furthermore, we show that a significant portion of the emitted photons can be directed into the waveguide by appropriately adjusting the dielectric and plasmonic dimensions of the antenna. These findings indicate that the proposed nanoantenna is highly suitable for applications involving the unidirectional generation of quantum emitters and their efficient coupling to optical waveguides. Additionally, we illustrate that this nanoantenna can be implemented using either gold or aluminum plasmonic materials alongside silicon dielectrics. The design is compact, with a total size of approximately 1.5 micrometers, and supports emitters operating in the near-infrared range. The methodology used to design and analyze the emitter and the light-matter coupling is broadly applicable to other sub-wavelength nanoantenna geometries. This approach holds promise for designing unidirectional emitters and nanoantenna-based quantum light sources that can be interfaced with optical waveguides. The interplay between gravity and friction in granular matter generates complex behaviors that defy conventional theories. A notable example is the "anomalous screening" effect, where the bulk compressibility of a granular assembly is significantly lower than that of individual grains. This study presents the first experimental confirmation of this phenomenon. We measured the compressibility of polystyrene beads within a vertical column subjected to a horizontal confining stress, comparing our results to the predictions of the recently developed force chain network model. Our findings demonstrate that the granular assembly's compressibility is orders of magnitude less than that of the individual beads. Furthermore, we show that the force chain network model accurately predicts this anomalous behavior. Finally, we confirm that the observed compressibility is independent of grain size, confirming a recent numerical prediction. These results establish a robust theoretical framework for understanding the mechanical properties of granular materials. This framework is anticipated to aid in the design of efficient bulk material handling systems and to enhance the stability of natural slopes and underground excavations. Additionally, it offers a pathway to unravel the complex behavior of other complex materials, such as colloidal suspensions and biological tissues. This study investigates the electronic structure of silicene supported on hexagonal boron nitride (hBN) using first-principles calculations. Our results indicate that while the free-standing system exhibits a zero-gap semiconductor characteristic, the interaction with the hBN substrate induces an energy gap of 0.05 eV, transforming the material into a direct band-gap semiconductor. Furthermore, we observe that Mn decoration shifts the Fermi level into the valence band, resulting in p-type semiconducting behavior. Additionally, the doping process enhances the material's magnetic properties, as evidenced by an increase in magnetic moment density from 2.00 $\mu_B$/cell to 2.05 $\mu_B$/cell. These findings suggest that Mn-doped silicene on hBN holds promise for spintronic applications. Finally, we demonstrate that the material exhibits strong magnetoresistance, with a percentage change of 100% at 0 K. These outcomes are attributed to the hybridization between Si and hBN atoms, the doping effect, and the magnetic interactions arising from Mn decoration. Consequently, Mn-decorated silicene on hBN is identified as a viable candidate for spintronic devices. Sgr A East is the Galactic Center's most luminous supernova remnant, yet its origin remains uncertain. While some researchers attribute it to a Type Ia supernova, others favor a core-collapse event. This study investigates the core-collapse hypothesis by analyzing the remnant's morphology and kinematics. We employed a Bayesian framework to determine the progenitor mass, supernova type, and explosion location, accounting for uncertainties in distance and inclination. Our analysis indicates that a core-collapse supernova from an 11 solar mass progenitor occurred 0.05 parsecs from Sgr A* with 90% confidence. This finding aligns with the remnant's observed morphology and kinematics and suggests a link to a nearby young stellar cluster. Our results support the hypothesis that a massive star within this cluster, which formed approximately 2.5 million years ago, exploded and triggered the cluster's dispersal. Furthermore, the supernova may have triggered star formation in the nearby Circumnuclear Disk. These conclusions are robust against uncertainties in distance and inclination. Additionally, we demonstrate that the proposed Sgr A East supernova is the most energetic core-collapse event in the Milky Way. We also rule out the possibility of a Type Ia supernova within the central parsec. Although a Type Ia event could have occurred 1.6 parsecs from Sgr A*, such an explosion would not explain the remnant's observed morphology and kinematics. These findings offer a novel perspective on the history of the Galactic Center. Finally, we discuss the implications of these results for the proposed connection between Sgr A East and the Great Starburst in the Magellanic Clouds. We show that the supernova could have triggered the Magellanic Clouds' starburst approximately 2.5 million years ago, though this scenario requires a distance to Sgr A East of less than 8.2 kiloparsecs. We also examine the potential for a supernova in the Magellanic Clouds to trigger the central parsec's star formation 2.5 million years ago, a hypothesis that is difficult to test due to the lack of a clear star formation signature in the Galactic Center. Ultimately, our findings suggest that the Galactic Center and its surrounding regions may be more interconnected than previously thought. This study underscores the need for a more comprehensive understanding of the Galactic Center's history and its relationship with the Magellanic Clouds. Our findings also highlight the necessity of conducting supernova simulations to better understand the remnant's morphology and kinematics.

Text classification is a fundamental task in natural language processing, yet multi-class classification often suffers from class imbalance, where some categories contain significantly fewer samples than others. This disparity can hinder model performance, particularly when the minority classes are linguistically distinct from the majority ones. To address this, researchers frequently employ oversampling techniques to generate additional training instances for underrepresented classes. This study evaluates the efficacy of various oversampling methods—specifically oversampling, SMOTE, SMOTE-NC, and ADASYN—across three publicly available text classification datasets. The experiments compare two popular deep learning architectures: CNN and Bi-LSTM. Our findings indicate that oversampling consistently enhances the performance of both CNN and Bi-LSTM models on all three datasets. Furthermore, we observed that the original oversampling approach generally yields superior results compared to the other methods tested. Finally, we present a comprehensive comparison of these techniques to guide future research in imbalanced multi-class text classification. This study examines the interconnections between local news online (LNO) coverage of COVID-19, including its sources, and the pandemic's progression in terms of cases, fatalities, and audience size within the United States. Utilizing data from the COVID-19 News Corpus, the LNO dataset, and the COVID-19 Data Platform, we apply a Bayesian structural time series model to analyze these relationships. Our findings indicate that LNO coverage of COVID-19 is driven by the disease's spread, while the volume of such coverage, in turn, influences the number of cases and deaths. Furthermore, we observe a negative correlation between LNO coverage and audience reach, suggesting that as news coverage intensifies, the audience diminishes. These results offer valuable insights for policymakers and media organizations aiming to leverage local online news for public health communication during the COVID-19 crisis. Additionally, the research demonstrates the utility of integrating large-scale, high-quality, real-time datasets for analyzing the dynamics of social phenomena. Finally, we outline several promising avenues for future inquiry. Specifically, we recommend investigating how LNO coverage varies across different topics and how this coverage influences audience perceptions of the pandemic. Moreover, we propose extending the current analysis to other emerging infectious diseases, such as Ebola and Zika, to determine if similar patterns exist. Finally, we suggest exploring the impact of media coverage on the public's behavioral responses to the virus. These directions are particularly relevant given the ongoing debate regarding the efficacy of media coverage in shaping public behavior during the COVID-19 outbreak. The Fast Multipole Method (FMM) is an algorithm designed to accelerate the calculation of pairwise particle interactions, reducing the computational complexity of N-body simulations from O(N^2) to O(N). This study investigates the FMM's precision within the context of fluid dynamics. Specifically, we examine an Eulerian simulation of a vortex ring, which conserves angular momentum, and compare results obtained using FMM against standard direct summation. Our findings indicate that FMM introduces significant errors in both energy and angular momentum. We attribute these discrepancies to truncation errors arising from the Taylor series expansion of particle potentials within FMM. Furthermore, we demonstrate that increasing the Taylor series order substantially mitigates these errors. Finally, we establish that the FMM error scales with the ratio of the particle spacing to the Taylor series radius. These insights enable the optimization of FMM parameters to achieve the desired level of accuracy. This work is pertinent to any simulation employing FMM for pairwise interactions where physical quantities such as energy and angular momentum must be conserved. Additionally, the derived error scaling law can be utilized to determine the appropriate Taylor series order required to achieve a specific error tolerance. This study presents a search for the double Higgs boson ($HH$) system produced in association with a single vector boson ($W$ or $Z$) during proton-proton collisions at $\sqrt{s} = 13$ TeV. The analysis utilizes data from the ATLAS detector collected by the Large Hadron Collider at CERN, amounting to an integrated luminosity of 139 fb$^{-1}$ from 2015 and 2016. The investigation examines $VH$ events where the vector boson decays leptonically and the Higgs bosons decay into $b\bar{b}WW^*$, $\tau\tau$, or $ZZ^*$. A multivariate discriminant is employed to separate signal from background, and the results are interpreted within the context of the Standard Model and various simplified models. No significant evidence for $VH$ production was observed. The 95% confidence level upper limits on the cross section times branching ratio relative to the Standard Model prediction range from 1.1 to 2.1 times. These findings are compared against predictions from the Standard Model and specific beyond-Standard-Model scenarios. Furthermore, this search represents the first observation of $W_H$ and $Z_H$ production in the $b\bar{b}$ final state. The combined results from the $VH$ and direct $HH$ searches are also included in the interpretation. The most stringent constraint on the production cross section of a Higgs-like resonance decaying to a pair of Standard Model vector bosons is established at 1.1 times the Standard Model prediction for a mass of 125 GeV. This constraint is derived from a combined analysis of the $VH$ and $hh$ channels, incorporating the $b\bar{b}$, $\tau\tau$, and $ZZ^*$ decay modes. The corresponding limits for the $hh$ channel alone are 1.3 to 2.1 times the Standard Model prediction across a mass spectrum of 125 to 625 GeV. These outcomes are also contrasted with those from other $HH$-like simplified models. The analysis concludes that the ATLAS detector has successfully identified a new class of Higgs boson production, specifically vector boson-associated production, and that the $VH$ search results are consistent with the Standard Model. We introduce a digital alkali spin maser that functions without an optical resonator, utilizing a chip-integrated photodetector alongside on- and off-resonance scattering. By employing a pulsed laser, we periodically reset the spin polarization, enabling maser action with lower laser power. This approach extends the maser's coherence time by a factor of three compared to continuous-wave operation using a similar resonatorless setup. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the maser's coherence time is directly proportional to the photodetector's gain. This device holds promise for applications in quantum sensing and metrology. Additionally, we outline potential pathways for integrating such spin masers into larger quantum circuits. Specifically, we illustrate that a single-photon-driven maser can be triggered by a quantum emitter, with the emission frequency contingent upon the emitter's quantum state. This capability establishes a fundamental interface between masers and quantum emitters, which is essential for the development of quantum information processors. Finally, we show that this interface can be leveraged to create a quantum switch capable of routing single photons based on the state of a remote qubit. These findings highlight the potential for masers to serve as critical components in future quantum information processing systems. The experimental data presented here are accessible via Zenodo. This paper investigates K3 surfaces that possess a Siegel disk of conformal modulus 1. We demonstrate that if such a surface is defined over $\overline{\mathbb{Q}}$, its automorphism group cannot be finite. Furthermore, we establish that if the Picard lattice $S$ of a K3 surface $X$ contains a unimodular sublattice $U$ isomorphic to the unimodular split hyperbolic lattice of rank 2, then $X$ admits a Siegel disk. Additionally, assuming Conjecture 1.1, we prove that $X$ must be defined over $\overline{\mathbb{Q}}$ and that its Picard number is at least 18. We also provide an example of a K3 surface $X$ featuring a Siegel disk, where the Picard lattice $S$ is the Kummer lattice derived from the singular Kummer fibration $f: K3 \to \mathbb{P}^1$. In this specific instance, $S$ is generated by the fibers of $f$ and the class of a section, resulting in a Picard number of 19. Finally, we outline an approach to determining the precise value of the modulus for the Siegel disk in this example. We investigate a scenario where dark matter consists of a stable, neutral, weakly interacting massive particle (WIMP) formed by a mixture of neutral superpartners. In this framework, the superpartner with the lowest mass does not exist as a free particle; instead, it is bound to a pion, reducing its mass through the pion's negative binding energy. This composite state decays into two pions and a Higgs boson, with the Higgs subsequently decaying into a gamma-ray pair. We analyze the implications of this model for LHC searches and future facilities, specifically regarding indirect detection via the predicted gamma-ray signature. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the gamma-ray spectrum from such dark matter decay can be distinguished from backgrounds produced by dark matter annihilation. Our findings indicate that the LHC could detect this decaying neutralino dark matter if its mass exceeds 110 GeV, while the High-Altitude Water Cherenkov (HAWC) observatory could detect it above 100 GeV. Additionally, a proposed gamma-ray telescope with a 1 km² effective area would be sensitive to this decaying neutralino up to approximately 1 TeV. We also show that such a particle could be detected by the Cherenkov Telescope Array (CTA) up to about 100 GeV. Finally, we highlight that this model offers a unique advantage: the gamma rays are emitted after dark matter decay, allowing them to be observed well after the last epoch of dark matter annihilation. This feature enables the use of gamma-ray spectra to constrain the dark matter density profile, thereby distinguishing the decay signal from annihilation background. We conclude that this decaying neutralino scenario represents a promising target for both collider and indirect detection experiments. We demonstrate that the genus of a dense graph can be computed with high precision by determining the genus modulo any integer. Building on this, we develop an efficient polynomial-time approximation scheme that is nearly tight, indicating that the genus of a dense graph is densely distributed. This advancement represents a significant enhancement to the tight bounds previously established by M\'{e}g\'{a}nne and Thomassen. Furthermore, we establish that the genus of a dense graph is well approximated by the expression $\left(\frac{1}{4\pi}\right)\left(\frac{n^2}{\max\{k, (n-k)^2\}}\right)$, where $n$ denotes the number of vertices and $k$ denotes the number of edges in the largest missing complete subgraph. This formula refines the asymptotic bounds originally set by Erd\H{o}s and Tur\'{a}n. Additionally, we prove that for sufficiently large $n$, the genus of a dense graph $G$ with $n$ vertices and $e$ edges is bounded by $\left(\frac{1}{4\pi}\right)\left(\frac{n^2}{(n-k)^2}\right) \le \mathfrak{g}(G) \le \left(\frac{1}{4\pi}\right)\left(\frac{n^2}{k^2}\right)$, where $k = \max\{e - \binom{n}{2}, 0\}$. These results are achieved through the application of the probabilistic method. Our approach also yields a straightforward proof of a conjecture by Erd\H{o}s and Gallai regarding the upper bound on the number of edges in a $K_{r+1}$-free graph. In a speech recognition task, the results confirm that the proposed algorithm outperforms competing methods in both convergence speed and generalization error. Additionally, the experiments illustrate that the computational cost of each iteration scales linearly with the size of the selected dataset. These properties suggest that the method is particularly well-suited for large-scale distributed learning applications. The Sinkhorn algorithm is a widely utilized iterative method for solving the Schrödinger problem, yielding the unique solution whenever one exists. This study examines the algorithm's behavior in instances where no such solution is present. We demonstrate that, under mild assumptions, the Sinkhorn iterates converge to a minimizer of a specific free energy functional. Furthermore, we establish a global convergence rate for these iterates in a weak metric, and, subject to additional conditions, derive a convergence result in a strong metric. These findings are illustrated through examples drawn from both continuous and discrete frameworks. The continuous proofs were developed in collaboration with J. Eckhoff, who previously established analogous results in the discrete setting. Eckhoff's work also addressed the additional convergence hypothesis required for the strong metric convergence, a hypothesis that we subsequently extend to the continuous case. Additionally, we generalize Eckhoff's counterexample to demonstrate a scenario where the extra hypothesis fails to hold. Finally, we provide a self-contained proof of the classical convergence of the Sinkhorn iterates for the case where a unique solution to the Schrödinger problem does hold. This result is derived using a novel approach that relies on the concept of free energy. Our methodology is sufficiently flexible to be applied to other contexts, such as the semi-discrete case. In this scenario, we show that the Sinkhorn iterates converge to a minimizer of the semi-discrete Schrödinger problem, thereby recovering and extending the findings of Benamou, Carlier, and Labbé. Furthermore, our approach yields a new, self-contained proof of the convergence of Sinkhorn to the optimal transport map in the Gaussian case, an application originally developed by Eckhoff. Urban environments are renowned for their social interactions and the exchange of diverse perspectives, a process driven by the movement of people across various social and economic backgrounds. These encounters are fundamental to the creative and innovative nature of cities. However, the pandemic-induced restrictions on movement and socializing, combined with the widespread adoption of remote work, have significantly reduced the frequency of such interactions. This study examines the impact of these behavioral shifts on the income diversity of urban interactions, utilizing a large-scale dataset of urban encounters derived from mobile phone data. Our findings indicate that the decline in income diversity was more pronounced in densely populated areas and among individuals with higher pre-pandemic incomes. Furthermore, the diversity of interactions linked to specific income brackets varied depending on the income levels of the other participants, revealing distinct patterns for interactions involving two high-income individuals, as well as those between high and low income groups. These results highlight the critical role of urban interactions in the functioning of cities and suggest that future urban planning must prioritize the maintenance of social connectivity. Additionally, our analysis of specific income brackets offers valuable insights for policymakers aiming to mitigate the social and economic disparities exacerbated by the pandemic. Finally, we explore the potential of artificial intelligence to foster new forms of social interaction that can help rebuild the social fabric damaged by lockdowns. This study introduces and evaluates two nonlinear field-splitting preconditioners designed for two-phase flow in heterogeneous porous media. Both methods utilize a nonlinear fixed-point approach combined with a field-splitting technique to construct these preconditioners. The initial strategy employs a multiphase black-oil model featuring a linear relative permeability approximation for gas, whereas the second replaces the linear gas permeability with a more accurate, albeit nonlinear, model. The field-splitting process is resolved through a simplified two-stage procedure: first, a linear flow problem is solved assuming constant pressure fields for both phases; second, a nonlinear diffusion problem is addressed using the pressure and saturation fields obtained from the initial step. The research demonstrates that preconditioning the second-stage problem with a suitable approximate solver enhances the overall efficiency of the field-splitting scheme. Furthermore, the study confirms that nonlinear field-splitting preconditioners are highly effective for multiphase flow in heterogeneous porous media, achieving superior performance compared to the widely used algebraic multigrid method. Finally, numerical experiments indicate that applying the field-splitting approach to the multiphase black-oil model results in a more efficient nonlinear fully implicit scheme than in two-phase flow scenarios. These findings are particularly significant for multiphase flow simulations involving strong nonlinear nonlinearities driven by relative and solution-dependent viscosities. The paper concludes by providing a detailed description of the field-splitting nonlinear preconditioners and their associated fixed-point and linear solvers. Additionally, it offers a comprehensive analysis of the algorithm's convergence behavior regarding model parameters, including relative and solution-dependent viscosities, as well as the distribution of permeability. The study also examines the relationship between these viscosities and the optimal field-splitting strategy, specifically addressing the impact of strong nonlinearities on convergence. Finally, the influence of capillary pressure on the field-splitting nonlinear preconditioner is explored. Numerical results indicate that while the method remains effective for cases with moderate capillary pressure, it fails to converge for scenarios characterized by high capillary pressure. This limitation is attributed to the field-splitting scheme's inability to adequately resolve the strong nonlinearities inherent in the capillary pressure function. However, the authors suggest that a more sophisticated field-splitting approach could potentially address this challenge. We introduce a theoretical framework for chiral optical cavities built from single-handedness metamaterials. Our model demonstrates that the single-handedness of these cavities enables the creation of two distinct and separable eigenmodes characterized by opposite circular polarizations. Furthermore, we show that a critical threshold exists for the refractive index of the metamaterial; surpassing this threshold allows for a tunable crossover between these two eigenmodes. This predictive model offers a new avenue for designing and manipulating chiral light-matter interactions. Additionally, we suggest that these single-handedness cavities could serve as highly efficient chiral sensors and facilitate the study of chiral molecules. Our findings have been validated through three-dimensional finite-difference time-domain simulations. These results underscore the significant potential of single-handedness optical cavities in advancing chiral photonics. Future research should focus on experimental verification and the development of practical applications. The Alcubierre metric represents a solution to Einstein's equations that theoretically enables superluminal travel. Originally derived as a vacuum solution, it has since been extended to include the energy-momentum tensor of a perfect fluid and the cosmological constant. This paper presents the metric's general solution incorporating a perfect fluid and the cosmological constant, demonstrating that such a solution exists only under specific conditions regarding the cosmological constant. Furthermore, it is established that the resulting warp drive geometry remains stable against linear scalar and gravitational perturbations. These findings suggest that a more robust theory of gravity may be necessary to achieve warp drive capabilities. Finally, the study examines the physical properties of the perfect fluid within this context, indicating that these properties are unsuitable for generating warp drive. Consequently, it is concluded that warp drive is unattainable within the framework of general relativity. Cities are increasingly adopting open data standards to foster innovation and enhance citizen engagement. However, transforming data from diverse city systems into these open standards is a labor-intensive and costly endeavor. This paper introduces GUIDES, a generic framework designed to streamline the integration of various city system data through a unified engineering solution. We demonstrate the GUIDES pipeline's application in ingesting data from multiple sources for two specific open data standards: GeoJSON and TAB Separated Values (TSV). Furthermore, we outline a cost model that enables cities to forecast the expenses associated with converting their system data to open standards. Our evaluation indicates that GUIDES significantly reduces both the time and financial resources required for data integration. Additionally, we have deployed GUIDES on the Google Cloud Platform to facilitate easy access to the tools for converting system data into open standards. We introduce and implement a spin-dependent motional probe to investigate the temperature, motional state distributions, and heating rates of individual ions within a two-dimensional crystal. By preparing ions in a phonon number distribution that mirrors the mode temperature and reading out the resulting spin-dependent dephasing, we can determine these parameters. This method is nondestructive to the ion crystal and enables repeated measurements on the same system. We apply this technique to a 2D crystal of $^{171}$Yb$^+$ ions, observing heating rates of approximately $0.001$ to $0.01$ phonons per millisecond. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the motional state distributions are non-thermal, characterized by a broader variance than predicted by a thermal distribution with the same average temperature. This distribution is fully characterized by two parameters: the average phonon number and its variance. We propose that such heating arises from the interaction between the ions and the cavity field. Our findings offer a robust approach for characterizing and controlling the motion of trapped ions, which is essential for scaling up quantum information processing. Additionally, this technique is applicable to other platforms, such as neutral atoms, where heating rates are typically lower. The accompanying open-source software can be utilized to analyze experimental data and characterize the motion of any trapped-ion or neutral-atom system. We introduce a method to investigate the chemical and electromagnetic contributions to the quantum-enhanced tip-enhanced Raman scattering (TERSC) of a single molecule. This approach is fully quantum and explicitly accounts for the molecule's coupling with the local electromagnetic field. Our findings indicate that electromagnetic effects can be incorporated into TERSC by adjusting the molecule's transition dipole moments, which are otherwise determined through time-independent, fully quantum calculations. This capability offers a straightforward and efficient means to isolate quantum electromagnetic effects within TERSC. Additionally, we demonstrate that these phenomena are particularly significant for molecules situated near a sharp metallic tip. The proposed methodology is implemented using the ALPSkit, an open-source software suite for quantum many-body systems. All computational details are provided in the supplementary material. Ammonium sulfate ((NH$_4$)$_2$SO$_4$) exhibits a large entropy-driven electrocaloric effect, yet the underlying mechanism remains unclear. This study investigates the entropy variation associated with the phase transition in (NH$_4$)$_2$SO$_4$ by analyzing its electronic structure and lattice dynamics. We demonstrate that the phase transition is linked to a symmetry-breaking process that lifts the degeneracy of the lowest Jahn-Teller pair of modes. This transition is further supported by a phase diagram derived from the temperature-dependent pressure-induced electrocaloric response. Our findings indicate that the significant entropy change is primarily attributed to the substantial volume difference between the high- and low-temperature phases, a result corroborated by high-pressure experiments. Additionally, we establish that the entropy difference between these phases can be accurately predicted using density functional theory. These results offer valuable insights into the entropy fluctuations occurring during the phase transition in (NH$_4$)$_2$SO$_4$. Finally, we discuss the potential for achieving even larger entropy changes in other materials by employing a similar theoretical methodology. This model incorporates a broad category of suboptimal mechanisms, where participants' trait-like scores indicate the extent to which they employ these tendencies. By integrating these components, we can better explain the complexity of human learning and predict individual differences in learning outcomes. This study addresses the Approximate Near Neighbor Search (ANN) problem under the Fréchet distance for polygonal representations of time series. We introduce an algorithm that, given a set $\mathcal{P}$ of $n$ such polygons, a radius $r$, and an approximation factor $\rho > 1$, preprocesses the input to build a data structure. This structure enables the identification of an $\rho$-approximate $r$-center for any query polygon $Q$ in $O(1)$ time. The algorithm achieves a worst-case bound of $O(n^{1+\epsilon})$ for the data structure size and $O(\log n)$ for the query time, where $\epsilon$ depends on $r$, $\rho$, and the maximum degree of the polygons. We demonstrate that these bounds are nearly tight by establishing a lower bound of $\Omega(n^{1-\epsilon})$ for the data structure size and $O(\log n)$ for query time, valid when $\rho$ is a sufficiently large constant. Furthermore, we prove that for any fixed $\rho > 1$, the combination of $O(1)$ query time and $O(n^{1-\epsilon})$ preprocessing time is unattainable for sufficiently large polygon sets. Additionally, we show that the preprocessing and query complexities are essentially tight for the specific case of polygon lines. Finally, we extend our results to ANN search for general metric spaces, deriving a lower bound of $\Omega(n^{1-\epsilon})$ for data structure size and $O(\log n)$ for query time, which holds for any metric admitting an $O(1)$-bi-Lipschitz embedding into the Hamming space. This lower bound is tight for the Euclidean plane when $\rho$ is a sufficiently large constant. Our findings rely on a novel lower bound for the Hamming nearest neighbor problem, which is of independent significance. Specifically, we establish that for any fixed $\rho > 1$, the combination of $O(1)$ query time and $O(n^{1-\epsilon})$ preprocessing time is impossible for large sets of polygon lines under the $L_1$ metric. This result is achieved through a reduction from the Element Uniqueness problem. To the best of our knowledge, this represents the first lower bound for ANN search in the Hamming metric that is independent of the approximation factor $\rho$. Addressing measurement errors in quantum experiments is essential for obtaining precise outcomes. While various mitigation strategies exist, they often demand substantial experimental resources or depend on characterizing errors through separate calibration runs. This study introduces a scalable mitigation method that eliminates the need for additional measurements. By applying iterative Bayesian unfolding to raw data, we enhance statistical significance while maintaining high fidelity. We validate this approach across several simulation-based quantum tasks, including quantum cloning, phase estimation, and the variational quantum eigensolver. Furthermore, we extend the technique to handle bin-wise fidelity, demonstrating its effectiveness in data analysis. This study examines how humans and socially intelligent robots can establish mutual expectations by negotiating conventions through shared autonomy. Drawing inspiration from human learning, the research investigates whether robots can acquire human preferences and whether humans can instruct robots on communication protocols. The paper details the experimental design, findings, and implications of a study involving 100 participants interacting with a social robot. Results indicate that humans can teach robots conventions, though the process is time-intensive. Furthermore, humans can rapidly infer robot expectations by observing its behavior across multiple trials. Finally, humans are capable of adjusting their own actions to align with established robot conventions. The paper concludes by discussing the broader implications of these findings. Autonomous navigation within unknown settings is a critical ability for mobile robots. While most current research focuses on mapless methods, utilizing maps can significantly boost performance by enabling efficient path planning and robust obstacle avoidance. However, existing map-based strategies often depend on specific map types, leading to suboptimal results. To address this, we introduce a novel hierarchical topological map representation called HiTMap, designed to facilitate navigation in unfamiliar areas. This representation is constructed from raw sensor data and decomposed into a coarse map for high-level path planning and a fine map for low-level, detailed planning. The system was tested in both simulated and real-world scenarios, demonstrating superior performance compared to other map-based methods. Furthermore, our approach exhibits greater robustness in highly dynamic environments than previous techniques. The implementation is accessible at https://github.com/robinwang1998/HiTMap. First, Multivariable Inter-Group Complementary Array Code Sets (MIGCCS) are constructed using multivariable functions, offering zero interference between groups while maintaining a large code size. Second, Multivariable Z-Complementary Array Code Sets (MZCCS) are developed via multiple array concatenation methods, providing zero interference and zero distortion across two dimensions. These new code sets are formulated using multivariable functions, which can be derived from one-variable functions through multivariable extension techniques. The study demonstrates that functions suitable for SIGCCS and ZCCS can be generated from existing single-variable code sets through these extensions. By applying multivariable extension, array code sets with larger sizes can be created from smaller primitive sets. This research extends those applications into two dimensions, yielding code sets with significantly larger capacities. Computed Tomography (CT) is a prevalent imaging technique in both medical and industrial contexts. However, acquiring high-quality CT images demands substantial computational resources and extended scan durations. Consequently, there is a pressing need to develop efficient reconstruction methods that produce accurate images from limited data. This study introduces a new variational framework capable of simultaneously reconstructing images, denoising polyenergetic sensor data, and performing material decomposition. The proposed model utilizes a non-convex approach to minimize the total data error, sensor noise, and material decomposition errors. To address the non-convexity inherent in this formulation, we developed an efficient algorithm utilizing the alternating direction method of multipliers (ADMM). Numerical experiments on both synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate that the proposed algorithm outperforms existing state-of-the-art techniques. Furthermore, the results confirm that the method effectively handles noisy polyenergetic data and executes accurate material decomposition. This work investigates how electron spill-out and nonlocality influence light propagation in the limit of vanishing gaps within plasmonic nanostructures. By employing a nonlocal hydrodynamic model, we demonstrate that while electron spill-out causes a minor redshift in the plasmonic resonance, certain nonlocal effects can induce significant enhancements. Specifically, we identify that under specific conditions, plasmons can sustain themselves even with zero-gap separations. Furthermore, these findings are applicable to designing new types of gap-plasmons, offering potential for achieving ultra-high sensitivity in sensing applications. Finally, we introduce a novel class of nonlocal surface modes that emerge in the vacuum side-by-side configuration. These modes exhibit exceptional field confinement and sensitivity to the width of the vacuum channel, making them promising candidates for sensing and detection. Additionally, we provide a theoretical framework to describe the evolution of these modes as the two nanostructures transition from being plasmonically coupled to separated by a vacuum gap. This study represents the first comprehensive analysis of light propagation in the gap-plasmon limit. It not only elucidates the physical mechanisms governing these phenomena but also paves the way for developing new types of nonlocal surface modes. The results are validated through numerical simulations. All associated numerical codes are publicly accessible. These findings are expected to significantly advance the understanding of light-matter interactions in plasmonic nanostructures and inspire the design of next-generation devices with unprecedented performance. Time series and longitudinal data are prevalent in scientific research, business analytics, and daily life. Although time is inherently multivariate, these data are typically visualized as one-dimensional lines. This paper introduces a method for interacting with time series and longitudinal data across multiple dimensions using spatial displays. The approach relies on two key concepts: data regions, which represent segments of the time series, and region operators, which manipulate these regions. We present two methods for defining data regions: one based on the natural temporal axis and another on selected dimensions. Furthermore, we offer two strategies for manipulating regions: direct manipulation through mouse interactions and indirect manipulation via region operators. To illustrate the method's utility, we introduce TimeCanvas, a system that implements this approach. Our evaluation demonstrates that TimeCanvas enables users to explore the relationships between data dimensions and to identify data regions exhibiting similar patterns. Additionally, we show that the system is intuitive and accessible to non-expert users. This method is applicable to any data where time serves as a common axis, including time series, time-ordered events, and longitudinal data. The system is available at https://github.com/TimeCanvas/TimeCanvas. Electronic Health Records (EHRs) are extensively utilized in healthcare, yet their potential for clinical decision support remains underexplored. While deep learning models have been applied to EHR data, they often overlook the heterogeneous nature of these records, which consist of diverse data types such as demographics, vital signs, and clinical measurements. This paper introduces the Heterogeneous Similarity Graph Neural Network (HSGNN), a novel framework designed to model EHRs as heterogeneous graphs. By representing each data point as a node and capturing both structural and semantic relationships between them, HSGNN learns a shared representation for all nodes. We validate the model's efficacy on a public EHR dataset using two tasks: disease classification and sepsis prediction. Experimental results demonstrate that HSGNN outperforms existing methods in both accuracy and robustness. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/ChenYi1993/HSGNN. Furthermore, the model has been integrated into the Kaggle EHR Challenge, where it secured first place in the individual track and a top-three finish in the ensemble track.
