Gapped graphene exhibits an intrinsic valley Hall effect, which is essential for the valley Hall sensor concept. However, this effect is typically restricted to very low electric fields due to the rapid closure of the valley-locked Landau levels. In this work, we demonstrate that the orbital Hall effect can alternatively drive a valley Hall current in gapped graphene across a broad spectrum of magnetic fields, extending well beyond the range of Landau level overlap. This phenomenon arises from the orbital magnetic moment associated with Landau levels, a property that is non-zero in gapped graphene but absent in gapless valley-dependent graphene. Consequently, the orbital Hall effect enables the observation of a valley Hall current across extensive domains of magnetic field, valley-landau-level curvature, and electron temperature. Furthermore, we show that the orbital Hall current is particularly pronounced in the quantum Hall regime, where only a single Landau level is occupied. This finding is significant for experimental efforts to detect a pure valley current using transport measurements in quantum Hall regimes. Finally, we propose a practical method for measuring the orbital Hall effect through nonlocal transport in a bilayer graphene Hall bar. This approach involves applying a transverse electric field to generate an orbital Hall current and then applying a longitudinal electric field to open a gap within the orbital Hall current channel, thereby allowing for the measurement of the valley Hall response. This protocol offers a viable alternative to the previously proposed anomalous Hall effect measurement. Additionally, we highlight that the orbital Hall effect is not unique to graphene but is a general phenomenon applicable to any two-dimensional system. We illustrate this by showing that both bilayer graphene and single-layer graphene exhibit orbital Hall currents, with bilayer graphene displaying a significantly enhanced effect. This suggests that the orbital Hall effect holds great promise for advancing valleytronics. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the orbital Hall effect can be tuned in gapped graphene by applying a perpendicular strain, which serves as a viable alternative to applying a magnetic field. This capability is expected to be highly beneficial for valleytronics applications. Finally, we discuss the potential for realizing a pure valley current using this strain-based approach. Our findings are based on a combination of analytical and numerical calculations. Specifically, we derive an analytical expression for the orbital magnetic moment of Landau levels in gapped graphene and for the orbital Hall conductivity in the quantum Hall regime. These results are corroborated by numerical calculations of the orbital Hall conductivity across a wide range of magnetic fields. This paper introduces a new data poisoning attack targeting graph neural networks (GNNs), aimed at maximizing the performance of a specific classification label within a predefined target set. Our primary motivation stems from the growing challenge of automating malicious activities, particularly in the context of GNNs, where graph structures are susceptible to poisoning. We propose employing reinforcement learning to identify the most effective poisoned node set that aligns with a constrained budget. Our attack strategy involves modifying node labels to a target value, thereby increasing the likelihood that the GNN will assign these values to the remaining unpoisoned nodes during classification. We evaluate this poisoning method against GNNs using both synthetic and real-world datasets. The experimental results demonstrate that our attack achieves a higher success rate compared to existing methods under identical budget conditions. Furthermore, we observe that the attack success rate is directly proportional to the budget available. Finally, our approach proves particularly devastating when targeting small sets of labels within the target set.

Catalogue matching is a critical process for identifying and characterizing sources in astronomical surveys. This study investigates how incorporating photometric data from the Pan-STARRS1 survey enhances the accuracy of matching sources in the 2MASS and WISE all-sky infrared catalogues. We developed two catalogues containing 1.1 million and 1.3 million sources, respectively, and conducted two experiments: the first utilized only photometric data, while the second combined both astrometry and photometric information. Our results demonstrate that the combination of astrometry and Pan-STARRS1 photometry yields a 10% improvement in matching accuracy for the 2MASS catalogue and a 20% improvement for the WISE catalogue. Furthermore, we found that including Pan-STARRS1 photometry significantly boosts the ability to distinguish real sources from spurious ones in both catalogues. Finally, we applied these findings to identify and characterize real sources in the 2MASS and WISE catalogues that were previously missed. Our analysis indicates that Pan-STARRS1 photometry enables the recovery of approximately 10% of missed real sources in the 2MASS catalogue and 20% in the WISE catalogue. These findings underscore the substantial potential of combining multi-wavelength photometric data with astrometry for catalogue matching. The two catalogues described in this work are publicly accessible at https://github.com/abhishekkumar12345/Catalogue-Matching. The source code used to generate them can be found at https://github.com/abhishekkumar12345/Catalogue-Matching/tree/main/2mass_wise_missed_real_sources. Future research will explore the application of these catalogues to other surveys, such as the upcoming Roman Space Telescope. Furthermore, we establish that the upper bound $\sigma(\kappa)$ is tight for vertex covers of size $\kappa \geq \aleph_1$, and the bound $\mathfrak{c}$ is sharp for finite vertex covers. We also present several hypergraph constructions that illustrate the tightness of these findings. Additionally, we explore hypergraphs possessing vertex covers of all possible cardinalities and present a construction of a hypergraph with a maximal vertex cover of size $\kappa$ that includes a vertex cover of size $\mathfrak{c}$ which cannot be extended to a minimal cover of size $\kappa$. Ontologies serve as formal conceptual models that define concepts and their interrelationships, enabling knowledge sharing and reuse across domains. While ontology visualization tools assist users in browsing and comprehending these structures, they often struggle with non-associative concepts and the sheer volume of associations, leading to cluttered and unreadable representations. This paper introduces OntoPlot, a new visualization method designed to handle non-hierarchical associations in large ontologies. By utilizing a space-filling curve to map multi-dimensional points and generating concentric rings, the tool effectively manages a high volume of associations. Furthermore, we propose a novel association filtering technique to further reduce visual complexity. Experimental results demonstrate that OntoPlot significantly improves both the density and readability of visualizations for large ontologies. The tool is accessible at https://ontoplot.net. This paper introduces a novel approach to enhance semi-supervised end-to-end automatic speech recognition (E2E-ASR) by employing CycleGAN for cross-domain feature mapping and incorporating specific losses to facilitate effective model training. The proposed method trains a generator to perform a mapping function between speech data domains, utilizing CycleGAN to enforce consistency within this process. Furthermore, we implement an intermediate model and a loss function designed to align the mapping results produced by the intermediate model with those from the generator. Experimental findings demonstrate that feature mappings generated by the proposed generator significantly improve ASR performance. Additionally, the experiments confirm that the features extracted by the intermediate model are highly relevant to the target domain, as evidenced by the performance gains achieved when using its outputs as priors. Overall, the proposed approach yields substantial performance improvements, achieving a 20% relative reduction in character error rate (CER) on the WSJ dataset and a 10% relative reduction in word error rate (WER) on the Switchboard dataset. To our knowledge, this represents the first study to apply CycleGAN for domain adaptation in semi-supervised ASR. The code is accessible at \url{https://github.com/ChenYiLi1993/CycleGAN_CycleConsistency}.

This paper introduces a new framework for autonomous robot navigation, grounded in the computational theory of active inference. Within this theory, perception and action are unified as free energy minimization, where agents select actions to reduce uncertainty about their sensory inputs. Our objective is to develop a model that replicates human-like perception and action by integrating hierarchical deep learning with biologically plausible mechanisms. We demonstrate the efficacy of this approach through a case study involving robot navigation in a room, where both the robot's position and obstacles are inferred and utilized to guide movement. The proposed model successfully replicates human behavior in this scenario. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the framework can be extended to more complex scenarios, such as navigating a maze, by employing a more sophisticated hierarchical deep learning architecture. This method enables the robot to infer its position using multiple sensory modalities, including visual and motor information. Ultimately, we show that the active inference model can navigate a maze by replicating the behavior of a human participant. The code is publicly available at https://github.com/DeepMind/iFog. Our findings indicate that active inference models can replicate human behavior in robot navigation tasks, offering a promising avenue for building intelligent systems capable of robust perception and decision-making. Additionally, the model's ability to balance computational efficiency with performance makes it suitable for deployment on robots. We anticipate that this work will inspire further research into active inference models for robot learning and control. The active inference model presented here offers a novel approach to robot control, distinct from traditional methods. By leveraging the theory's capacity for robust perception and decision-making, the model can adapt to changing environments and learn from interactions. Moreover, the model can be trained using reinforcement learning, enabling it to improve its behavior over time. We believe that active inference models will play a crucial role in the future of robot learning and control. Furthermore, our predictions regarding the temperature dependence of the Soret coefficient successfully explain the observed reversal of the Soret coefficient's sign. Automated Essay Scoring (AES) has been a primary driver for developing natural language processing (NLP) systems, as it offers clear metrics for assessing model performance. This study introduces a new dataset designed to train and evaluate AES models. The data originates from 1,000 essays, each annotated with scores from three human raters. We benchmark this dataset against existing state-of-the-art AES models and further assess their capabilities using GPT-2 and XLM-R, which are trained on massive language corpora. Our findings indicate that models trained on this dataset generalize effectively to unseen essays. Additionally, we demonstrate that these models can identify essay quality by analyzing textual features such as syntax, vocabulary, and semantics. The dataset is publicly accessible at https://github.com/abhi-1989/automated-essay-scoring. The source code for all experiments can be found at https://github.com/abhi-1989/automated-essay-scoring/tree/master/essay_scoring. False positives are a primary challenge in automatic object detection, particularly in domain-adaptive pedestrian detection. While box re-ranking is a widely used technique to filter these false positives, it has not been fully explored in the context of domain adaptation. This paper introduces Box Re-Ranking, a novel method that leverages the efficiency of pre-trained models on large-scale datasets and the robustness of self-supervised pre-training to suppress false positives during adaptation. Box Re-Ranking operates unsupervisedly by generating additional candidate boxes, which are then re-ranked using a domain-adaptive detector. The approach's effectiveness is demonstrated through extensive experiments across multiple cross-domain pedestrian detection tasks. The code is accessible at https://github.com/robinliang1997/Box-Re-Ranking. The source code for a self-supervised pre-training framework, which serves as a key component of this method, is available at https://github.com/robinliang1997/SelfSupervisedPretraining. Furthermore, the paper is supported by an extended video presentation at https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=2222222222. Finally, the authors acknowledge the contributions of all individuals who have assisted in the development of this work.

Low-quality music recordings, such as those captured by mobile devices or voice memo apps, often suffer from background noise, echo, and distortions, rendering them unsuitable for listening. This paper introduces a deep learning framework designed to enhance music through a two-stage process: first, an image-to-image translation network converts monochrome audio spectra into high-quality spectra, and second, the enhanced spectrum is synthesized into audio using music vocoding. We specifically employ a Generative Adversarial Network (GAN) to address the non-stationary characteristics of music signals. Experimental results demonstrate that our model significantly outperforms existing methods in enhancing music signals. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/leeyongjun/music-enhancement. Furthermore, the model can be utilized to improve music playlists on streaming services like Spotify. This paper introduces a new dataset designed to investigate the visual cues of human throwing. Our findings indicate that observers can identify the point of release in throwing animations with greater than 90% accuracy, a capability that relies on the object's flight trajectory. To examine the visual mechanisms behind this skill, we developed a 3D simulation of a throwing motion, varying the point of release across 100% of the kinematic profile. We extracted object motion data from these simulations and integrated them into natural scenes. In a forced-choice experiment, 20 participants viewed pairs of images with distinct points of release and were asked to distinguish between them. The results demonstrate that incorrect points of release can be detected with over 90% accuracy. Furthermore, we conducted a computational analysis of the visual differences between correct and incorrect throws, revealing that the direction of object motion is the most significant feature enabling human discrimination. These insights are crucial for developing computer vision systems capable of detecting anomalies in human throwing actions. Our results also suggest that computer vision models could be trained to identify incorrect throws by analyzing motion trajectories, a task for which we have provided a novel dataset. Finally, we demonstrate the utility of this dataset in training a computer vision model to classify throws as correct or incorrect based on the point of release. Our findings indicate that a simple throw detector could achieve over 90% accuracy in identifying correct throws and approximately 60% accuracy in detecting faulty throws. This research holds significant potential for applications in human-computer interaction, including gesture recognition, activity monitoring, and anomaly detection. Neural Machine Translation (NMT) models typically generate translations via a left-to-right, word-by-word strategy, which often results in syntactically incoherent outputs. This study presents a top-down, tree-structured decoding algorithm that leverages syntactic dependencies to guide word generation. By integrating this algorithm with an NMT framework enhanced with explicit syntactic connections, we achieve superior performance in both machine translation and parsing compared to standard NMT systems. Furthermore, we demonstrate that our top-down approach yields more diverse syntactic structures than previous hierarchical methods, such as beam search over NMT+Syntax models. Finally, experimental results indicate that our method produces smoother, more fluent, and more accurate translations. The code is accessible at https://github.com/taehyungkim/TDS. This study introduces the Binding Energy Evaluation Platform (BEEP), a database designed to facilitate the assessment of binding energies for molecules of astrochemical significance. We present the platform's initial release, which encompasses data on 125 molecules. The information is derived from 1,150 distributions generated using 1,000 individual quantum chemical calculations. These distributions were constructed by analyzing 100 binding distances per molecule, calculated via the Potential Energy Surface Evolution (PESE) method. The platform's primary objective is to streamline the evaluation of binding energy distributions for both well-known and newly identified molecules. To achieve this, we have made the code and scripts used to generate the binding energy distributions publicly accessible. This work demonstrates the platform's efficacy in accelerating the computation of binding energy distributions. We introduce a new method for estimating expectations of random Pauli operators that achieves a sample complexity independent of the operator's support size. Our approach involves measuring a low-depth random Clifford circuit and subsequently applying classical shadow techniques to the resulting state. This method surpasses direct expectation estimation, where complexity scales with support, and directly estimating the corresponding quantum state, which requires complexity that grows exponentially with support. The current study examines the large $|k|$ asymptotics of the reflection coefficient $r(k)$ for data arising from Cauchy problems with the Davey-Stewartson II equations. This reflection coefficient is derived from the scattering data of a Riemann-Hilbert problem, which is constructed from the large $z$ asymptotics of a matrix solution to a linear system linked to the stationary equation of the DSII system. The primary challenge lies in the fact that the stationary DSII equation is not integrable in the conventional sense, meaning its Lax pair components do not satisfy a zero-curvature condition. Consequently, the stationary equation must be solved using a method that extends the technique introduced by McLeod and Sire in 2005. A further complication arises because the associated scattering problem is non-isospectral, requiring the introduction of a specific matrix function to address this issue. Additionally, the stationary equation exhibits a non-trivial behavior at the origin, necessitating the use of a Jost-type matrix solution that differs from standard approaches. To derive the large $|k|$ asymptotics of $r(k)$, the stationary equation is solved in a specific sector, and a novel approach is employed to analyze the resulting integral equation. This method involves a transformation of the unknown function to a new one, followed by an asymptotic expansion of the integral term as $|k|$ becomes large. The asymptotic behavior of the transformed unknown function is subsequently determined using a technique inspired by the work of Deift and Zhou. Ultimately, the large $|k|$ asymptotics of $r(k)$ are established, and it is demonstrated that the phase of the stationary equation possesses a non-trivial contribution. These findings provide a foundation for addressing the direct problem of the DSII system. Furthermore, the results indicate that the stationary equation exhibits a phase contribution, a phenomenon that appears to be unique to this specific equation. The methodology developed here is also applicable to other non-integrable equations. Finally, the paper concludes with an outline of the strategy for solving the inverse problem. This approach involves deforming the contour of the Riemann-Hilbert problem to the large $z$ asymptotics of the matrix solution, thereby reducing the problem to a model equation. The solution to this model equation is then determined via a limiting argument. We introduce a straightforward yet potent strategy for creating robust classifiers, grounded in the concept of model transformations. These transformations enable the training of a classifier on a broad spectrum of synthetic data, thereby enhancing its generalization capabilities. We demonstrate that applying Sibylvariant transformations to text—such as inserting or deleting spaces, altering capitalization, or inserting/deleting punctuation—significantly boosts classification performance. This approach is straightforward to implement and incurs no additional computational expense, as robustness is improved directly within the training phase. We validate the efficacy of Sibylvariant transformations across various text classification tasks, including sentiment analysis and topic classification, using diverse datasets like MNIST, IMDB, and AG News. Our findings indicate that the proposed method surpasses state-of-the-art performance on these datasets. Furthermore, we show that the approach is highly effective even with limited training data. Finally, we examine the application of Sibylvariant transformations to other forms of synthetic data, such as images and speech. The source code is accessible at: https://github.com/DeepMind/sibylvariant-transformations.

Meta-learning seeks to create algorithms capable of rapidly acquiring new skills by leveraging prior experience. This paper focuses on linear meta-learning, a specific category where meta-learned representations are linear combinations of historical tasks. Although this approach is highly efficient, it is often difficult to analyze. We introduce a provable framework for meta-learning a wide range of linear observation models, extending beyond the limitations of previous studies. Our analysis demonstrates that the algorithm learns a generalization that adapts to incoming tasks with a sample complexity that scales linearly with the dimensionality of the learned representation. Furthermore, we present experimental results that validate our theoretical findings. The code is accessible at https://github.com/ashwinb2000/provable-linear-meta. Keywords: meta-learning, representation learning, linear models, provable guarantees.

Although recent years have seen significant advancements in machine translation, certain language pairs remain underrepresented due to data scarcity. To address this, researchers have explored model distillation and quantization as methods to enhance performance and efficiency for low-resource translation. This study evaluates the robustness of these approaches by analyzing their impact on both performance and efficiency, aiming to guide future research in these areas. Our findings indicate that quantized models exhibit greater resilience to degradation than distilled models. Consequently, we recommend investigating knowledge distillation techniques that prioritize efficiency and robustness over absolute performance. The experimental code and data are accessible at https://github.com/abhi-1999/Comparing-the-Stability-of-Quantization-and-KD. Additionally, the paper includes a new benchmark for assessing the stability of lightweight low-resource models. We hope this work inspires further research into model distillation and quantization, particularly regarding their stability characteristics. The associated repository also offers a comprehensive suite of utilities for quantization and knowledge distillation. Finally, the paper presents a novel, user-friendly framework designed to facilitate the quantization and distillation of machine translation models. The repository includes a tutorial to assist users in utilizing these tools. The code is licensed under the Apache License 2.0. We examine a collection of $N$ undirected single hypergraphs, where each hypergraph consists of $M$ vertices and $\mathcal{E}$ edges. The number of vertices and edges is defined as $M = \lfloor \alpha M_0 \rfloor$ and $\mathcal{E} = \lfloor \beta \mathcal{E}_0 \rfloor$, with $\alpha$ and $\beta$ serving as irrational parameters. The constants $M_0$ and $\mathcal{E}_0$ represent the mean vertex and edge counts, respectively, given by $M_0 = N \langle M \rangle$ and $\mathcal{E} = N \langle \mathcal{E} \rangle$, where $\langle M \rangle$ and $\langle \mathcal{E} \rangle$ denote the average values per undirected single hypergraph. The undirected single hypergraphs are assumed to be randomly and independently generated. We introduce a Lagrangian density for this system, which is itself an irrational quantity. Furthermore, we derive the corresponding equation of motion and analyze its solutions. Finally, we demonstrate that the partition function can be expressed as the trace of a product of $N$ matrices, each of dimension $2^M$. This formulation indicates that the partition function is also an irrational quantity. Additionally, we show that the partition function can be represented as a trace involving the product of $2^{\mathcal{E}}$ matrices, each of dimension $2^M$. We also provide an expression for the free energy. Our results suggest that the partition function and free energy are independent of both the parameters $\alpha$ and $\beta$, as well as the specific values of $M$ and $\mathcal{E}$. Consequently, we conclude that the collection of undirected single hypergraphs exhibits a high degree of symmetry. Finally, we discuss the implications of these findings. This work extends the symmetry analysis previously conducted for directed single hypergraphs. Our findings are significant for the fields of combinatorics and combinatorial optimization. We also discuss the potential applications of these results in the study of complex systems. This research represents an extension of our previous study on the symmetry analysis of directed single hypergraphs. This study addresses the challenge of segmenting COVID-19 lesions within chest X-rays, a critical step for analyzing disease progression and monitoring patient outcomes. While deep learning models excel in medical image analysis, they typically demand extensive labeled datasets. To mitigate this, we employed image augmentation to generate synthetic training data. We evaluated various augmentation techniques and selected the optimal combination for our model. Our primary objective was to assess the impact of these augmentations on model performance and to determine the minimum quantity of original images required for effective training. We trained the U-Net architecture using both the original and minimum sets of images, applying different augmentation strategies. The experimental results demonstrated that our approach achieved state-of-the-art segmentation performance while significantly reducing the reliance on labeled data. This paper introduces a new approach to controllable image captioning that leverages prompt tuning to generate diverse and varied captions for the same image. While previous prompt-based methods have primarily focused on natural language understanding, we explore their potential for natural language generation within the field of computer vision. Our proposed model, Controllable Image Captioning via Prompting (CICP), demonstrates that it can produce a range of diverse captions for a single image without requiring any retraining. We evaluate CICP across various tasks, including zero-shot and few-shot caption generation, caption diversity, and zero-shot captioning based on natural language prompts. The term "harmful" is frequently employed in AI safety and policy contexts, yet its definition remains ambiguous. This paper introduces a causal framework for harm, positing that an entity is detrimental if its presence or actions elevate the probability of negative outcomes. The proposed model is demonstrated through both formal analysis and informal discussions. We argue that this definition is sufficiently precise for practical application in AI systems, such as moderating social media content. Furthermore, we illustrate how the framework can guide the development of a moderate AI system by addressing specific design choices. Ultimately, we contend that adopting a causal perspective on harm is essential for the responsible deployment of AI. Speech translation involves converting spoken language from one language into another language. This paper introduces a zero-shot approach to speech translation, which utilizes a pre-trained multilingual speech model to extract semantic representations from speech and translates them into target languages for which no specific speech encoder was pre-trained. We demonstrate that our model can translate across up to 11 languages, including English, German, and Japanese. We evaluate the model using two automated metrics: sentence-level BLEU scores and an audio-based Carrot metric. Our results show that the model performs comparably to fully end-to-end systems when English is involved and achieves reasonable performance when translating between non-English languages. Additionally, we conduct a human assessment to evaluate the quality of speech outputs, finding that the model generates natural-sounding translations that accurately convey the original meaning. Finally, we explore the model's ability to handle various speech phenomena, such as code-switching and disfluencies, during translation. Overall, this model represents a promising step toward zero-shot speech translation systems capable of processing a broader range of languages and diverse speech inputs. Our code and data are publicly available at https://github.com/ashishkumar123/zero-shot-st. The paper can be accessed at https://arxiv.org/abs/2105.04001. This study examines a class of Coleman-Gurtin equations defined on a domain $\Omega$ subject to dynamic boundary conditions on $\partial\Omega$. Initially, the problem is reformulated as a system of two equations, both featuring integral terms. Subsequently, employing the Faedo-Galerkin method, we establish the existence and uniqueness of the solution. Finally, under specific conditions, we demonstrate the asymptotic stability of this solution. The proofs rely on several novel inequalities and lemmas, some of which may hold independent interest. Furthermore, we derive an inequality that extends the scope of a recently published result by the first author. Finally, utilizing a suitable Lyapunov functional, we prove asymptotic stability for the solution. The methodology for deriving the inequality and the associated Lyapunov functional is applicable to a broader category of problems. Additionally, the analysis of asymptotic stability can be extended to a more general setting. This work serves as a precursor to our subsequent paper, where we will investigate the asymptotic behavior of solutions to a system of Coleman-Gurtin type equations incorporating time delays. In that context, time delays appear in the integral terms, and the domain $\Omega$ includes dynamic boundary conditions. Our approach for this delayed system draws inspiration from the method used in this current study. Specifically, we will adapt the Faedo-Galerkin method to address the delayed problem. To achieve this, we will construct an appropriate approximate solution and subsequently prove the existence and uniqueness of the solution to the original problem. The core challenge in this extension lies in the additional delays, which introduce new terms into the a priori estimates. To manage these terms, we will utilize a technique inspired by this paper, thereby extending the analysis to the delayed scenario. This paper also serves as a foundation for our forthcoming study, which addresses a different type of delay problem. In that work, we will analyze a Coleman-Gurtin type problem incorporating time delays within the integrodifferential equations. The primary difficulty in this case stems from the presence of integrodifferential terms. To address this, we will adapt the approach presented in this paper to handle the delayed problem. Specifically, we will utilize Faedo-Galerkin approximations and construct an appropriate Lyapunov functional to derive estimates for the time derivatives of the solution. These estimates will then be employed to establish the asymptotic stability of the solution. This research also builds upon our prior work, which addressed a related but distinct delay problem. Accurate distribution load forecasts are essential for the efficient planning and operation of power grids. For distribution system operators (DSOs), this is particularly critical due to their management of the low voltage (LV) network, where the integration of distributed energy resources (DER) and the shift toward electric mobility introduce significant challenges. This study evaluates the impact of forecast fusion and the characteristics of daily peak demand at the LV substation level. Probabilistic forecasts are generated using the quantile regression random forest method, with probabilistic metrics assessed via the Continuous Ranked Probability Score (CRPS). The analysis utilizes one-year of smart meter data from 1,000 households, along with weather and temporal features. Results indicate that forecast accuracy improves when probabilistic load data is aggregated, specifically through the calculation of the median of individual household forecasts. Furthermore, the CRPS metric demonstrates that forecast accuracy is highest during daily peak demand periods. These findings suggest that probabilistic load forecasting will be most effective during times of high electricity consumption, such as the daily peaks observed in the LV network. Additionally, the research confirms that the uncertainty in the forecasted probabilistic load decreases as the number of households included in the aggregation increases. Finally, the study shows that incorporating weather and temporal features into the quantile regression random forest model enhances accuracy, especially during daily peak demand. These conclusions are supported by an analysis of the impact of various input features on the CRPS. Overall, this study provides valuable insights for DSOs regarding the accuracy of probabilistic load forecasts for LV networks, the influence of smart meter data aggregation, and the identification of critical periods for distribution planning. These results can guide future research and the development of new probabilistic forecasting methods. To ensure the reproducibility of this work, all data and code are available at: https://github.com/fernando-fernandez-l/forecasting-fusion-and-lv-peaks. The source code is written in Python and utilizes the following libraries: scikit-learn, scikit-postprocesses, and pymc3. The dataset comprises smart meter readings from 1,000 households in Spain, collected at a 15-minute interval. The dataset is accessible at: https://zenodo.org/record/6112522. The data was provided by the Spanish company Iberdrola Distribution.

This roadmap details the current state of domain knowledge integration in machine learning, emphasizing the knowledge representation layer. It begins by defining key concepts and surveying existing approaches for integrating domain knowledge into machine learning workflows. Subsequently, it surveys ontology engineering methods, followed by an examination of knowledge representation languages and formal reasoning. The roadmap then highlights learning techniques used to embed domain knowledge within these structures. Finally, it outlines current and future directions in this field, accompanied by a discussion on open challenges. This document serves as a comprehensive guide to the field of domain knowledge integration in machine learning, with a specific focus on learning-based integration. It is particularly valuable for researchers and practitioners entering this domain, as well as for those in related fields such as knowledge representation, reasoning, and neural-symbolic AI. Recent studies indicate that deep learning models are heavily reliant on high-quality supervision, where model performance is directly tied to the accuracy of annotations. However, obtaining precise annotations for COVID-19 lesions in CT scans is labor-intensive and demands specialized expertise. To address this, we introduce a weakly supervised framework designed to localize and segment COVID-19 lesions using only image-level labels. Our approach employs a two-stage strategy: first, a lesion-localization module identifies candidate regions via a region-proposal module and filters them using a binary classification module; second, these selected proposals are aggregated into a final segmentation mask through a mask fusion module. We evaluated our model on the public LIDC-IQHI dataset, which includes both healthy and COVID-19 affected scans. The experimental results demonstrate that our model achieves state-of-the-art performance in both lesion localization and segmentation. Furthermore, we conducted an ablation study to assess the impact of various model components and explored the potential for unbiased localization and segmentation by examining the effects of data augmentation and class imbalance. The source code is accessible at \url{https://github.com/ChenYi1998/COVID-19-Weakly-Supervised-Segmentation}. This paper introduces a novel technique for automatic localization and identification of vertebrae in abdominal CT scans. The approach begins by extracting a 3D volume from the CT image, which is then rectified into a spine-aligned coordinate system using an automatically determined transformation. Vertebra localization is achieved by optimizing a cost function that assesses the likelihood of a vertebra's presence within a local region, while identification is performed by selecting the vertebra with the highest probability across the entire volume. The system's performance is evaluated using a dataset of 100 anonymized CT scans, and results are compared against those of two existing methods. The proposed method demonstrates superior performance relative to the other approaches. Furthermore, the method is robust to significant abdominal organ displacement caused by conditions such as obesity, pregnancy, or respiratory motion. Finally, the method is accessible as open-source software. We investigate how vacuum fluctuations influence electron scattering within a cavity, specifically examining the interaction between the electron's charge and an electromagnetic field mode. Our findings indicate that the vacuum field can either enhance or suppress scattering, with suppression occurring in the ultra-coupling regime where the electron's motion resonates with the cavity field. This phenomenon, termed "dynamical stabilization," demonstrates that vacuum fluctuations can impede electron scattering when the light-matter interaction reaches the strong or ultrastrong regime. We further show that the rate constant for the inverse process, electron attachment, can be significantly amplified under these conditions. These results are corroborated by simulations of resonant electron scattering and attachment in a 3D model featuring a point charge inside a 3D cavity. Additionally, we establish that the rate constant for dynamical stabilization scales inversely with the cavity volume, a relationship that remains valid even outside the cavity. These insights offer a pathway to controlling electron scattering and attachment through vacuum fluctuations. Our findings are particularly relevant to emerging fields such as cavity quantum electrodynamics, electron microscopy, and electron microscopy combined with ultrafast light sources. Notably, our results suggest that vacuum fluctuations can inhibit electron scattering in the strong and ultrastrong light-matter coupling regimes, a phenomenon that could be experimentally verified using electron pulses in cavities. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the vacuum field can significantly increase electron capture by atoms and molecules, a process known as electron attachment. This enhancement is especially pronounced in cavities with small volumes, where the electromagnetic field is strongly confined. This study investigates the potential of elastic actuators in enhancing quadruped locomotion. While prior research has primarily concentrated on developing efficient control strategies, this work shifts focus to the design of the elastic actuator itself. We propose an optimization framework that utilizes reinforcement learning to determine optimal elastic actuator parameters. Our results demonstrate that the reinforcement learning policy can effectively identify these parameters, surpassing the performance of both rigid-actuated and linearly-actuated robots. Furthermore, we observe that the learned policy successfully infers the necessary parameters to adapt to various terrains. We introduce a global variational method designed to determine whether an $N$-mode quantum state is entangled within the Gaussian framework. This approach identifies a specific set of symplectic transformations that convert the target state into a GCS state featuring $k$ distinct GCS components, where $k \geq N$. The value of $k$ subsequently indicates the level of complexity regarding the state's separability. We demonstrate that the proposed cost function is non-increasing and possesses a global minimum that clearly delineates the path to the optimal separability structure. Furthermore, we establish a direct connection between the complexity of the variational problem and the existence of analytical methods for calculating the covariance matrix elements. We have implemented this algorithm on both classical and quantum computing platforms to examine the separability of quantum states across 2, 3, and 4 modes. The results confirm that the variational algorithm converges rapidly to a solution, effectively navigating out of local minima to reach the global optimum. Additionally, we show that the quantum algorithm can be enhanced by integrating a layer of symplectic transformations to facilitate state optimization. Finally, we outline the potential for extending this algorithm to non-Gaussian states. Our findings indicate that the method is highly efficient for low-mode-count states, with a computational complexity that scales linearly with the number of modes. This efficiency is attributed to the use of a cost function that avoids the need for gradient calculations. Consequently, the algorithm offers a valuable tool for investigating the properties of quantum states in quantum information processing. This study examines the initial evolution of a tearing mode within a collisionless, current-carrying slab plasma under a weakly nonuniform background magnetic field. The analysis focuses on the physics governing the initial linear phase of the mode as it transitions into the intermediate phase, a critical stage where the reconnection rate stabilizes. The initial linear phase is categorized into three distinct subphases, each defined by the tearing-mode's growth rate relative to the local ion Larmor frequency. The first subphase mirrors the initial linear growth observed in tearing modes under uniform background fields. The second subphase is characterized by a magnetic perturbation that varies with distance from the current sheet as the square root of the background field. In the third subphase, the magnetic perturbation exhibits a logarithmic dependence on the distance from the current sheet. The study also addresses the formation of magnetic islands during the initial linear phase and the subsequent evolution of their growth rates. Furthermore, the impact of finite ion Larmor radius effects on the transition from the initial linear to the intermediate phase is analyzed. Finally, the results are compared with those of a tearing mode in a collisional slab plasma. The findings indicate that, in a small-scale tearing-mode regime, the transition from the initial linear to the intermediate phase occurs more rapidly in a collisionless plasma than in a collisional one. Additionally, the magnetic island growth rate in a collisionless plasma is observed to be smaller than in a collisional plasma. These outcomes suggest that the initial growth of small-scale tearing modes in a collisionless plasma is slower than in a collisional plasma. This conclusion is validated by comparing the growth rates in both regimes with those of a large-scale tearing mode in a collisional plasma. The comparison demonstrates that the initial growth rate of a small-scale tearing mode in a collisionless plasma is significantly lower than that of a large-scale tearing mode in a collisional plasma. This finding underscores the potential for small-scale tearing modes to act as a mechanism for the early generation of magnetic islands in collisionless plasmas. Finally, the implications of these findings for the initial growth of small-scale tearing modes in magnetized plasmas are explored. This paper examines the Fokas-Lenells equation, a fourth-order nonlinear integrable evolution equation, utilizing the bilinear method. We derive dark, bright, and singular solitary wave solutions, alongside various solitary wave interaction patterns, including elastic and inelastic scattering. Furthermore, we analyze the rational solution, which exhibits a pole of order two at the origin, and a two-hump rational solution. We also present the corresponding Lax pair and conservation laws for the Fokas-Lenells equation. These findings offer novel insights into the Fokas-Lenells model, which was recently formulated by Fokas and Lenells in 2007 as an integrable hierarchy within the 2+1 dimensional nonlinear Schrödinger equation framework. The study employs the bilinear method to derive these results, which were previously obtained through the inverse scattering transform method by the same authors. Additionally, we have implemented a numerical scheme to simulate the Fokas-Lenells equation, validating the existence of various solutions, including dark, bright, and rational solitary waves. The simulation results align well with the theoretical predictions. Specifically, we examine two scenarios: a totally flat solution where all fields are constant, and a constant curvature solution where the Ricci tensor remains constant. Additionally, we identify the specific gauge transformations that can be eliminated through appropriate field redefinitions in both contexts. We also identify potential issues with certain actions, such as frame dependence and the presence of ghosts. Finally, we demonstrate that all proposed actions are equivalent when ghost-free. Furthermore, we identify the actions corresponding to the two main classes of non-Riemannian solutions found in non-Riemannian gravity. Finally, we examine the field content of these actions, revealing that all fields are non-propagating except for the dilaton in the ghost-free scenarios. Consequently, these actions represent the most general form of the double field theory scalar equation when restricted to non-Riemannian solutions. In this framework, the sole propagating field is the dilaton, which exhibits a non-linear profile. The IEEE 802.11 standard is widely adopted in wireless local area networks (WLANs), yet its performance often degrades in dense environments. To address this, the 802.11k/v amendments introduce mechanisms for neighbor reporting and client steering, respectively. This paper proposes a channel load-aware AP selection algorithm that leverages IEEE 802.11k/v to enhance the user experience within IEEE 802.11ac WLANs. The algorithm utilizes real-time channel load data from neighboring access points to identify the optimal connection. Furthermore, it incorporates 802.11v features to accelerate association by gathering and applying association parameters. Testing across various channel loads and network topologies demonstrates that the proposed method significantly improves overall performance. Additionally, the algorithm is designed for easy deployment on existing 802.11ac networks with minimal modifications. To further improve performance, the study also examines the impact of signal strength and interference on both the algorithm and the network's overall efficiency. Finally, the research explores the application of this algorithm in extending wireless coverage using home repeaters. Experimental results indicate that the proposed algorithm enhances the user experience by approximately 10% compared to the default 802.11ac implementation.
